author: charles-h-spurgeon
fields.title: Talks to the Farmer
fields.description: Have you ever wondered how the ordinary scenes of farm life can reveal deep spiritual truths? In Talks to the Farmer, Charles Spurgeon draws vivid lessons from seeds, soil, labour, and harvest, turning everyday rural life into profound reflections on repentance, grace, and the work of God in the heart. Open these pages and let their timeless wisdom challenge, encourage, and nourish your faith.

fields.title: The Sluggard's Farm
fields.body_html:
“I passed by the field of a sluggard, by the vineyard of a man lacking sense, and behold, it was all overgrown with thorns; the ground was covered with nettles, and its stone wall was broken down.

Then I saw and considered it; I looked and received instruction.” — Proverbs 24:30–32 (ESV) No doubt Solomon was sometimes glad to set aside his royal robes, escape the formalities of court, and travel through the countryside unnoticed. On one such occasion, he looked over the broken wall of a small estate belonging to one of his countrymen. This property consisted of a piece of ploughed land and a vineyard. One glance showed him that it belonged to a sluggard who had neglected it. The weeds had grown thickly and covered the entire ground. From this sight, Solomon received instruction. People generally learn wisdom if they already possess wisdom. The artist’s eye sees beauty in a landscape because he has beauty in his mind. “To him who has will more be given,” and he shall have abundance, for he will reap a harvest even from a field covered with thorns and nettles.

There is a great difference between one person and another in how they use the mind’s eye. I have a book entitled The Harvest of a Quiet Eye, and it is a good one. The harvest of a quiet eye can be gathered from a sluggard’s land just as much as from a well-managed farm. When we were children, we were taught a small poem called Eyes and No Eyes. It contained much truth. Some people have eyes but do not see, which is much the same as having no eyes at all. Others, however, have sharp eyes for discovering instruction. Some look only at the surface, while others see not only the outer shell but the living kernel of truth hidden within outward things.

We may find instruction everywhere. To a spiritual mind, nettles have their purpose and weeds have their lesson. Are not thorns and thistles meant to teach sinful people?

Do they not grow from the earth to show us what sin has done, and the kind of produce that results when we sow seeds of rebellion against God? “I passed by the field of a sluggard, by the vineyard of a man lacking sense,” says Solomon. “I saw and considered it; I looked and received instruction.” Whatever you see, take care to consider it carefully, and you will not see it in vain.

You will find books and sermons everywhere — in the land and in the sea, in the earth and in the skies. You may learn from every living beast, bird, fish, and insect, and from every useful or useless plant that springs from the ground. We may also gather valuable lessons from things we do not like. Solomon certainly did not admire the thorns and nettles that covered the vineyard, yet he still found instruction in them. Many are stung by nettles, but few are taught by them. Some are hurt by briars, yet here was one who was improved by them. Wisdom has a way of gathering grapes from thorns and figs from nettles. She draws good from plants that seem unpleasant and harmful.

Do not complain about thorns; instead, gain good from them. Do not sting yourself on nettles; grasp them firmly and use them for the health of your soul.

Trials and troubles, worries and disturbances, small irritations and disappointments, may all help you if you allow them. Like Solomon, see and consider them carefully — look at them and receive instruction. As for us, we will now first consider Solomon’s description of a sluggard: he is “a man lacking sense.” Secondly, we will notice his description of the sluggard’s land: “it was all overgrown with thorns; the ground was covered with nettles.” When we have considered these two matters, we will conclude by gathering the instruction this neglected land may provide.

First, think of Solomon’s description of a slothful man. Solomon was not someone we would contradict, for he possessed great wisdom, and he wrote under divine inspiration in the Book of Proverbs. Solomon says a sluggard is “a man lacking sense.” The slothful man does not think so.

He places his hands in his pockets, and from his confident manner you would think he owned the Bank of England. He appears very wise in his own estimation and carries himself in a way meant to impress others with his supposed ability. How he gained this wisdom is difficult to say. He has never taken the trouble to think. I cannot say he leaps to conclusions, for he never leaps at all; he simply settles lazily into them. Yet he believes he knows everything and has resolved every issue.

Meditation is too much effort for him. Learning is something he has never been willing to endure.

Yet he delights in thinking himself naturally clever. He does not wish to know more than he already knows, for in his own mind he knows enough — though in truth he knows nothing.

The proverb is not flattering, but Solomon was correct in calling him “a man lacking sense.”

According to modern polite society, this may sound blunt, especially since the man owned a field and a vineyard. As the saying goes, “When I have a horse and a cow, every man bids me good morning.”

How can a man be said to lack understanding if he owns land and property? Is it not commonly assumed that a person’s intelligence is measured by his wealth? Wealth often brings praise for supposed ability. Such is the way of the world.

But it is not the way of Scripture. Whether he owns a field and a vineyard or not, Solomon says that if he is a sluggard, he is foolish — or to put it plainly, he is empty of understanding.

Not only does he fail to understand, but he also lacks the capacity to understand. If he is slothful, he is empty-headed. He may be called a gentleman. He may be a landowner. He may possess a vineyard and a field.

Yet these possessions make him no better. Indeed, they make him worse, for he is a man lacking sense and therefore unable to make proper use of what he has.

I am glad that Solomon tells us so plainly that a slothful man is lacking sense, for that is useful information. I have met people who believed they fully understood the doctrines of grace. They could clearly explain the election of the saints, the predestination of God, the certainty of the divine decree, the necessity of the Spirit’s work, and all the glorious doctrines that build the structure of our faith.

Yet from these truths they concluded that they had nothing to do, and so they became sluggards.

Doing nothing became their creed. They would not even encourage others to labour for the Lord because, they said, “God will do his own work. Salvation is all of grace.”

Their idea was that a man should simply wait and do nothing — sit still and let the grass grow to his ankles while hoping for heavenly help. To stir himself, in their view, would interfere with God’s eternal purpose.

I have known such a man look sour, shake his aged head, and speak harshly against earnest believers who were trying to win souls. I have seen him discourage young people and, like a heavy steam hammer, crush them by calling them unsound and ignorant.

How are we to endure the criticism of such a dogmatic person? How are we to escape this supposedly knowledgeable and fault-finding sluggard? Solomon comes to our aid and silences him by declaring that he is lacking sense. He may consider himself the standard of orthodoxy and judge everyone else, yet Solomon applies a different standard and says he lacks understanding. He may know the doctrine, but he does not truly understand it. If he did, he would know that the doctrines of grace lead us to seek the grace those doctrines proclaim.

When we see God at work, we learn that he works in us, not to make us idle, but “to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13, ESV). God’s predestination of a people means he has ordained them “for good works” (Ephesians 2:10, ESV), that they may display his praise. If you or I draw from any doctrine — however true — the conclusion that we may be idle and indifferent about the things of God, then we lack understanding. We misuse the gospel. We take what was meant as nourishment and turn it into poison. The sluggard, whether lazy in business or careless about his soul, is a man lacking sense.

As a general rule, we may measure a person’s understanding by his useful activity. Some call themselves “cultured,” yet they cultivate nothing. Much modern thought, from what I have observed, is like a bottle of smoke — impressive in appearance, but producing nothing solid. There are people who can analyse, debate, refine, and refute, yet meanwhile the hemlock grows in the furrow and the plough rusts unused. If your knowledge, culture, or education does not lead you to serve God practically in your own generation, then you have not learned what Solomon calls wisdom. You are not like the Blessed One — incarnate Wisdom — of whom it is written, “He went about doing good” (Acts 10:38, ESV).

A lazy person is not like our Saviour, who said, “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17, ESV). True wisdom is practical. Empty culture only speaks and theorises.

Wisdom ploughs its field. Wisdom hoes its vineyard. Wisdom watches its crops. Wisdom makes the best of everything. Whoever does not do so, whatever knowledge he may claim, is a man lacking sense. Why does he lack understanding? Is it not because he has opportunities he does not use? His day has come and is passing, yet he lets the hours slip away without purpose. Let each of us examine ourselves seriously. Am I using the minutes as they pass? This man had a vineyard but did not cultivate it. He had a field but did not till it. Do we use our opportunities? Each of us has some ability to serve God. Do we employ it?

If we are his children, he has not placed us where we must be useless. He has given us somewhere we may shine with the light he has given us, even if it is only a small candle. Are we shining? Do we “sow beside all waters”? Do we sow our seed in the morning and not withhold our hand in the evening? (Ecclesiastes 11:6, ESV) If not, Solomon’s verdict stands: the slothful is a man lacking sense; a man void of understanding. This man had opportunities he did not use. He also had duties he did not fulfil. When God gave each Israelite a portion of land, he did not intend it to lie waste, but to be cultivated.

When God placed Adam in the garden of Eden, it was not merely to admire its beauty, but “to work it and keep it” (Genesis 2:15, ESV). Likewise, each Israelite’s land was meant to reach its full fruitfulness through faithful labour. Ownership brought responsibility. The sluggard failed in that responsibility, and so he lacked understanding.

What is your role? A father? A master? A servant? A minister? A teacher? In these roles you have your fields and vineyards. If you fail to use them rightly, you neglect the purpose of your existence and fall short of the calling God has given you. The slothful farmer also had abilities he did not use. He could have worked his land if he had chosen to do so. He was not ill; he was simply lazy by choice.

God does not require from us what we do not have. “It is required according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have” (2 Corinthians 8:12, ESV). The man with two talents is not expected to produce five, but he is expected to use his two. This sluggard refused to attempt what was clearly within his power. Many have abilities lying dormant. Others use their gifts for themselves rather than for the One who gave them. If God has granted us any power to do good, let us use it. This world is weary and wicked. We should not hide even a glow-worm’s light in such darkness. We should not withhold even a single word of truth in a world filled with error.

However weak our voice, let us raise it for truth and righteousness. Let us not lack understanding by neglecting opportunities, ignoring duties, and failing to use our abilities. In matters of the soul, the sluggard is especially lacking in sense, for he trifles with matters that require utmost seriousness.

Have you never cultivated your heart? Has the plough never broken the hard soil of your soul? Has the seed of the Word never been sown — or has it taken no root?

Have you never watered the young shoots of desire? Never tried to pull up the weeds of sin? You care for your body by spending time in front of the mirror, yet neglect your soul. You adorn the flesh, which will soon return to dust, while your soul remains unwashed and uncared for. This is folly of the highest order. He who is lazy regarding the vineyard of his heart is truly lacking sense.

And if you are a Christian, truly saved, yet negligent in the Lord’s work, then you show little understanding. If you know the danger of lost souls, how can you not strive to rescue them? Time does not delay. Death does not delay. Hell does not delay. Satan is not idle. The powers of darkness are active. How then can we be sluggish if the Master has placed us in his vineyard? If we have been saved by God’s infinite love, should we not spend and be spent in his service? The very order of things demands that a saved person be earnest.

The Christian who is lazy in service does not realise what he loses. The richest part of fellowship with God is wholehearted consecration to God. Some possess just enough religion to make it doubtful whether they have any at all. They display a little godliness, yet little evidence of the Spirit’s work. We are meant to reflect Christ. Instead, some bring reproach upon him. When we see lazy servants, we assume their master must also be indifferent.

Let the world never think that Christ is indifferent to suffering or lacking in zeal. Yet they may think so if those who claim to serve him are mere sluggards. The slothful person loses honour and joy in service. He dishonours the cause he claims to love and prepares thorns for his dying pillow.

Let it stand settled: the slothful, whether minister, deacon, or private Christian, is a man lacking sense.

Now, secondly, let us consider the sluggard’s land: “I passed by the field of a sluggard, by the vineyard of a man lacking sense, and behold, it was all overgrown with thorns; the ground was covered with nettles, and its stone wall was broken down.” (Proverbs 24:30–31, ESV) Land will always produce something. Soil fit for a field or vineyard will yield fruit of some kind. Likewise, our hearts and our spheres of influence will produce something. We cannot live as blanks. We will do good or evil.

If you are idle in Christ’s work, you are active in the devil’s. By sleeping, the sluggard cultivated thorns more effectively than by any effort. If we do not produce wheat for Christ, we will grow weeds fit only for burning. If the soul is not cultivated for God, it will produce its natural fruit.

And what is that natural fruit? Sin and misery. If children are left untrained, what will they produce? If a city is left without the Gospel, what will grow there? Crime and corruption. There will always be a harvest. If we are slothful, that harvest will be painful even to ourselves. No one rests comfortably on thorns. While you sleep, Satan sows. If you withhold good seed, he will scatter evil seed freely. From that will come regret, perhaps for eternity.

“Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you” (Genesis 3:18, ESV). Often the evil growth will be abundant. Good land yields abundant weeds if neglected. The person who might have done much for God will do much harm if left idle. The best, when neglected, becomes the worst. If you want salvation, effort must be made to show you the way. But if you want to be lost, it requires only neglect: “How shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation?” (Hebrews 2:3, ESV) The sluggard says, “A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest” (Proverbs 24:33, ESV), and the thorns multiply beyond number and prepare many a sting for him.

As we look at the lazy man’s vineyard, let us also look into the heart of the ungodly sluggard. He does not care about repentance and faith. To think seriously about his soul or eternity is too much effort for him. He prefers to take life easily, with “a little folding of the hands to rest.” What is growing in his mind and character? In some of these spiritual sluggards, you see drunkenness, impurity, greed, anger, pride, and many other thistles and nettles. In others, where such obvious sins are restrained by respectable surroundings, you find different varieties of evil. The heart cannot remain empty. Either Christ or the devil will occupy it. My friend, if you are not decided for God, you cannot remain neutral. In this conflict, each person stands either with God or against him.

You cannot remain like a blank sheet of paper. The clear handwriting of Satan is upon you; can you not see the marks? Unless Christ has written his own gracious name across the page, the signature of Satan remains. You may say, “I do not live in open sin; I am moral.” Yet if you would examine your heart carefully, you would see hostility towards God and his ways. You do not love his law, nor his Son, nor his gospel. You are estranged in heart, filled with vain thoughts and wrong desires.

These will grow and increase as long as you remain a spiritual sluggard and leave your heart uncultivated. May the Spirit of God awaken you. May he stir you to serious and earnest reflection.

Then you will see that these harmful growths must be uprooted, that your heart must be broken up by conviction, and sown with the good seed of the gospel until it yields a harvest for the great Husbandman. Friend, if you believe in Christ, allow me also to look into your heart, especially if you are a sluggish Christian. I fear that nettles and thistles may be growing there as well. Did I not hear you sing recently, “‘Tis a point I long to know”? That question will often trouble you, for doubt readily grows in idle minds.

I do not recall reading in John Wesley’s diary that he questioned his salvation. He was so busy in his Master’s harvest that it did not occur to him to distrust his God.

Some Christians have little faith because they have never sown the mustard seed they were given.

If you do not use your faith, how can it grow? When faith is actively exercised in Christ’s service, it takes root, grows strong, and eventually chokes out doubt. Others suffer from gloomy forebodings. They become discontented, irritable, selfish, and complaining — often because they are idle. These are the weeds that grow in a sluggard’s garden.

I have known lazy believers become so peevish that nothing pleased them. The most earnest Christian could not satisfy them. The most loving believers were never affectionate enough. The most active church was never energetic enough. They found fault everywhere, even where God was clearly at work. This spirit of criticism, contention, and constant complaint is one of the nettles that surely grow where there is spiritual laziness.

If your heart does not bear fruit for God, it will certainly produce what harms you and others.

Thorns often choke good seed, but it is a blessed thing when good seed grows so abundantly that it chokes the thorns. God enables some believers to become so fruitful that when Satan sows tares, they cannot grow. The Holy Spirit weakens evil in the heart so that it no longer dominates. If you are slothful, examine the field of your heart and grieve over what you see.

Now consider your home. It is a serious matter when a person fails to cultivate their own family.

In my early days, I knew a man who often accompanied me into villages where I preached. I appreciated his company until I learned more about him. He spent every evening attending meetings, yet neglected his many children. They grew into ungodly young people because their father never sought to lead them to Christ. What is the use of zeal abroad if there is neglect at home? How sad to say, “My own vineyard I have not kept” (Song of Solomon 1:6, ESV).

I once heard of a man who refused to teach his children about God because he did not wish to prejudice them. He preferred to let them choose their religion later. One of his sons broke his arm, and while the doctor was setting it, the boy was swearing. The doctor remarked, “You feared to prejudice your son towards good, but the devil had no such hesitation.” It is our duty to cultivate the field in favour of good crops, or it will soon be overrun with weeds. Train a child towards good, or he will naturally drift towards evil. As it is with homes, so it is with schools. A man who later joined this church had once been an atheist. He traced his unbelief partly to his school experience.

On Sundays, the boys were confined to a distant gallery in church where they could scarcely hear a word. They endured endless prayers, but nothing touched their hearts. Eventually, he became so weary of religion that he resolved to abandon it once free. Sunday-school teachers must take care.

Classes can be made so dull that children come to dislike Sunday itself. Time can be wasted without bringing young hearts to Christ.

Some Christian parents, through harshness and lack of tenderness, have sown seeds of resentment instead of love. May we live among our children in such a way that they love not only us but our Father in heaven. Let parents show cheerful and genuine faith, so that children may desire to follow their example. If faith does not rule in the home, we will see disorder, pride, folly, and the beginnings of vice. Let not your home become a sluggard’s field. Let every deacon, class leader, and minister examine the field entrusted to him. If we neglect our responsibilities, we become like barren trees occupying space that fruitful trees could have used. We will hinder rather than help unless we render real service. Consider this seriously. You cannot remain neutral. If you produce no gain, you create loss. May God grant that we become profitable servants.

Now look at the vast field of the world. See how it is overgrown with thorns. Vast regions are covered with error, unbelief, and false religion. The world abounds in cruelty, oppression, impurity, and misery. To what extent is this due to a negligent church? Nearly two thousand years have passed, yet much of the vineyard remains overgrown. Wherever the church has ceased missionary labour, she has declined. When she stops reclaiming the wilderness, she becomes barren herself. Rather than asking what the church has done in past centuries, let us ask what we will do now.

Will we continue cultivating the same ground repeatedly while vast fields remain untouched? May God awaken us from our sluggishness. If not, the report may be: “I passed by the field of the sluggish church, and it was all overgrown with thorns.” There is a lesson here. Left to itself, human nature produces only thorns and nettles. Apart from grace, this is all we would have yielded. If we now produce good fruit, it is entirely due to grace. Let us then display the fruit of grace in our lives. Shall we serve Christ less earnestly than we once served sin? Shall we sacrifice less for him than we did for our former desires? May the Holy Spirit produce abundant fruit in us.

We also learn the emptiness of good intentions without action. This man always meant to work hard one day. He said, “A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest” (Proverbs 24:33, ESV). Only a little delay — then he would begin. But that day never came. Many hear serious sermons and intend to respond. They mean to turn to God “one day.” Some have delayed for forty years. When will you turn? “Before I die,” you say. Will you postpone it to your final hour? Is that wise? You may die suddenly. Life is uncertain. Take heed of small delays. You have wasted enough time already. Decide now. May the Holy Spirit bring you to decide.

“Surely you do not object to my having a little more sleep?” says the sluggard. “You have waked me so soon. I only ask another little nap.” “My dear man, it is far into the morning.” He answers, “It is rather late, I know; but it will not be much later if I take just another doze.” You wake him again, and tell him it is noon. He says, “It is the hottest part of the day: I daresay if I had been up I should have gone to the sofa and taken a little rest from the hot sun.” You knock at his door when it is almost evening, and then he cries, “It is of no use to get up now, for the day is almost over.”

You remind him of his overgrown field and weedy vineyard, and he answers, “Yes, I must get up, I know.” He shakes himself and says, “I do not think it will matter much if I wait till the clock strikes. I will rest another minute or two.”

He is glued to his bed, dead while he lives, buried in his laziness. If he could sleep forever he would, but he cannot, for the judgment day will rouse him. It is written, “And in Hades, being in torment, he lifted up his eyes” (Luke 16:23, ESV). God grant that you spiritual sluggards may wake before that; but you will not unless you bestir yourselves in time, for “now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2, ESV). And it may be now or never.

Tomorrow is only to be found in the calendar of fools; today is the time of the wise man, the chosen season of our gracious God. Oh that the Holy Spirit may lead you to seize the present hour, that you may at once give yourselves to the Lord by faith in Christ Jesus, and then from his vineyard— “Quick uproot The noisome weeds, that without profit suck The soil’s fertility from wholesome plants.”

God’s predestination of a people means he has ordained them “for good works” (Ephesians 2:10, ESV), that they may display his praise. If you or I draw from any doctrine — however true — the conclusion that we may be idle and indifferent about the things of God, then we lack understanding. We misuse the gospel. We take what was meant as nourishment and turn it into poison. The sluggard, whether lazy in business or careless about his soul, is a man lacking sense. As a general rule, we may measure a person’s understanding by his useful activity. Some call themselves “cultured,” yet they cultivate nothing. Much modern thought, from what I have observed, is like a bottle of smoke — impressive in appearance, but producing nothing solid. There are people who can analyse, debate, refine, and refute, yet meanwhile the hemlock grows in the furrow and the plough rusts unused. If your knowledge, culture, or education does not lead you to serve God practically in your own generation, then you have not learned what Solomon calls wisdom. You are not like the Blessed One — incarnate Wisdom — of whom it is written, “He went about doing good” (Acts 10:38, ESV). A lazy person is not like our Saviour, who said, “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17, ESV). True wisdom is practical. Empty culture only speaks and theorises. Wisdom ploughs its field. Wisdom hoes its vineyard. Wisdom watches its crops. Wisdom makes the best of everything. Whoever does not do so, whatever knowledge he may claim, is a man lacking sense. Why does he lack understanding? Is it not because he has opportunities he does not use? His day has come and is passing, yet he lets the hours slip away without purpose. Let each of us examine ourselves seriously. Am I using the minutes as they pass? This man had a vineyard but did not cultivate it. He had a field but did not till it. Do we use our opportunities? Each of us has some ability to serve God. Do we employ it? If we are his children, he has not placed us where we must be useless. He has given us somewhere we may shine with the light he has given us, even if it is only a small candle. Are we shining? Do we “sow beside all waters”? Do we sow our seed in the morning and not withhold our hand in the evening? (Ecclesiastes 11:6, ESV) If not, Solomon’s verdict stands: the slothful is a man lacking sense; a man void of understanding. This man had opportunities he did not use. He also had duties he did not fulfil. When God gave each Israelite a portion of land, he did not intend it to lie waste, but to be cultivated. When God placed Adam in the garden of Eden, it was not merely to admire its beauty, but “to work it and keep it” (Genesis 2:15, ESV). Likewise, each Israelite’s land was meant to reach its full fruitfulness through faithful labour. Ownership brought responsibility. The sluggard failed in that responsibility, and so he lacked understanding. What is your role? A father? A master? A servant? A minister? A teacher? In these roles you have your fields and vineyards. If you fail to use them rightly, you neglect the purpose of your existence and fall short of the calling God has given you. The slothful farmer also had abilities he did not use. He could have worked his land if he had chosen to do so. He was not ill; he was simply lazy by choice. God does not require from us what we do not have. “It is required according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have” (2 Corinthians 8:12, ESV). The man with two talents is not expected to produce five, but he is expected to use his two. This sluggard refused to attempt what was clearly within his power. Many have abilities lying dormant. Others use their gifts for themselves rather than for the One who gave them. If God has granted us any power to do good, let us use it. This world is weary and wicked. We should not hide even a glow-worm’s light in such darkness. We should not withhold even a single word of truth in a world filled with error. However weak our voice, let us raise it for truth and righteousness. Let us not lack understanding by neglecting opportunities, ignoring duties, and failing to use our abilities. In matters of the soul, the sluggard is especially lacking in sense, for he trifles with matters that require utmost seriousness. Have you never cultivated your heart? Has the plough never broken the hard soil of your soul? Has the seed of the Word never been sown — or has it taken no root? Have you never watered the young shoots of desire? Never tried to pull up the weeds of sin? You care for your body by spending time in front of the mirror, yet neglect your soul. You adorn the flesh, which will soon return to dust, while your soul remains unwashed and uncared for. This is folly of the highest order. He who is lazy regarding the vineyard of his heart is truly lacking sense. And if you are a Christian, truly saved, yet negligent in the Lord’s work, then you show little understanding. If you know the danger of lost souls, how can you not strive to rescue them? Time does not delay. Death does not delay. Hell does not delay. Satan is not idle. The powers of darkness are active. How then can we be sluggish if the Master has placed us in his vineyard? If we have been saved by God’s infinite love, should we not spend and be spent in his service? The very order of things demands that a saved person be earnest. The Christian who is lazy in service does not realise what he loses. The richest part of fellowship with God is wholehearted consecration to God. Some possess just enough religion to make it doubtful whether they have any at all. They display a little godliness, yet little evidence of the Spirit’s work. We are meant to reflect Christ. Instead, some bring reproach upon him. When we see lazy servants, we assume their master must also be indifferent. Let the world never think that Christ is indifferent to suffering or lacking in zeal. Yet they may think so if those who claim to serve him are mere sluggards. The slothful person loses honour and joy in service. He dishonours the cause he claims to love and prepares thorns for his dying pillow. Let it stand settled: the slothful, whether minister, deacon, or private Christian, is a man lacking sense. Now, secondly, let us consider the sluggard’s land: “I passed by the field of a sluggard, by the vineyard of a man lacking sense, and behold, it was all overgrown with thorns; the ground was covered with nettles, and its stone wall was broken down.” (Proverbs 24:30–31, ESV) Land will always produce something. Soil fit for a field or vineyard will yield fruit of some kind. Likewise, our hearts and our spheres of influence will produce something. We cannot live as blanks. We will do good or evil. If you are idle in Christ’s work, you are active in the devil’s. By sleeping, the sluggard cultivated thorns more effectively than by any effort. If we do not produce wheat for Christ, we will grow weeds fit only for burning. If the soul is not cultivated for God, it will produce its natural fruit. And what is that natural fruit? Sin and misery. If children are left untrained, what will they produce? If a city is left without the Gospel, what will grow there? Crime and corruption. There will always be a harvest. If we are slothful, that harvest will be painful even to ourselves. No one rests comfortably on thorns. While you sleep, Satan sows. If you withhold good seed, he will scatter evil seed freely. From that will come regret, perhaps for eternity. “Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you” (Genesis 3:18, ESV). Often the evil growth will be abundant. Good land yields abundant weeds if neglected. The person who might have done much for God will do much harm if left idle. The best, when neglected, becomes the worst. If you want salvation, effort must be made to show you the way. But if you want to be lost, it requires only neglect: “How shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation?” (Hebrews 2:3, ESV) The sluggard says, “A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest” (Proverbs 24:33, ESV), and the thorns multiply beyond number and prepare many a sting for him. As we look at the lazy man’s vineyard, let us also look into the heart of the ungodly sluggard. He does not care about repentance and faith. To think seriously about his soul or eternity is too much effort for him. He prefers to take life easily, with “a little folding of the hands to rest.” What is growing in his mind and character? In some of these spiritual sluggards, you see drunkenness, impurity, greed, anger, pride, and many other thistles and nettles. In others, where such obvious sins are restrained by respectable surroundings, you find different varieties of evil. The heart cannot remain empty. Either Christ or the devil will occupy it. My friend, if you are not decided for God, you cannot remain neutral. In this conflict, each person stands either with God or against him. You cannot remain like a blank sheet of paper. The clear handwriting of Satan is upon you; can you not see the marks? Unless Christ has written his own gracious name across the page, the signature of Satan remains. You may say, “I do not live in open sin; I am moral.” Yet if you would examine your heart carefully, you would see hostility towards God and his ways. You do not love his law, nor his Son, nor his gospel. You are estranged in heart, filled with vain thoughts and wrong desires. These will grow and increase as long as you remain a spiritual sluggard and leave your heart uncultivated. May the Spirit of God awaken you. May he stir you to serious and earnest reflection. Then you will see that these harmful growths must be uprooted, that your heart must be broken up by conviction, and sown with the good seed of the gospel until it yields a harvest for the great Husbandman. Friend, if you believe in Christ, allow me also to look into your heart, especially if you are a sluggish Christian. I fear that nettles and thistles may be growing there as well. Did I not hear you sing recently, “‘Tis a point I long to know”? That question will often trouble you, for doubt readily grows in idle minds. I do not recall reading in John Wesley’s diary that he questioned his salvation. He was so busy in his Master’s harvest that it did not occur to him to distrust his God. Some Christians have little faith because they have never sown the mustard seed they were given. If you do not use your faith, how can it grow? When faith is actively exercised in Christ’s service, it takes root, grows strong, and eventually chokes out doubt. Others suffer from gloomy forebodings. They become discontented, irritable, selfish, and complaining — often because they are idle. These are the weeds that grow in a sluggard’s garden. I have known lazy believers become so peevish that nothing pleased them. The most earnest Christian could not satisfy them. The most loving believers were never affectionate enough. The most active church was never energetic enough. They found fault everywhere, even where God was clearly at work. This spirit of criticism, contention, and constant complaint is one of the nettles that surely grow where there is spiritual laziness. If your heart does not bear fruit for God, it will certainly produce what harms you and others. Thorns often choke good seed, but it is a blessed thing when good seed grows so abundantly that it chokes the thorns. God enables some believers to become so fruitful that when Satan sows tares, they cannot grow. The Holy Spirit weakens evil in the heart so that it no longer dominates. If you are slothful, examine the field of your heart and grieve over what you see. Now consider your home. It is a serious matter when a person fails to cultivate their own family. In my early days, I knew a man who often accompanied me into villages where I preached. I appreciated his company until I learned more about him. He spent every evening attending meetings, yet neglected his many children. They grew into ungodly young people because their father never sought to lead them to Christ. What is the use of zeal abroad if there is neglect at home? How sad to say, “My own vineyard I have not kept” (Song of Solomon 1:6, ESV). I once heard of a man who refused to teach his children about God because he did not wish to prejudice them. He preferred to let them choose their religion later. One of his sons broke his arm, and while the doctor was setting it, the boy was swearing. The doctor remarked, “You feared to prejudice your son towards good, but the devil had no such hesitation.” It is our duty to cultivate the field in favour of good crops, or it will soon be overrun with weeds. Train a child towards good, or he will naturally drift towards evil. As it is with homes, so it is with schools. A man who later joined this church had once been an atheist. He traced his unbelief partly to his school experience. On Sundays, the boys were confined to a distant gallery in church where they could scarcely hear a word. They endured endless prayers, but nothing touched their hearts. Eventually, he became so weary of religion that he resolved to abandon it once free. Sunday-school teachers must take care. Classes can be made so dull that children come to dislike Sunday itself. Time can be wasted without bringing young hearts to Christ. Some Christian parents, through harshness and lack of tenderness, have sown seeds of resentment instead of love. May we live among our children in such a way that they love not only us but our Father in heaven. Let parents show cheerful and genuine faith, so that children may desire to follow their example. If faith does not rule in the home, we will see disorder, pride, folly, and the beginnings of vice. Let not your home become a sluggard’s field. Let every deacon, class leader, and minister examine the field entrusted to him. If we neglect our responsibilities, we become like barren trees occupying space that fruitful trees could have used. We will hinder rather than help unless we render real service. Consider this seriously. You cannot remain neutral. If you produce no gain, you create loss. May God grant that we become profitable servants. Now look at the vast field of the world. See how it is overgrown with thorns. Vast regions are covered with error, unbelief, and false religion. The world abounds in cruelty, oppression, impurity, and misery. To what extent is this due to a negligent church? Nearly two thousand years have passed, yet much of the vineyard remains overgrown. Wherever the church has ceased missionary labour, she has declined. When she stops reclaiming the wilderness, she becomes barren herself. Rather than asking what the church has done in past centuries, let us ask what we will do now. Will we continue cultivating the same ground repeatedly while vast fields remain untouched? May God awaken us from our sluggishness. If not, the report may be: “I passed by the field of the sluggish church, and it was all overgrown with thorns.” There is a lesson here. Left to itself, human nature produces only thorns and nettles. Apart from grace, this is all we would have yielded. If we now produce good fruit, it is entirely due to grace. Let us then display the fruit of grace in our lives. Shall we serve Christ less earnestly than we once served sin? Shall we sacrifice less for him than we did for our former desires? May the Holy Spirit produce abundant fruit in us. We also learn the emptiness of good intentions without action. This man always meant to work hard one day. He said, “A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest” (Proverbs 24:33, ESV). Only a little delay — then he would begin. But that day never came. Many hear serious sermons and intend to respond. They mean to turn to God “one day.” Some have delayed for forty years. When will you turn? “Before I die,” you say. Will you postpone it to your final hour? Is that wise? You may die suddenly. Life is uncertain. Take heed of small delays. You have wasted enough time already. Decide now. May the Holy Spirit bring you to decide. “Surely you do not object to my having a little more sleep?” says the sluggard. “You have waked me so soon. I only ask another little nap.” “My dear man, it is far into the morning.” He answers, “It is rather late, I know; but it will not be much later if I take just another doze.” You wake him again, and tell him it is noon. He says, “It is the hottest part of the day: I daresay if I had been up I should have gone to the sofa and taken a little rest from the hot sun.” You knock at his door when it is almost evening, and then he cries, “It is of no use to get up now, for the day is almost over.” You remind him of his overgrown field and weedy vineyard, and he answers, “Yes, I must get up, I know.” He shakes himself and says, “I do not think it will matter much if I wait till the clock strikes. I will rest another minute or two.” He is glued to his bed, dead while he lives, buried in his laziness. If he could sleep forever he would, but he cannot, for the judgment day will rouse him. It is written, “And in Hades, being in torment, he lifted up his eyes” (Luke 16:23, ESV). God grant that you spiritual sluggards may wake before that; but you will not unless you bestir yourselves in time, for “now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2, ESV). And it may be now or never. Tomorrow is only to be found in the calendar of fools; today is the time of the wise man, the chosen season of our gracious God. Oh that the Holy Spirit may lead you to seize the present hour, that you may at once give yourselves to the Lord by faith in Christ Jesus, and then from his vineyard— “Quick uproot The noisome weeds, that without profit suck The soil’s fertility from wholesome plants.”

fields.title: The Broken Fence
fields.body_html:
“I passed by the field of a sluggard, by the vineyard of a man lacking sense, and behold, it was all overgrown with thorns; the ground was covered with nettles, and its stone wall was broken down.

Then I saw and considered it; I looked and received instruction.” Proverbs 24:30–32 (ESV) This slothful man did no harm to his fellow men: he was not a thief, nor a ruffian, nor a meddler in other men’s business. He did not trouble himself about other men’s concerns, for he did not even attend to his own—it required too much effort. He was not openly vicious; he had not have enough energy for that. He liked to take things easily. He always let well enough alone, and, for that matter, he let ill alone too, as the nettles and thistles in his garden plainly proved.

What was the use of disturbing himself? It would all be the same a hundred years from now; and so he took things as they came. He was not a bad man, so some said of him; and yet, perhaps, it will be found at last that there is no worse man in the world than the man who is not good. In some respects he is not good enough to be bad; he has not enough strength of character to serve either God or Baal. He simply serves himself, worshiping his own ease and adoring his own comfort.

Yet he always meant to be right. Dear me! he was not going to sleep much longer; he would only have forty winks more, and then he would be at his work and show you what he could do. One of these days he meant to be thoroughly earnest and make up for lost time. The time never actually came for him to begin, but it was always coming. He always meant to repent, but he went on in his sin. He meant to believe, but he died an unbeliever. He meant to be a Christian, but he lived without Christ. He halted between two opinions because he would not trouble himself to decide; and so he perished through delay.

This picture of the slothful man and his garden and field overgrown with nettles and weeds represents many a man who has professed to be a Christian, but who has become slothful in the things of God. Spiritual life has withered in him. He has backslidden. He has come down from healthy spiritual energy into listlessness and indifference to the things of God. While things have gone wrong within his heart, and all sorts of mischiefs have entered him, grown up, and taken root in him, mischief is also taking place outwardly in his daily conduct. The stone wall that guarded his character is broken down, and he lies open to every evil. Upon this point we will now meditate: “the stone wall thereof was broken down.”

Come, then, let us walk with Solomon, and stand with him, and consider, and receive instruction while we look at this broken-down fence. When we have examined it, let us consider the consequences of broken-down walls; and then, in the last place, let us try to rouse up this sluggard so that his wall may yet be repaired. If this slothful person should be one of ourselves, may God’s infinite mercy rouse us before this ruined wall has let in a herd of prowling vices.

I. Let Us Look at This Broken Fence In the beginning it was a very good fence, for it was a stone wall. Fields are often surrounded with wooden fences that soon decay, or with hedges that may easily have gaps made in them; but this was a stone wall. Such walls are very common in the East, and also in some of our own counties where stone is plentiful. It was solid protection to begin with, and it securely enclosed the little estate that had fallen into such bad hands. The man had a field for farming, and another strip of land for a vineyard or garden. It was fertile soil, for it produced thorns and nettles in abundance; and where these grow, better things can grow as well. Yet the idler took no care of his property, but allowed the wall to fall into disrepair, and in many places to be completely broken down.

Let me mention some of the stone walls that men allow to crumble when they backslide. In many cases, sound principles were instilled in youth, but these are forgotten. What a blessing Christian education is. Our parents, both by instruction and example, taught many of us what is pure, honorable, and of good repute. We saw in their lives how to live. They opened the Word of God before us, and taught us what is right toward God and toward men. They prayed for us, and they prayed with us, until the things of God surrounded us and enclosed us like a stone wall.

We have never been able to rid ourselves of those early impressions. Even in times of wandering, before we knew the Lord savingly, those truths had a healthy influence over us. We were restrained when we would have done evil. We were helped when we were struggling toward Christ. It is very sad when people allow these first principles to be shaken and removed like stones falling from a boundary wall. Young people begin by speaking lightly of the old-fashioned ways of their parents.

Soon it is not merely the old-fashioned aspect they despise, but the ways themselves. They seek other company, and from that company they learn nothing but evil. They seek pleasure in places that would horrify their parents. This leads to worse. If they do not bring their father’s gray hairs down with sorrow to the grave, it is no credit to them.

I have known young men, who truly were Christians, sadly backslide because they were persuaded to modify, conceal, or alter those holy principles in which they were trained from their mother’s knee. It is a great calamity when professing believers become unstable and are carried about with every wind of doctrine. It shows weakness of mind and unsoundness of heart when we can trifle with those serious and sacred truths that were watered with a mother’s tears and upheld by a father’s faithful life.

“I am your servant, the son of your maidservant” (Psalm 116:16, ESV). David felt it to be both an honor and a sacred bond that he was the son of one who was called God’s servant.

Take care, you who have received Christian training, that you do not trifle with it. “My son, keep your father’s commandment, and forsake not your mother’s teaching.

Bind them on your heart always; tie them around your neck.” (Proverbs 6:20–21, ESV) Protection of character is also found in solid doctrine. This too is a strong stone wall. Many among us have been taught the gospel of the grace of God and have learned it well, so that they are able to contend earnestly for the faith once delivered to the saints. Happy are those whose religion rests upon clear knowledge of eternal truth.

A religion that is all excitement and little instruction may serve for a time; but for lifelong strength there must be knowledge of those great doctrines that are foundational to the gospel. I tremble when I hear of a man giving up, one by one, the vital truths of the gospel and boasting of his liberality. I hear him say, “These are my views, but others have a right to theirs.” That is proper when speaking of mere opinions; but we may not speak so of truth revealed by God. That truth is one and unchanging, and all are bound to receive it. It is not your personal view of truth that saves you, but truth itself as God has revealed it, embraced by faith.

I will gladly give up my way of stating a doctrine, but not the doctrine itself. One man may express it this way, another in a different way; but the truth itself must never be surrendered. The spirit of the Broad School robs us of certainty. I would ask some of its leaders whether they believe that anything taught in Scripture is worth dying for, and whether the martyrs were fools for giving their lives for what might be merely opinions. This broad-church spirit breaks down stone walls. It lets in the devil and all his company, and it will do immeasurable harm to the church of God if it is not resisted. A loose state of belief damages any man’s soul.

We are not bigots; yet we would be none the worse if we lived so faithfully that men called us such. I met a man recently who was accused of bigotry, and I said, “Give me your hand. I like to meet with bigots now and then. They are becoming rare, and the material they are made of is so strong that if there were more of it we might see more men among us and fewer creatures without backbone.”

Lately we have seen few men with backbone; most have been like jellyfish. There was a time when I would have said, “Be liberal and cast-off narrowness.” Now I must say, “Be steadfast in the truth.” The faith once delivered to the saints is more precious to me now that it is called narrow, for I am tired of that breadth which comes from broken hedges.

There are fixed truths and definite certainties of faith, and woe to you if you allow these stone walls to crumble. I fear that the slothful are many, and that future generations may lament the carelessness applauded in this negligent age.

Another fence often neglected is that of godly habits already formed. The sluggard lets this wall fall into ruin. Let me mention some important safeguards of life and character.

One is the habit of secret prayer. Private prayer should be regularly offered, at least morning and evening. We cannot do without set times of drawing near to God. To look into the face of man without first looking into the face of God is dangerous. To go into the world without committing your heart to God is to leave it open to every spiritual intruder. At night, to go to bed like animals into their stall, without thanking God for the mercies of the day, is shameful. The evening sacrifice should be offered as surely as we enjoy the evening fire. We should place ourselves beneath the wings of the Preserver of men.

It is said, “We can pray at all times.” That is true; but I fear those who do not pray at stated times seldom pray at all. Those who pray regularly are most likely to pray continually. Spiritual life does not thrive on rigid formalism, but since life always takes some outward form, we should care for its outward habits as well as its inward power. Never allow large gaps in the wall of habitual private prayer.

I go further. There is great protective power in family prayer, and I am deeply grieved that many Christian families neglect it. There was a time when Romanism could make little progress in England because it offered only a shadow of what Christian homes already possessed in substance.

“Do you hear that bell in the morning?”

“What is it for?”

“To go to church to pray.” The Puritan replied, “I have no need to go there. I have gathered my children. We have read Scripture, prayed, and sung God’s praise. We have a church in our house.” The evening bell rang again. It was for vespers. But he had already held his evening worship around his own table, with the large Bible as its chief ornament. They said there could be no service without a priest. He answered that every godly man should be a priest in his own home.

Thus the saints resisted priest craft and preserved the faith from generation to generation.

Household devotion and the pulpit are, under God, the stone walls of Protestantism. My prayer is that these walls may not be broken down.

Another protective fence is the weeknight service. When people abandon weeknight meetings, the power of their religion declines. I do not speak of those providentially hindered by sickness, work, or duty. Exceptions exist. I speak of those who could attend but choose not to. When someone says, “Sunday sermons are enough for me. I do not want prayer meetings or lectures,” it shows a lack of appetite for the Word, and that is a bad sign. If you build a fence around Sunday and leave the rest of the week exposed, Satan’s cattle will enter and cause great destruction.

Take care also to maintain the wall of Bible reading and of Christian conversation. Associate with the godly. Commune with God. By the Spirit’s blessing, you will maintain a strong fence against temptation. Otherwise, temptations will enter the fields of your soul and consume all the good fruit. Many have found great protection for the field of daily life in the stone wall of a public profession of faith. I am speaking to you who are true believers, and you know that it has often been a strong safeguard to be openly known and recognized as a follower of Jesus.

I have never regretted—and I never shall regret—the day when I walked to the little River Lark in Cambridgeshire and was there buried with Christ in baptism. In doing so, I acted contrary to the opinions of all my respected friends; but having read the Greek Testament for myself, I felt bound to be immersed upon a profession of my faith, and so I was. By that act I declared to the world, “I am dead to you, and buried to you in Christ, and I hope from this time forward to walk in newness of life.”

That day, by God’s grace, I followed the strategy of a general who intended to fight until he conquered, and therefore burned his boats so there could be no retreat. I believe that a solemn confession of Christ before men is like a thorn hedge, keeping a man within bounds and keeping away those who would draw him aside. Of course, it is only a hedge, and it is useless if it surrounds a field of weeds; but when wheat is growing, a hedge is of great importance.

You who imagine that you can belong to the Lord and yet lie open like common ground are greatly mistaken. You ought to be distinct from the world and obey the voice that says, “Come out from among them, and be separate” (2 Corinthians 6:17, ESV).

The promise of salvation is to the one who believes in the heart and confesses with the mouth (Romans 10:9–10). Say boldly, “As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord” (Joshua 24:15, ESV). By such a confession you step onto the King’s highway and place yourself under the protection of the Lord of pilgrims, and he will care for you.

Often, when you might otherwise hesitate, you will say, “The vows of the Lord are upon me; how can I draw back?” Therefore I urge you: set up the stone wall and maintain it. If at any point it has been thrown down, build it up again. Let it be evident by your conduct and conversation that you are a follower of Jesus and not ashamed to be known as such.

Hold firmly to your religious principles like true men and women. Do not turn aside for the sake of gain or social respectability. Do not allow wealth to break down your wall. I have known some who made a wide gap to let their carriage pass through, and to welcome wealthy worldlings into their company for the sake of their status. Those who forsake principle to please men will eventually be lightly esteemed; but the one who is faithful will receive honor from God. Guard this hedge of steadfast adherence to the faith, and you will find great blessing in it.

There is yet another stone wall to mention: firmness of character. Our holy faith teaches a person to be decisive for Christ and resolute in removing sinful habits. “If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away” (Matthew 5:29, ESV). It does not say to cover it with a patch.

“If your right hand causes you to sin, cut it off and throw it away” (Matthew 5:30, ESV). It does not say to put it in a sling. True religion is thorough. It says, “Touch no unclean thing” (2 Corinthians 6:17, ESV).

But many are so idle in the ways of God that they have no firmness of their own. Evil companions tempt them, and they cannot say, “No.” They need a stone wall made of repeated refusals. Here are the stones: “No. No. No.” Dare to be different. Resolve to cling closely to Christ. Make a firm determination to allow nothing in your life—however profitable or pleasurable—if it would dishonor the name of Jesus. Be unwavering in truth, unyielding in holiness, immovable in honesty, steadfast in kindness, and fixed in uprightness. If God’s grace builds such a hedge around you, even Satan will recognize it and say, “Have you not put a hedge around him?” (Job 1:10, ESV).

I have kept you long enough looking over the wall. Let me now invite you inside and consider the consequences of a broken-down fence.

First, the boundary disappears. The lines of separation once maintained by sound principles, godly habits, open confession, and firm resolve are gone. Now the question arises: is this man a Christian or not? The fence has fallen so far that he no longer knows what belongs to the Lord and what lies open as common ground. He does not know whether he himself is part of the King’s domain or merely wasteland under the world’s rule.

This happens when fences are not maintained. If that man had lived near to God, walked in integrity, and enjoyed the rich presence of the Spirit in holy living and patient waiting, he would know exactly where the boundary lies. He would know whether his land belonged to the parish of All-Saints, to No-Man’s-Land, or to the territory where Satan rules.

I heard of a dear elderly saint who, near death, was assaulted by Satan. She gently waved her finger and said, “Chosen! Chosen! Chosen!” She knew she was chosen, and she remembered the words, “The Lord who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you” (Zechariah 3:2, ESV). When the wall stands firm around the field, we can resist the devil and say, “Leave the Lord’s property alone. I belong to Christ, not to you.” To speak like this, you must mend the fences carefully, so that the boundary is clear and you can declare, “Trespassers, beware.” Yield not an inch to the enemy. Raise the wall higher when he attempts to climb it. May he never find a gap through which to enter.

Second, when the wall falls, protection is lost. When a man’s heart is unfenced, his thoughts wander across the mountains of vanity. Like sheep, thoughts must be enclosed, or they will stray.

David said, “I hate vain thoughts” (Psalm 119:113, ESV). Slothful men have plenty of them, for unless every gap is stopped and every gate secured, vain thoughts will rush in. Holy reflections, comforting meditations, devout longings, and gracious fellowship with God will disappear if we lazily allow the wall to crumble.

As good things depart, bad things enter. When the wall is down, every passerby sees an invitation.

The gate is open, and in they come. Are there fruits? They pluck them. They roam as if in a public park and pry into every corner. Is there a private place in your heart for Jesus alone? Satan and the world will invade it. Why should we be surprised? Every stray animal tramples and spoils more than it consumes when gaps are wide open. So too, every kind of evil desire and imagination feeds upon an unguarded soul.

It is useless to pray, “Lead us not into temptation” (Matthew 6:13, ESV), if you deliberately walk toward it. God will not lead you into temptation, but you may lead yourself. If you expose yourself to evil influences, you grieve the Spirit of God, and he may leave you to reap the results of your folly. Would it not be wiser to repair the fence at once?

There is yet another consequence: the land itself may be lost. In England, a broken wall does not remove ownership; but in Palestine, fields on hillsides were held in place by terraced walls. When those walls collapsed, the soil slipped away, terrace by terrace, and vines and trees went with it.

Then rains washed the soil away entirely, leaving only barren rock.

So it is spiritually. A man may neglect himself and the things of God—becoming careless about doctrine and holy living—until his power for good is gone. His mind, heart, and strength seem to disappear. The prophet said, “Ephraim is like a dove, silly and without sense” (Hosea 7:11, ESV).

Many are such silly doves. The man who trifles with religion trifles with his soul and soon becomes incapable of serious thought or useful service.

Therefore, stand firm in this evil day. When religious thought slides like mud into the Dead Sea of unbelief, build solid walls around your life, faith, and character. “Stand therefore” (Ephesians 6:14, ESV), and having done all, still stand. May the Holy Spirit root and establish you, so that you do not cast away your confidence, “which has a great reward” (Hebrews 10:35, ESV).

Lastly, let me try to wake the sluggard. It is time to rise. The sun has already dried the dew. You ask for “a little more sleep.” If you sleep a little longer, you may not wake until you lift up your eyes in another world. Rise now. Leap from your bed before it becomes your grave.

Look at your heart. Neglect has allowed sins to grow like weeds. You have neglected God and Christ until you have become worldly, careless, indifferent. Some of you once bore the sacred name; now you resemble the world. Examine the results of your neglected walls. Compare yourself with diligent believers—poor and uneducated perhaps—who serve Christ faithfully. With all your gifts and opportunities, you have become an unprofitable servant. Is it not time to stir yourself?

Consider others who once intended to wake later. Some have fallen into open sin and dishonored Christ. They only went a little farther than you. Your heart is much the same. Under similar temptation, you might fall as they did. A slothful professor is ready for anything. A lazy heart is tinder for the devil’s sparks.

Remember the coming of the Lord Jesus Christ. Will he find you sleeping? Remember the judgment. What excuse will you offer for wasted time and unused talents, when the Master returns?

And you, my unconverted friend, if you drift through life without concern for your soul, you will surely be lost. “If the righteous is scarcely saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner?”

(1 Peter 4:18, ESV). Salvation is entirely of grace; but grace does not produce laziness or indifference. It produces energy, zeal, fervency, persistence, and self-denial.

May God grant us the indwelling of his Holy Spirit, that all may be set in order, sins uprooted from the heart, and the whole person guarded by sanctifying grace from the destroyers that lurk near every low wall. O Lord, in mercy remember us. Fence us by your power. Keep us from sloth that would expose us to evil, for Jesus’ sake. Amen.
fields.body_text: “I passed by the field of a sluggard, by the vineyard of a man lacking sense, and behold, it was all overgrown with thorns; the ground was covered with nettles, and its stone wall was broken down. Then I saw and considered it; I looked and received instruction.” Proverbs 24:30–32 (ESV) This slothful man did no harm to his fellow men: he was not a thief, nor a ruffian, nor a meddler in other men’s business. He did not trouble himself about other men’s concerns, for he did not even attend to his own—it required too much effort. He was not openly vicious; he had not have enough energy for that. He liked to take things easily. He always let well enough alone, and, for that matter, he let ill alone too, as the nettles and thistles in his garden plainly proved. What was the use of disturbing himself? It would all be the same a hundred years from now; and so he took things as they came. He was not a bad man, so some said of him; and yet, perhaps, it will be found at last that there is no worse man in the world than the man who is not good. In some respects he is not good enough to be bad; he has not enough strength of character to serve either God or Baal. He simply serves himself, worshiping his own ease and adoring his own comfort. Yet he always meant to be right. Dear me! he was not going to sleep much longer; he would only have forty winks more, and then he would be at his work and show you what he could do. One of these days he meant to be thoroughly earnest and make up for lost time. The time never actually came for him to begin, but it was always coming. He always meant to repent, but he went on in his sin. He meant to believe, but he died an unbeliever. He meant to be a Christian, but he lived without Christ. He halted between two opinions because he would not trouble himself to decide; and so he perished through delay. This picture of the slothful man and his garden and field overgrown with nettles and weeds represents many a man who has professed to be a Christian, but who has become slothful in the things of God. Spiritual life has withered in him. He has backslidden. He has come down from healthy spiritual energy into listlessness and indifference to the things of God. While things have gone wrong within his heart, and all sorts of mischiefs have entered him, grown up, and taken root in him, mischief is also taking place outwardly in his daily conduct. The stone wall that guarded his character is broken down, and he lies open to every evil. Upon this point we will now meditate: “the stone wall thereof was broken down.” Come, then, let us walk with Solomon, and stand with him, and consider, and receive instruction while we look at this broken-down fence. When we have examined it, let us consider the consequences of broken-down walls; and then, in the last place, let us try to rouse up this sluggard so that his wall may yet be repaired. If this slothful person should be one of ourselves, may God’s infinite mercy rouse us before this ruined wall has let in a herd of prowling vices. I. Let Us Look at This Broken Fence In the beginning it was a very good fence, for it was a stone wall. Fields are often surrounded with wooden fences that soon decay, or with hedges that may easily have gaps made in them; but this was a stone wall. Such walls are very common in the East, and also in some of our own counties where stone is plentiful. It was solid protection to begin with, and it securely enclosed the little estate that had fallen into such bad hands. The man had a field for farming, and another strip of land for a vineyard or garden. It was fertile soil, for it produced thorns and nettles in abundance; and where these grow, better things can grow as well. Yet the idler took no care of his property, but allowed the wall to fall into disrepair, and in many places to be completely broken down. Let me mention some of the stone walls that men allow to crumble when they backslide. In many cases, sound principles were instilled in youth, but these are forgotten. What a blessing Christian education is. Our parents, both by instruction and example, taught many of us what is pure, honorable, and of good repute. We saw in their lives how to live. They opened the Word of God before us, and taught us what is right toward God and toward men. They prayed for us, and they prayed with us, until the things of God surrounded us and enclosed us like a stone wall. We have never been able to rid ourselves of those early impressions. Even in times of wandering, before we knew the Lord savingly, those truths had a healthy influence over us. We were restrained when we would have done evil. We were helped when we were struggling toward Christ. It is very sad when people allow these first principles to be shaken and removed like stones falling from a boundary wall. Young people begin by speaking lightly of the old-fashioned ways of their parents. Soon it is not merely the old-fashioned aspect they despise, but the ways themselves. They seek other company, and from that company they learn nothing but evil. They seek pleasure in places that would horrify their parents. This leads to worse. If they do not bring their father’s gray hairs down with sorrow to the grave, it is no credit to them. I have known young men, who truly were Christians, sadly backslide because they were persuaded to modify, conceal, or alter those holy principles in which they were trained from their mother’s knee. It is a great calamity when professing believers become unstable and are carried about with every wind of doctrine. It shows weakness of mind and unsoundness of heart when we can trifle with those serious and sacred truths that were watered with a mother’s tears and upheld by a father’s faithful life. “I am your servant, the son of your maidservant” (Psalm 116:16, ESV). David felt it to be both an honor and a sacred bond that he was the son of one who was called God’s servant. Take care, you who have received Christian training, that you do not trifle with it. “My son, keep your father’s commandment, and forsake not your mother’s teaching. Bind them on your heart always; tie them around your neck.” (Proverbs 6:20–21, ESV) Protection of character is also found in solid doctrine. This too is a strong stone wall. Many among us have been taught the gospel of the grace of God and have learned it well, so that they are able to contend earnestly for the faith once delivered to the saints. Happy are those whose religion rests upon clear knowledge of eternal truth. A religion that is all excitement and little instruction may serve for a time; but for lifelong strength there must be knowledge of those great doctrines that are foundational to the gospel. I tremble when I hear of a man giving up, one by one, the vital truths of the gospel and boasting of his liberality. I hear him say, “These are my views, but others have a right to theirs.” That is proper when speaking of mere opinions; but we may not speak so of truth revealed by God. That truth is one and unchanging, and all are bound to receive it. It is not your personal view of truth that saves you, but truth itself as God has revealed it, embraced by faith. I will gladly give up my way of stating a doctrine, but not the doctrine itself. One man may express it this way, another in a different way; but the truth itself must never be surrendered. By such a confession you step onto the King’s highway and place yourself under the protection of the Lord of pilgrims, and he will care for you. Hold firmly to your religious principles like true men and women. Do not turn aside for the sake of gain or social respectability. Do not allow wealth to break down your wall. Those who forsake principle to please men will eventually be lightly esteemed; but the one who is faithful will receive honor from God. Guard this hedge of steadfast adherence to the faith, and you will find great blessing in it. There is yet another stone wall to mention: firmness of character.
