fields.title: Frost And Thaw
fields.body_html:
“He gives snow like wool; he scatters the frost like ashes. He hurls down his crystals of ice like crumbs; who can stand before his cold? He sends out his word, and melts them; he makes his wind blow and the waters flow.” — Psalm 147:16–18 (ESV) Looking out of our window one morning, we saw the earth clothed in a white covering; for in only a few short hours the ground had been covered to a considerable depth with snow. We looked out again a few hours later and saw the fields as green as ever, and the ploughed land as bare as if not a single flake had fallen.

It is not uncommon for a heavy fall of snow to be followed by a rapid thaw. These interesting changes are brought about by God, not only with a purpose toward the outward world, but with some design toward the spiritual realm. God is always a teacher. In every action he performs he is instructing his own children and opening to them the way into deeper mysteries.

Happy are those who find food for their heaven-born spirits, as well as for their minds, in the works of the Lord’s hands.

I shall ask your attention, first, to the operations of nature spoken of in the text; and secondly, to those operations of grace of which they are the most fitting symbols.

I. Consider, First, the Operations of Nature We shall not think a few minutes wasted if we call your attention to the hand of God in frost and thaw, even upon natural grounds.

1. Observe the Directness of the Lord’s Work Observe the directness of the Lord’s work. I rejoice, as I read these words, to find how present our God is in the world.

It is not written, “the laws of nature produce snow,” but, “He gives snow,” as though every flake came directly from the palm of his hand.

We are not told that certain natural processes form moisture into frost; no — but just as Moses took ashes from the furnace and scattered them over Egypt, so it is said of the Lord, “He scatters the frost like ashes.” It is not said that the Eternal set the world in motion and that ice is produced merely by the operation of machinery. Oh no — every single fragment of ice descending in the hail is from God; “He hurls down his crystals of ice like crumbs.” Even as a slinger distinctly sends a stone from his sling, so the path of every hailstone is marked by divine power.

The ice is called, you observe, his ice; and in the next sentence we read of his cold. These words make nature wonderfully majestic. When we look upon every hailstone as God’s hail, and upon every fragment of ice as his ice, how precious those watery diamonds become. When we feel the cold biting our limbs and penetrating every garment, it consoles us to remember that it is his cold.

When the thaw comes, see how the text speaks of it: “He sends out his word.” He does not leave it to certain forces of nature, but like a king — “He sends out his word and melts them; he makes his wind blow.” He has a special ownership in every wind; whether it comes from the north to freeze, or from the south to melt, it is his wind.

Behold how in God’s temple everything speaks of his glory. Learn to see the Lord in all scenes of the visible universe, for truly he works all things. This thought of the directness of the divine operations must be carried into providence. It will greatly comfort you if you can see God’s hand in your losses and hardships; surely you will not complain against the direct action of your God.

This will put an extraordinary sweetness into daily mercies and make the comforts of life more comfortable still, because they are from a Father’s hand. If your table is scantily furnished, it shall suffice for your contented heart when you know that your Father has spread it for you in wisdom and love.

This shall bless your bread and your water. This shall make the bare walls of an unfurnished room as splendid as a palace, and turn a hard bed into a couch of down — my Father does it all. We see his smile of love even when others see nothing but the dark hand of death striking those we love most. We see a Father’s hand when disease lays our cattle dead upon the field. We see God at work in mercy when we ourselves are stretched upon a bed of illness.

It is always our Father’s act and deed. Do not let us move beyond this. Rather, let us enlarge our understanding of this truth, and remember that it is true of the small as well as of the great.

Let the lines of a true poet strike you: “If pestilence stalks through the land, you say the Lord has done it — Has he not done it when an aphis creeps upon the rosebud? If an avalanche tumbles from the Alps, you tremble at the will of Providence — Is not that will as much concerned when the dry leaves fall from the poplar?”

Let your hearts sing over everything: Jehovah-Shammah — the Lord is there.

2. Notice the Ease of Divine Working Next, I beg you to notice, with thanksgiving, the ease of divine working. These verses read as if the making of frost and snow were the simplest matter in all the world. A man puts his hand into a sack of wool and throws it out — God gives snow as easily as that: “He gives snow like wool.” A man takes up a handful of ashes and throws them into the air, so that they fall around — “He scatters the frost like ashes.” Rime and snow are marvels of nature. Those who have observed the extraordinary beauty of ice crystals have been enraptured, and yet they are easily formed by the Lord. “He hurls down his crystals of ice like crumbs” — just as easily as we cast crumbs of bread outside the window for the robins during wintry days.

When the rivers are frozen solid and the earth is held in iron chains, then the melting of it all — how is that done? Not by kindling countless fires, nor by sending electric shocks through the interior of the earth. No — “He sends out his word, and melts them; he makes his wind blow, and the waters flow.”

The whole matter is accomplished with a word and a breath. If you and I had any great thing to do, what puffing and straining there would be. Even great engineers, who perform marvels by machinery, make much noise and commotion about it. It is not so with the Almighty. Our globe spins round in twenty-four hours, and yet it does not make as much noise as a child’s spinning top.

Those vast worlds rolling in space trace their paths in silence. If I enter a factory, I hear a deafening roar. If I stand near the village mill turned by water, there is an unceasing clatter. But God’s great wheels revolve without noise or friction. Divine machinery works smoothly. This ease is seen in providence as well as in nature. Your heavenly Father is as able to deliver you as he is to melt the snow, and he will deliver you in as simple a manner if you rest upon him. He opens his hand and supplies the needs of every living thing as readily as he works in nature. Mark the ease of God’s working — he simply opens his hand.

3. Notice the Variety of the Divine Operations Notice, in the next place, the variety of the divine operations in nature. When the Lord is at work with frost as his tool, he creates snow — a wonderful production, every crystal a marvel of design.

But he is not content with snow. From the same water he makes another form of beauty which we call frost, and yet a third shining substance — glittering ice — all by the one agency of cold. What marvellous variety the trained eye can detect in the several forms of frozen water.

The same God who solidified the flood with cold soon melts it with warmth. But even in thaw there is no monotony. At one time the streams rush with such force from their imprisonment that rivers swell and floods cover the plain. At another time, by slow degrees and in small trickles, the drops regain their freedom. The same variety is seen in every department of nature.

So in providence, the Lord has a thousand forms of frosty trial with which to test his people, and ten thousand beams of mercy with which to cheer and comfort them. He can afflict you with the snow trial, or with the frost trial, or with the ice trial, if he wills. And then, at once, he can by his word loosen the bonds of adversity — and that in countless ways. Whereas men are limited to a few methods in accomplishing their purposes, God is infinite in understanding and works as he wills by ways beyond mortal imagination.

4. Consider the Swiftness of God’s Work I shall ask you also to consider the works of God in nature in their swiftness. It was thought a wonderful thing in the days of Ahasuerus that letters were sent by post on swift animals. In our own land we thought we had reached the age of wonders when railway axles glowed with speed, and now with the telegraph we seem to stretch our hands into infinity. But what is our speed compared with that of God’s operations?

Well does the Scripture say: “He sends out his command to the earth; his word runs swiftly.” — Psalm 147:15 (ESV) Forth went the word, “Open the storehouses of snow,” and the flakes descended in countless multitudes. Then it was said, “Let them be closed,” and not another snowflake appeared. Then the Master spoke, “Let the south wind blow and the snow be melted,” and it disappeared at the voice of his word. Believer, you cannot tell how soon God may come to your help.

“He rode on a cherub and flew; he came swiftly on the wings of the wind.” — Psalm 18:10 (ESV) He will come from above to rescue his beloved. He will rend the heavens and come down. With such speed will he descend that he will not pause to draw aside heaven’s curtains, but will tear them in his haste, and make the mountains flow down at his feet, that he may deliver those who cry to him in the hour of trouble. That mighty God who can melt the ice so swiftly can take to himself the same eagle wings and hasten to your deliverance.

Arise, O God, and let your children be helped — and that right early. 5. One Other Thought: Consider the Goodness of God One other thought: consider the goodness of God in all the operations of nature and providence.

Think of that goodness negatively. “Who can stand before his cold?” You cannot help thinking of the poor in a harsh winter — only a hard heart could forget them when you see the snow lying deep. But suppose that snow continued to fall. What is there to hinder it? The same God who sends us snow for one day could send it for fifty days if he pleased. Why not? And when the frost grips us so severely, why should it not continue month after month? We can only thank that goodness which does not send “his cold” to such an extent that our spirits fail. Travellers towards the North Pole tremble as they consider that question, “Who can stand before his cold?”

For cold has a kind of overwhelming power when God is pleased to let it loose. Let us thank God for the restraining mercy by which he holds the cold in check.

Not only negatively, but positively there is mercy in the snow. Is not that a suggestive metaphor?

“He gives snow like wool.” Snow is said to warm the earth. It protects the little plants that have just begun to peep above the ground and might otherwise be frostbitten. Like a garment of down, the snow shields them from extreme cold. Hence Watts sings, in his version of the hundred and forty-seventh Psalm: “His flakes of snow like wool he sends, And thus the springing corn defends.”

It was an idea among the ancients that snow warmed the heart of the soil and gave it fertility, and therefore they praised God for it. Certainly there is much mercy in frost. Pestilence might run a far longer course if frost did not cry to it, “Thus far shall you come, and no farther.” Harmful insects would multiply until they devoured the precious fruits of the earth if sharp nights did not destroy millions of them, so that these pests are swept away. Though man may think himself a loser by the cold, he is in the end a great gainer by the decree of Providence that appoints winter. The quaint saying of one of the old writers, that “snow is wool, and frost is fire, and ice is bread, and rain is drink,” is true, though it sounds like a paradox. There is no doubt that frost, by breaking up the soil, promotes fruitfulness, and so the ice becomes bread.

Thus those agencies which for the moment deprive workers of their means of livelihood are the very means by which God supplies every living thing. Mark, then, God’s goodness as clearly in the snow and frost as in the thaw which clears away winter’s work. Christian, remember the goodness of God in the frost of adversity. Rest assured that when God is pleased to send the biting winds of affliction, he is in them, and he is always love — as much love in sorrow as when he breathes upon you the soft south wind of joy.

See the lovingkindness of God in every work of his hand. Praise him — he makes summer and winter — let your song run through the whole year. Praise him — he gives the day and sends the night — thank him at all hours. Cast not away your confidence; it has great reward.

As David wove the snow, and rain, and stormy wind into a song, so weave your trials, your troubles, your difficulties and adversities into a sweet psalm of praise, and say continually: “Let us, with a gladsome mind, Praise the Lord, for he is kind.”

Thus much upon the operations of nature. It is a very inviting theme, but other fields call me. II. The Operations of Grace I would now address you very earnestly and solemnly upon those operations of grace of which frost and thaw are the outward symbols. There is a season with God’s own people when he comes to deal with them by the frost of the law. The law is to the soul as the cutting north wind. Faith can see love in it, but the natural eye cannot. It is a cold, terrible, comfortless blast. To be exposed to the full force of the law of God would be to be frostbitten with everlasting destruction. Even to feel it for a season would chill one’s very being and make the whole person rigid with fear. “Who can stand before his cold?” When the law comes forth thundering from its treasuries, who can endure it?

The effect of the law upon the soul is to bind up the rivers of human delight. No one can rejoice when the terrors of conscience are upon him. When the law of God sweeps through the soul, music and dancing lose their joy, the cup loses its power to cheer, and the enchantments of earth are broken. The rivers of pleasure freeze into icy despondency. The buds of hope are suddenly nipped, and the soul finds no comfort. It once found satisfaction in growing rich, but now rust and decay seem upon all gold and silver. Every promising hope is frostbitten, and the spirit is bound in winter despair. This cold makes the sinner feel how ragged his garments are. In summer weather he could parade about and think his rags were royal robes, but now the frost finds every tear in his clothing, and in the hands of the terrible law he trembles like leaves upon the aspen.

The north wind of judgment searches the man through and through. He did not know what was within him, but now he sees his inward parts filled with corruption and decay. These are some of the terrors of the wintry breath of the law. This frost of law and terror alone tends only to harden.

Nothing splits the rock or makes the cliff fall like frost when followed by thaw, but frost by itself makes the earth like iron, breaking the ploughshare that tries to pierce it.

A sinner under the influence of the law of God, apart from the gospel, is hardened by despair and says, “There is no hope; therefore I will follow my own desires. Since there is no heaven for me after this life, I will make a heaven out of this earth; and since hell awaits me, I will at least enjoy whatever sweetness sin can give me here.”

This is not the fault of the law. The blame lies with the corrupt heart that is hardened by it. Yet such is its effect. When the Lord has worked by the frost of the law, he sends the thaw of the gospel. When the south wind blows from the land of promise, bringing precious reminders of God’s fatherly pity and tender mercy, then at once the heart begins to soften. A sense of blood-bought pardon quickly dissolves it. The eyes fill with tears, the heart melts in tenderness, rivers of joy flow freely, and buds of hope open in the cheerful air.

A heavenly spring whispers to the flowers that were sleeping in the cold earth. They hear its voice and lift up their heads, for: “For behold, the winter is past; the rain is over and gone. The flowers appear on the earth, the time of singing has come, and the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land.” — Song of Solomon 2:11–12 (ESV) God sends his word, saying, “Your warfare is ended, your iniquity is pardoned.” — Isaiah 40:2 (ESV) When that blessed, cheering word comes with power to the soul, and the sweet breath of the Holy Spirit acts like the warm south wind upon the heart, then the waters flow, and the mind is filled with holy joy, light, and liberty.

“The legal wintry state is gone, The frosts are fled, the spring comes on, The sacred turtle-dove we hear Proclaim the new, the joyful year.” Having shown you that there is a parallel between frost and thaw in nature and law and gospel in grace, I would now repeat the same thoughts concerning grace that I gave you concerning nature.

1. Remark the Directness of God’s Work in Grace We began with the directness of God’s works in nature. Now, beloved friends, remark the directness of God’s works in grace. When the heart is truly affected by the law of God, when sin is made to appear exceedingly sinful, when earthly hopes are frozen by the law, when the soul feels its barrenness and utter ruin — this is the finger of God.

Do not speak merely of the minister. It was right that he preached earnestly. God used him as an instrument, but God works all. When the thaw of grace comes, I pray you discern the distinct hand of God in every beam of comfort that gladdens the troubled conscience, for it is the Lord alone who “heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds.” — Psalm 147:3 (ESV) We are far too ready to stop at instruments. Folly leads men to look to sacraments for heart-breaking or heart-healing, but sacraments say, “It is not in us.” Some look to the preaching of the Word and look no higher, but faithful preachers will tell you, “It is not in us.” Eloquence and earnestness, even at their highest, can neither break nor heal a heart. This is God’s work — not secondary, as though God merely stood behind natural law — but his personal and immediate work. He stretches out his own hand when the conscience is humbled, and by his own right hand the conscience is relieved and cleansed.

I desire that this thought remain with you, for otherwise you will not praise God properly, nor will you remain sound in doctrine. All departures from sound teaching on conversion arise from forgetting that it is a divine work from beginning to end. The faintest desire after Christ is as much the work of God as the gift of his dear Son. From Alpha to Omega, the Holy Spirit works in us both to will and to work for his good pleasure. — Philippians 2:13 (ESV) As you have clearly seen the finger of God in casting forth his ice and in sending thaw, so I pray you recognise the handiwork of God in giving you a sense of sin and in bringing you to the Saviour’s feet. Join together in heartfelt praise to the wonder-working God, who does all things according to the counsel of his will.

“Our seeking Your face Was all of Your grace; Your mercy demands and shall have all the praise.

No sinner can be Beforehand with You; Your grace is preventing, almighty and free.” 2. The second thought about nature is the ease with which the Lord works. There is no struggle or disturbance. Apply this to the work of grace. How easy it is for God to bring conviction into a person’s heart! You stubborn sinner cannot touch Him, and even the circumstances of life have failed to awaken you. You are dead—completely dead in your sins. But if the glorious Lord sends the wind of His Spirit, He will melt you. The person who curses and lives in sin, whose words are full of profanity—if the Lord looks upon them and reveals His irresistible grace, they will yet praise God, bless His name, and live for His glory.

Do not limit God. Saul, the persecutor, became Paul, the apostle. Why should not someone you almost despair of also be saved? Your husband may seem unreachable, your son may have offended both heaven and you—but no one is beyond the reach of God. Even the hardest, most stubborn sin must yield to the warmth of His grace. Even the largest iceberg of wrongdoing can melt in the ocean of God’s love.

Dear sinner, perhaps God has sent a long, cold winter into your soul, and it feels like it will never end. Let me encourage you to hope and to pray for His gracious visitation. Miss Steele’s poem captures this feeling perfectly: “Stern winter throws his icy chains, Encircling nature round; How bleak, how comfortless the plains, Late with green so richly crowned!

The sun withdraws its vital beams, And light and warmth depart; And, drooping lifeless, nature seems An emblem of my heart— My heart, where mental winter reigns In night’s dark mantle clad, Confined in cold, inactive chains; How desolate and sad!

Return, O blissful sun, and bring Thy soul-reviving ray; This mental winter shall be spring, This darkness cheerful day.”

It is easy for God to save you. He says, “I have blotted out your transgressions like a thick cloud” (Isaiah 44:22, ESV). I remember looking up at a black cloud one evening, certain it would rain; I went inside, and when I came back out, the sky was clear—the wind had blown the cloud away.

So it is with your soul. God can remove all your sins in an instant. All obstacles were removed by Jesus on the cross, and if you believe in Him, He has cast your sins into the depths of the sea. “If you can believe, all things are possible for the one who believes” (Mark 9:23, ESV).

3. The next thought about God’s work in nature is its variety. Frost produces a trinity of effects— snow, hoarfrost, and ice—and the thaw comes in many forms. So it is with God in the heart.

Conviction is different for everyone. Some experience it gently, like falling snow—they scarcely notice it at first. True repentance can begin quietly and softly. Others experience it like hailstones, harsh and noisy, striking the heart with a sense of terror. God works in different ways, but every method accomplishes His purpose. Be thankful for His visitation, but do not try to dictate how He works.

As for the Gospel thaw, do not demand a particular way for God’s grace. Thawing is gradual and universal. The surface ice melts first, and slowly the warmth penetrates the entire mass until every frozen rock gives way. In the same way, the Spirit works gradually in the heart—enlightening the mind, freeing the will, removing fear, inspiring hope, awakening the spirit, and producing peace and joy. You cannot see Him at work any more than you can see the wind, but you can feel the effects. Do not be surprised if your experience is different from others’. There is a pattern in God’s work, like the likeness between snow, hoarfrost, and ice, but the details vary.

4. Notice the speed of God’s work: “His word runs very swiftly” (Psalm 147:15, ESV). It did not take long for God to remove the last snow. A human might need days to finish such work, but God’s Word acts instantly. So it is with the soul. The Lord can work quickly when He blesses a heart. Even if you have been under the weight of sin and law for a long time, God can free you in an instant. He can bring you from death to life, from condemnation to justification. “Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in Paradise” (Luke 23:43, ESV), Jesus told a dying thief.

Only believe in Christ’s sacrifice, and you will be saved.

5. Finally, consider God’s goodness. How merciful that He did not burden us with more law than we could bear! “Who can stand before his cold?” (Psalm 147:17, ESV). When God reveals His wrath to a soul, it is terrifying. Sin can weigh a person down like a crushing burden, but Jesus has borne it for us. Even on the Rock of Ages, we do not rejoice because we carry it ourselves, but because He has carried it. The frost of conviction humbles pride, destroys self-righteousness, and keeps us from folly. But how wonderful the thaw of God’s lovingkindness! As soon as His mercy touches the soul, hardness disappears, cold fades, warmth and love flow, and life returns.

We rise from despair as seeds rise from the earth. Faith opens itself like the crocus to receive the sun; hope looks up like the primrose, delighting in God’s promises. Thank God that spring has come in our hearts, and winter has gone forever.

“Where everlasting spring abides, And never withering flowers.

A thread-like stream alone divides That heavenly land from ours.” Believe in the Lord, you who shiver in the frost of the law, and His love will bring you warm days of joy and peace. Amen.

The Operations of Grace I would now address you very earnestly and solemnly upon those operations of grace of which frost and thaw are the outward symbols. Faith can see love in it, but the natural eye cannot. It is a cold, terrible, comfortless blast. To be exposed to the full force of the law of God would be to be frostbitten with everlasting destruction. Even to feel it for a season would chill one’s very being and make the whole person rigid with fear. “Who can stand before his cold?” When the law comes forth thundering from its treasuries, who can endure it? The effect of the law upon the soul is to bind up the rivers of human delight. No one can rejoice when the terrors of conscience are upon him. When the law of God sweeps through the soul, music and dancing lose their joy, the cup loses its power to cheer, and the enchantments of earth are broken. The rivers of pleasure freeze into icy despondency. The buds of hope are suddenly nipped, and the soul finds no comfort. It once found satisfaction in growing rich, but now rust and decay seem upon all gold and silver. Every promising hope is frostbitten, and the spirit is bound in winter despair. This cold makes the sinner feel how ragged his garments are. In summer weather he could parade about and think his rags were royal robes, but now the frost finds every tear in his clothing, and in the hands of the terrible law he trembles like leaves upon the aspen. The north wind of judgment searches the man through and through. He did not know what was within him, but now he sees his inward parts filled with corruption and decay. These are some of the terrors of the wintry breath of the law. This frost of law and terror alone tends only to harden. Nothing splits the rock or makes the cliff fall like frost when followed by thaw, but frost by itself makes the earth like iron, breaking the ploughshare that tries to pierce it. A sinner under the influence of the law of God, apart from the gospel, is hardened by despair and says, “There is no hope; therefore I will follow my own desires. Since there is no heaven for me after this life, I will make a heaven out of this earth; and since hell awaits me, I will at least enjoy whatever sweetness sin can give me here.” This is not the fault of the law. The blame lies with the corrupt heart that is hardened by it. Yet such is its effect. When the Lord has worked by the frost of the law, he sends the thaw of the gospel. When the south wind blows from the land of promise, bringing precious reminders of God’s fatherly pity and tender mercy, then at once the heart begins to soften. A sense of blood-bought pardon quickly dissolves it. The eyes fill with tears, the heart melts in tenderness, rivers of joy flow freely, and buds of hope open in the cheerful air. A heavenly spring whispers to the flowers that were sleeping in the cold earth. They hear its voice and lift up their heads, for: “For behold, the winter is past; the rain is over and gone. The flowers appear on the earth, the time of singing has come, and the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land.” — Song of Solomon 2:11–12 (ESV) God sends his word, saying, “Your warfare is ended, your iniquity is pardoned.” — Isaiah 40:2 (ESV) When that blessed, cheering word comes with power to the soul, and the sweet breath of the Holy Spirit acts like the warm south wind upon the heart, then the waters flow, and the mind is filled with holy joy, light, and liberty. “The legal wintry state is gone, The frosts are fled, the spring comes on, The sacred turtle-dove we hear Proclaim the new, the joyful year.” Having shown you that there is a parallel between frost and thaw in nature and law and gospel in grace, I would now repeat the same thoughts concerning grace that I gave you concerning nature. 1. Remark the Directness of God’s Work in Grace We began with the directness of God’s works in nature. Now, beloved friends, remark the directness of God’s works in grace. When the heart is truly affected by the law of God, when sin is made to appear exceedingly sinful, when earthly hopes are frozen by the law, when the soul feels its barrenness and utter ruin — this is the finger of God. Do not speak merely of the minister. It was right that he preached earnestly. God used him as an instrument, but God works all. When the thaw of grace comes, I pray you discern the distinct hand of God in every beam of comfort that gladdens the troubled conscience, for it is the Lord alone who “heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds.” — Psalm 147:3 (ESV) We are far too ready to stop at instruments. Folly leads men to look to sacraments for heart-breaking or heart-healing, but sacraments say, “It is not in us.” Some look to the preaching of the Word and look no higher, but faithful preachers will tell you, “It is not in us.” Eloquence and earnestness, even at their highest, can neither break nor heal a heart. This is God’s work — not secondary, as though God merely stood behind natural law — but his personal and immediate work. He stretches out his own hand when the conscience is humbled, and by his own right hand the conscience is relieved and cleansed. I desire that this thought remain with you, for otherwise you will not praise God properly, nor will you remain sound in doctrine. All departures from sound teaching on conversion arise from forgetting that it is a divine work from beginning to end. The faintest desire after Christ is as much the work of God as the gift of his dear Son. From Alpha to Omega, the Holy Spirit works in us both to will and to work for his good pleasure. — Philippians 2:13 (ESV) As you have clearly seen the finger of God in casting forth his ice and in sending thaw, so I pray you recognise the handiwork of God in giving you a sense of sin and in bringing you to the Saviour’s feet. Join together in heartfelt praise to the wonder-working God, who does all things according to the counsel of his will. “Our seeking Your face Was all of Your grace; Your mercy demands and shall have all the praise. No sinner can be Beforehand with You; Your grace is preventing, almighty and free.” 2. The second thought about nature is the ease with which the Lord works. There is no struggle or disturbance. Apply this to the work of grace. How easy it is for God to bring conviction into a person’s heart! You stubborn sinner cannot touch Him, and even the circumstances of life have failed to awaken you. You are dead—completely dead in your sins. But if the glorious Lord sends the wind of His Spirit, He will melt you. The person who curses and lives in sin, whose words are full of profanity—if the Lord looks upon them and reveals His irresistible grace, they will yet praise God, bless His name, and live for His glory. Do not limit God. Saul, the persecutor, became Paul, the apostle. Why should not someone you almost despair of also be saved? Your husband may seem unreachable, your son may have offended both heaven and you—but no one is beyond the reach of God. Even the hardest, most stubborn sin must yield to the warmth of His grace. Even the largest iceberg of wrongdoing can melt in the ocean of God’s love. Dear sinner, perhaps God has sent a long, cold winter into your soul, and it feels like it will never end. Let me encourage you to hope and to pray for His gracious visitation. Miss Steele’s poem captures this feeling perfectly: "Stern winter throws his icy chains, Encircling nature round; How bleak, how comfortless the plains, Late with green so richly crowned! The sun withdraws its vital beams, And light and warmth depart; And, drooping lifeless, nature seems An emblem of my heart— My heart, where mental winter reigns In night’s dark mantle clad, Confined in cold, inactive chains; How desolate and sad! Return, O blissful sun, and bring Thy soul-reviving ray; This mental winter shall be spring, This darkness cheerful day." It is easy for God to save you. He says, “I have blotted out your transgressions like a thick cloud” (Isaiah 44:22, ESV). I remember looking up at a black cloud one evening, certain it would rain; I went inside, and when I came back out, the sky was clear—the wind had blown the cloud away. So it is with your soul. God can remove all your sins in an instant. All obstacles were removed by Jesus on the cross, and if you believe in Him, He has cast your sins into the depths of the sea. “If you can believe, all things are possible for the one who believes” (Mark 9:23, ESV). 3. The next thought about God’s work in nature is its variety. Frost produces a trinity of effects— snow, hoarfrost, and ice—and the thaw comes in many forms. So it is with God in the heart. Conviction is different for everyone. Some experience it gently, like falling snow—they scarcely notice it at first. True repentance can begin quietly and softly. Others experience it like hailstones, harsh and noisy, striking the heart with a sense of terror. God works in different ways, but every method accomplishes His purpose. Be thankful for His visitation, but do not try to dictate how He works. As for the Gospel thaw, do not demand a particular way for God’s grace. Thawing is gradual and universal. The surface ice melts first, and slowly the warmth penetrates the entire mass until every frozen rock gives way. In the same way, the Spirit works gradually in the heart—enlightening the mind, freeing the will, removing fear, inspiring hope, awakening the spirit, and producing peace and joy. You cannot see Him at work any more than you can see the wind, but you can feel the effects. Do not be surprised if your experience is different from others’. There is a pattern in God’s work, like the likeness between snow, hoarfrost, and ice, but the details vary. 4. Notice the speed of God’s work: “His word runs very swiftly” (Psalm 147:15, ESV). It did not take long for God to remove the last snow. A human might need days to finish such work, but God’s Word acts instantly. So it is with the soul. The Lord can work quickly when He blesses a heart. Even if you have been under the weight of sin and law for a long time, God can free you in an instant. He can bring you from death to life, from condemnation to justification. “Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in Paradise” (Luke 23:43, ESV), Jesus told a dying thief. Only believe in Christ’s sacrifice, and you will be saved. 5. Finally, consider God’s goodness. How merciful that He did not burden us with more law than we could bear! “Who can stand before his cold?” (Psalm 147:17, ESV). When God reveals His wrath to a soul, it is terrifying. Sin can weigh a person down like a crushing burden, but Jesus has borne it for us. Even on the Rock of Ages, we do not rejoice because we carry it ourselves, but because He has carried it. The frost of conviction humbles pride, destroys self-righteousness, and keeps us from folly. But how wonderful the thaw of God’s lovingkindness! As soon as His mercy touches the soul, hardness disappears, cold fades, warmth and love flow, and life returns. We rise from despair as seeds rise from the earth. Faith opens itself like the crocus to receive the sun; hope looks up like the primrose, delighting in God’s promises. Thank God that spring has come in our hearts, and winter has gone forever. "Where everlasting spring abides, And never withering flowers. A thread-like stream alone divides That heavenly land from ours." Believe in the Lord, you who shiver in the frost of the law, and His love will bring you warm days of joy and peace. Amen.

fields.title: The Corn Of Wheat Dying To Bring Forth Fruit
fields.body_html:
“And Jesus answered them, ‘The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified. Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit. Whoever loves his life loses it, and whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life.’” John 12:23-25 (ESV) Certain Greeks wanted to see Jesus. These were Gentiles, and it was remarkable that they sought an audience with our Lord at this time. When they said, “We want to see Jesus,” they did not mean merely to look at Him, as one might observe someone in the street. They wanted to “see” Him in the sense of meeting and conversing with Him, to receive instruction from Him. These Greeks represented the first of the great multitude of people from every nation, language, and people group who would one day come to Christ. The Saviour naturally felt a measure of joy at seeing them, though He did not speak much about it because His mind was focused on His approaching sacrifice and its significance. Yet He noticed these Gentiles enough that it influenced the way His servant John recorded His words.

Here, the Saviour shows His broad humanity and identifies Himself as the “Son of Man.” He had done so before, but now with special intent. He says, “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.” He does not speak as the “Son of David” here, but as the “Son of Man.”

In this moment, Jesus emphasises His connection to all humanity. He is not highlighting His Jewish heritage or mission alone. Though He had been sent to the lost sheep of Israel, as the dying Saviour, He presents Himself as fully human, fully brother to every person—Jew or Gentile alike. The Lord Jesus embodies universal humanity; in Him, all people are joined as one family. Black and white, rich and poor, wise and simple, all share the same human nature. As the Son of Man, Jesus is closely related to every human being who lives.

With the arrival of these Greeks, our Lord begins to speak about His glory. “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.” He does not yet mention His crucifixion, though it is coming, but the sight of these first Gentile believers makes Him reflect on the glory that will result from His sacrifice. Remember, Christ is glorified in the souls He saves. Just as a doctor gains honour by healing, so the Physician of souls gains glory through those He redeems. When the Greeks said, “Sirs, we want to see Jesus,” it was a simple desire, like the sprouting of a green blade, yet Jesus rejoiced in it as the first sign of the harvest and saw in it the early promise of the glory of His cross.

The presence of these Greeks also explains the metaphor of the buried grain of wheat. Wheat had associations with Greek culture, but that is not the main point. More importantly, the Saviour was beginning the process that would break through the Jewish “husk” surrounding His human life.

Previously, Jesus had stated that His mission was limited to Israel, and He had reminded the Syrophenician woman of this restriction. When He sent out the seventy disciples, He told them not to enter Samaritan towns but to focus on Israel.

Now, however, the grain of wheat—the Son of Man—is breaking through. Even before being “planted” in death, He demonstrates His life-giving power. The Christ of God, though the Son of David, is on the Father’s side neither exclusively Jew nor Gentile, but fully human, with sympathy for all people. He regards all whom He has chosen as His brethren, regardless of sex, nation, or the era in which they live. At the sight of these Greeks, the true Christ manifests Himself openly in a way He had not before. This explains the metaphor of the grain of wheat.

In this passage, we see two main lessons: doctrinal teaching and practical moral principle. Doctrinal Teaching Jesus presents a number of profound paradoxes to His disciples.

First, although He was already glorious, He was still to be glorified. “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.” Jesus was always glorious. His human life was united with the Godhead. His moral perfection on earth also reflected His glory. But the purpose for which He came—to be the Saviour of humanity—added further honour. His life of obedience, resisting temptation, and serving God faithfully was itself glorious.

The apostle John writes: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14, ESV). This refers not only to the transfiguration but also to His ordinary life among men. Spiritual minds recognised the glory of His grace and truth in the everyday life of Jesus.

Even so, Jesus had yet to be glorified fully. Further honour would come through His death, resurrection, and ascension. Though already glorious, the Son of Man’s ultimate glory was tied to His obedience and sacrifice.

A second paradox is that His glory would come through shame. He says, “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified,” yet He speaks of His death. The supreme expression of His glory is His self-emptying, His obedience to death—even death on the cross. His highest honour comes from His humility and suffering. His cheeks were spat upon, His eyes dimmed by agony, His hands pierced by nails. As Son of God, His glory was inherent; as Son of Man, His glory comes through the cross and the suffering He endured for our sins.

We must never separate the crucified Saviour from the coming King. The atonement is central to His honour. When people say, “Let Him come down from the cross, and we will believe,” they misunderstand that it is through the cross that Jesus ascends to the throne. The Son of Man is glorified today because He died and redeemed us through His blood.

Another paradox is that Jesus must be alone—or He will remain alone. “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone.” The Son of Man had to die and experience the isolation of the grave, or He would be alone. Unless He entered the loneliness of Gethsemane, the suffering of the cross, and cried out, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46, ESV), He could not save us.

Though He was never without the Father or the Spirit, there was no human companionship in His suffering. The Son of Man could not rely on another human.

A head without its body is incomplete, and without His people, Jesus would have been a shepherd without sheep. The church is His body, the fullness of Him who fills all things.

He would have been a husband without his spouse, but He loves His bride so deeply that for this purpose He left His Father and became one flesh with her whom He had chosen. He clung to her and died for her; had He not done so, He would have been a bridegroom without a bride. This could never be. His heart is not capable of enjoying a selfish happiness shared by no one.

If you have read the Song of Solomon, where the heart of the Bridegroom is revealed, you will have seen that He desires the company of His love, His dove, His undefiled. His delights are with the sons of men. Simon Stylites on top of a pillar is not Jesus Christ; a hermit in a cave may mean well, but finds no example for his solitude in the one whose cross he claims to honour. Jesus was the friend of humanity, not avoiding people but seeking the lost. As it is written: “This man welcomes sinners and eats with them” (Luke 15:2, ESV).

He draws all people to Himself, and for this reason, He was lifted up from the earth. Yet this great, attractive man must have been alone in heaven if He had not been alone in Gethsemane, alone before Pilate, alone when mocked by soldiers, and alone upon the cross. If this precious grain of wheat had not descended into the loneliness of death, it would have remained alone. But since He died, He “bears much fruit.”

This leads us to the fourth paradox: Christ must die to give life. “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24, ESV). Jesus must die to give life to others. Many people misunderstand death, confusing it with non-existence, and life with mere existence. “The soul who sins shall die” (Ezekiel 18:4, ESV): it does not cease to exist, but it dies by being separated from God, its true life. Many live and yet have no true life, and they shall not see it, for “the wrath of God remains on them” (John 3:36, ESV).

The grain of wheat, when planted in the earth, dies—does it cease to exist? Not at all. Death is the dissolution of what possesses life into its basic elements. For us, it is the separation of body and soul; for a grain, it is the breaking down of the parts that make up the seed. When our divine Lord was put into the earth, His body did not see decay, but His soul was separated from His body for a time; thus He truly died. Unless He had actually died, He could not have given life to any of us.

Beloved, this reveals the heart of Christianity: Christ’s death is the source of all life in His teaching.

If His preaching or His example alone were enough, He could have produced disciples by teaching and living among men. Yet He declares that unless He dies, He will not bear fruit. One might argue that His death completes His example and seals His teaching; true, but even if He had lived on, performing miracles and teaching as He did, it would not have produced spiritual life in humanity.

No one can access spiritual life except through the atonement. There is no way to know God apart from the precious blood of Jesus Christ, through which we have access to the Father. If the ethical teachings of Christianity were more important than its doctrines, why did Jesus die at all? A long life of holiness could have taught ethics, yet it would not have saved a single soul. Only through death could He produce spiritual life. Not by living, not by teaching, not by miracles—but only through dying and rising from the dead could He bring life to others.

All spiritual life in the world comes from Christ’s death. The Old Testament provides shadows of this truth. Life first entered the world at creation but was lost in the fall. Later, through Noah, life came again by a symbolic death, burial, and resurrection: Noah entered the ark, shut himself in, and emerged into a new world when the waters subsided. Similarly today, we are dead with Christ, buried with Christ, and risen with Him. There is no true spiritual life except that which comes through death, burial, and resurrection with Christ.

Do you know this experientially? If not, you know the theory, but not the power of God within your spirit. Whenever the doctrine of the atonement is attacked, we must defend it. We value Christ’s life, but it is not His example alone that saves—it is His death for us. If Christ had lived another nineteen hundred years, teaching and living as He did, it would not have produced one spark of spiritual life among humanity. Without dying, He bears no fruit. If you want life, you must believe that Jesus died for you. You must understand that His blood cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7, ESV). Only when you understand that the grain of wheat is cast into the ground to die can you bear fruit in your soul and see fruit in the lives of others.

Another lesson: since Jesus truly fell into the ground and died, we may expect great results. “If it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24, ESV). Some imagine that only a few receive Christ’s saving benefits, thinking only a small, select group will glorify God.

But we cannot yet know the full fruit of our Lord Jesus. There may come a day when millions worship God with one voice, when the knowledge of His glory covers the earth as the waters cover the sea.

Yes, missions may progress slowly, but the seed is planted, and the corn of wheat that fell into the ground and died will bring forth much fruit. When we consider Christ’s sacrifice, the infinite love He displayed, we must believe that His travail will not produce a scant result. The outcome will match the greatness of the sacrifice. The Lord will reign for ever and ever! Hallelujah! Just as the groans of the cross amazed the angels, so will the results of the cross astonish the hosts of heaven.

Great things are still to come from Jesus. Take courage, you who are weary. Be steadfast, work with hope, suffer with joy, for the kingdom belongs to the Lord, and He rules among the nations.

Finally, a few practical lessons: what is true of Christ is, in measure, true of every child of God.

“Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24, ESV). This applies to us, as the next verse indicates: “Whoever loves his life loses it, and whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life” (John 12:25, ESV).

First, we must die if we are to live. There is no spiritual life except through dying into it. Your own self-righteousness must die. Any trust in yourself must die. The Spirit of God must slay the old nature before He can quicken you. “The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever” (Isaiah 40:8, ESV). You must experience the pruning and cutting of the Spirit before you can enjoy the life He gives.

Next, we must surrender everything to keep it. “Whoever loves his life loses it.” You cannot have spiritual life, hope, joy, peace, or heaven except by giving up everything to God. You will gain all in Christ only when you are willing to have nothing of your own. Pride, rebellion, and self-will must be laid down. If you do not surrender everything, you have already lost it. Full surrender is the only way to keep it. Many of God’s people have learned this through painful experience.

Next, we must lose self to find self. “Whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life.” Give up living for yourself, and you will truly live. A person who lives for themselves loses the essence, pleasure, and crown of life. But if you live for God and others, you find true life.

“Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew 6:33, ESV). There is no greater joy than losing yourself in service to others.

Finally, if you wish to bring life to others, you must die to yourself in some measure. Perhaps not literally, but you must be prepared. History shows this: the gospel spread most widely through men and women who suffered and died for it—Lollards, Anabaptists, martyrs of all ranks. They gave their lives, and their deaths produced life for countless others. Self-sacrifice is the law of divine increase. Death precedes growth. The Saviour of others cannot save Himself. And you, dear friend, must not say, “I cannot continue teaching, I am too tired.” You know what it means to be weary, but consider your Lord. He knew exhaustion, yet He never tired of doing good. Will you remain like the grain of wheat, unfruitful and forgotten, or will you bear fruit? Will you let God place you where you may grow—Sunday school, tract distribution, street ministry? Even if it costs everything, remember: “If it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24, ESV).

Let us rise to a higher level of consecration, hidden, dying to self, yet bearing abundant fruit for the glory of our Lord. I have merely glanced at the text; another time, we may dive even deeper.

A head without its body is incomplete, and without His people, Jesus would have been a shepherd without sheep. The church is His body, the fullness of Him who fills all things. He would have been a husband without his spouse, but He loves His bride so deeply that for this purpose He left His Father and became one flesh with her whom He had chosen. He clung to her and died for her; had He not done so, He would have been a bridegroom without a bride. This could never be. His heart is not capable of enjoying a selfish happiness shared by no one. If you have read the Song of Solomon, where the heart of the Bridegroom is revealed, you will have seen that He desires the company of His love, His dove, His undefiled. His delights are with the sons of men. Simon Stylites on top of a pillar is not Jesus Christ; a hermit in a cave may mean well, but finds no example for his solitude in the one whose cross he claims to honour. Jesus was the friend of humanity, not avoiding people but seeking the lost. As it is written: “This man welcomes sinners and eats with them” (Luke 15:2, ESV). He draws all people to Himself, and for this reason, He was lifted up from the earth. Yet this great, attractive man must have been alone in heaven if He had not been alone in Gethsemane, alone before Pilate, alone when mocked by soldiers, and alone upon the cross. If this precious grain of wheat had not descended into the loneliness of death, it would have remained alone. But since He died, He “bears much fruit.” This leads us to the fourth paradox: Christ must die to give life. “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24, ESV). Jesus must die to give life to others. Many people misunderstand death, confusing it with non-existence, and life with mere existence. “The soul who sins shall die” (Ezekiel 18:4, ESV): it does not cease to exist, but it dies by being separated from God, its true life. Many live and yet have no true life, and they shall not see it, for “the wrath of God remains on them” (John 3:36, ESV). The grain of wheat, when planted in the earth, dies—does it cease to exist? Not at all. Death is the dissolution of what possesses life into its basic elements. For us, it is the separation of body and soul; for a grain, it is the breaking down of the parts that make up the seed. When our divine Lord was put into the earth, His body did not see decay, but His soul was separated from His body for a time; thus He truly died. Unless He had actually died, He could not have given life to any of us. Beloved, this reveals the heart of Christianity: Christ’s death is the source of all life in His teaching. If His preaching or His example alone were enough, He could have produced disciples by teaching and living among men. Yet He declares that unless He dies, He will not bear fruit. One might argue that His death completes His example and seals His teaching; true, but even if He had lived on, performing miracles and teaching as He did, it would not have produced spiritual life in humanity. No one can access spiritual life except through the atonement. There is no way to know God apart from the precious blood of Jesus Christ, through which we have access to the Father. If the ethical teachings of Christianity were more important than its doctrines, why did Jesus die at all? A long life of holiness could have taught ethics, yet it would not have saved a single soul. Only through death could He produce spiritual life. Not by living, not by teaching, not by miracles—but only through dying and rising from the dead could He bring life to others. All spiritual life in the world comes from Christ’s death. The Old Testament provides shadows of this truth. Life first entered the world at creation but was lost in the fall. Later, through Noah, life came again by a symbolic death, burial, and resurrection: Noah entered the ark, shut himself in, and emerged into a new world when the waters subsided. Similarly today, we are dead with Christ, buried with Christ, and risen with Him. There is no true spiritual life except that which comes through death, burial, and resurrection with Christ. Do you know this experientially? If not, you know the theory, but not the power of God within your spirit. Whenever the doctrine of the atonement is attacked, we must defend it. We value Christ’s life, but it is not His example alone that saves—it is His death for us. If Christ had lived another nineteen hundred years, teaching and living as He did, it would not have produced one spark of spiritual life among humanity. Without dying, He bears no fruit. If you want life, you must believe that Jesus died for you. You must understand that His blood cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7, ESV). Only when you understand that the grain of wheat is cast into the ground to die can you bear fruit in your soul and see fruit in the lives of others. Another lesson: since Jesus truly fell into the ground and died, we may expect great results. “If it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24, ESV). Some imagine that only a few receive Christ’s saving benefits, thinking only a small, select group will glorify God. But we cannot yet know the full fruit of our Lord Jesus. There may come a day when millions worship God with one voice, when the knowledge of His glory covers the earth as the waters cover the sea. Yes, missions may progress slowly, but the seed is planted, and the corn of wheat that fell into the ground and died will bring forth much fruit. When we consider Christ’s sacrifice, the infinite love He displayed, we must believe that His travail will not produce a scant result. The outcome will match the greatness of the sacrifice. The Lord will reign for ever and ever! Hallelujah! Just as the groans of the cross amazed the angels, so will the results of the cross astonish the hosts of heaven. Great things are still to come from Jesus. Take courage, you who are weary. Be steadfast, work with hope, suffer with joy, for the kingdom belongs to the Lord, and He rules among the nations. Finally, a few practical lessons: what is true of Christ is, in measure, true of every child of God. “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24, ESV). This applies to us, as the next verse indicates: “Whoever loves his life loses it, and whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life” (John 12:25, ESV). First, we must die if we are to live. There is no spiritual life except through dying into it. Your own self-righteousness must die. Any trust in yourself must die. The Spirit of God must slay the old nature before He can quicken you. “The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever” (Isaiah 40:8, ESV). You must experience the pruning and cutting of the Spirit before you can enjoy the life He gives. Next, we must surrender everything to keep it. “Whoever loves his life loses it.” You cannot have spiritual life, hope, joy, peace, or heaven except by giving up everything to God. You will gain all in Christ only when you are willing to have nothing of your own. Pride, rebellion, and self-will must be laid down. If you do not surrender everything, you have already lost it. Full surrender is the only way to keep it. Many of God’s people have learned this through painful experience. Next, we must lose self to find self. “Whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life.” Give up living for yourself, and you will truly live. A person who lives for themselves loses the essence, pleasure, and crown of life. But if you live for God and others, you find true life. “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew 6:33, ESV). There is no greater joy than losing yourself in service to others. Finally, if you wish to bring life to others, you must die to yourself in some measure. Perhaps not literally, but you must be prepared. History shows this: the gospel spread most widely through men and women who suffered and died for it—Lollards, Anabaptists, martyrs of all ranks. They gave their lives, and their deaths produced life for countless others. Self-sacrifice is the law of divine increase. Death precedes growth. The Saviour of others cannot save Himself. And you, dear friend, must not say, “I cannot continue teaching, I am too tired.” You know what it means to be weary, but consider your Lord. He knew exhaustion, yet He never tired of doing good. Will you remain like the grain of wheat, unfruitful and forgotten, or will you bear fruit? Will you let God place you where you may grow—Sunday school, tract distribution, street ministry? Even if it costs everything, remember: “If it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24, ESV). Let us rise to a higher level of consecration, hidden, dying to self, yet bearing abundant fruit for the glory of our Lord. I have merely glanced at the text; another time, we may dive even deeper.

fields.title: The Ploughman
fields.body_html:
“Does the ploughman plough all day to sow?” — Isaiah 28:24 (ESV) Unless fields are cultivated, they yield nothing but briers and thistles. In this we see ourselves.

Unless the great Husbandman tills us by His grace, we will produce nothing good, but only what is evil. If one day I hear that a country has been found where wheat grows without the work of the farmer, perhaps then I may hope to find someone who will bring forth holiness without the grace of God. So far, every land where the foot of man has trodden has required labour and care; and in men the need for gracious tillage is universal.

Jesus says to all of us, “You must be born again.” Unless God the Holy Spirit breaks up the heart with the plough of the law and sows it with the seed of the gospel, not a single ear of holiness will be produced by any of us, even if we are children of godly parents or regarded as morally excellent by those around us.

Yes, the plough is needed not only to produce what is good, but to destroy what is evil. There are diseases that, over the course of ages, wear themselves out and do not reappear; and there may be forms of vice which under changed circumstances do not abound as they once did. But human nature remains the same, and therefore there will always be plentiful crops of the weeds of sin in humanity’s field. Only spiritual husbandry carried out by the Spirit of God can keep these weeds down.

You cannot destroy weeds by exhortations, nor can you tear out the roots of sin from the soul by moral persuasion. Something sharper and more effective must be brought to bear on them. God must put His own right hand to the plough, or the hemlock of sin will never give way to the wheat of holiness. Good never arises spontaneously in unrenewed humanity, and evil is never cut out until the ploughshare of almighty grace is driven through it.

The text guides our thoughts in this direction and helps us practically by asking a simple question: “Does the ploughman plough all day to sow?” This question may be answered in two ways. First, in the affirmative: “Yes, in the proper season he does plough all day to sow.” Secondly, in the negative: “No, the ploughman does not plough every day to sow; he has other work to do according to the season.”

I. The Affirmative Answer: “Yes, the ploughman does plough all day to sow.” When it is ploughing time, he continues until his work is finished. If it takes one day or twenty, he perseveres while the weather allows. The ploughman’s perseverance is instructive, teaching us two lessons.

First, when the Lord comes to plough the human heart, He ploughs all day — and here we see His patience. Secondly, so ought the Lord’s servants to labour with people’s hearts, showing perseverance in their work.

“Does the ploughman plough all day?” So God ploughs the heart of man, and here lies His patience. For some of us, the team was in the field very early in the morning of life; our first recollections involve conscience and the furrows of pain it made in our youthful minds. As little children, we walk in the night conscious of sin. Our parents’ teaching and prayers made deep and painful impressions, and though we did not then yield our hearts to God, we were greatly stirred, and indifference to religion became impossible.

At school, reading a chapter of God’s Word, the death of a playmate, an address at a Bible class, or a solemn sermon often affected us deeply, leaving us uneasy for weeks. The Spirit of God within urged us to think of higher and better things. Though we quenched the Spirit and stifled conviction, we still bore the marks of the ploughshare. Furrows were made in our souls, and certain foul weeds of evil were cut up by the roots, although no seed of grace had yet been sown in our hearts. Some have remained in this state for many years — ploughed but not sown. Blessed be God, it was not so with others of us, for we had not left boyhood before the good seed of the gospel fell on our hearts.

Alas, many do not yield to grace, and with them the ploughman ploughs all day to sow. I have seen young men come to London in their youth, yielding to its temptations, drinking in its poisoned pleasures, violating conscience, yet unhappy all the while. Fearful and restless, they were stirred within, like soil turned up by the plough. In many cases this work goes on for years without result.

I have known men reach middle age without receiving the good seed, their hard hearts never thoroughly broken up. They go on in business without God; day after day they rise and sleep with no more religion than their horses. All the while warnings of judgment and the chidings of conscience ring in their ears, so they lack peace.

After a powerful sermon they cannot enjoy meals or sleep, asking themselves, “What shall I do in the end of this?” The ploughman has ploughed all day, until evening shadows fall and the day comes to a close. What a mercy it is when the furrows are finally ready and the good seed is cast in to be received, nurtured and multiplied a hundredfold. It is sad to remember how often this ploughing continues until the sun touches the horizon and night dews begin to fall. Even then, the long-suffering God continues His work — ploughing and ploughing until darkness ends all.

Do I address any aged ones whose time is short? Consider your position. What! Sixty years old and yet unsaved? Forty years God bore with Israel in the wilderness; He has borne with you for sixty years. Seventy years old and still unregenerate! How little time remains to serve your Saviour before you go to heaven. But will you go there at all? Is it not terribly likely that you may die in your sins and perish forever?

How happy are those brought to Christ in early life; yet remember: “While the lamp holds out to burn, The vilest sinner may return.”

It may be late, very late, but it is not too late. The ploughman ploughs all day; and the Lord waits to be gracious to you. I have seen many aged people converted, and therefore I encourage other older souls to believe in Jesus.

I once read a sermon in which a minister claimed he had seldom known anyone converted over the age of forty who had been a Gospel hearer all their lives. We must caution against delay, but we must not invent facts.

Whatever that minister thought, my observation leads me to believe that, accounting for the greater number of young people, about as many are converted to God at one age as at another. It is dreadful to remain an unbeliever for so many years; yet God’s grace does not stop at a certain age. Those who enter the vineyard at the eleventh hour shall receive their pay, and grace shall be glorified in both the old and the young.

Come along, old friend — Jesus Christ invites you to come to Him even now, though you have resisted so long. You have been a tough piece of ground, and the ploughman has ploughed all day.

But if at last the sods are turned and your heart lies in ridges, there is still hope for you.

“Does the ploughman plough all day?” I answer — Yes. However long the day may be, God in mercy still ploughs; He is patient, tender, full of mercy and grace. Do not reject such patience, but yield to the Lord who has shown you gentle love.

Perseverance in Seeking God The text not only shows God’s patience but also teaches perseverance on our part. “Does the ploughman plough all day?” Yes, he does. Then if I am seeking Christ, should I be discouraged because I do not find Him immediately? The promise is: “For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened” (Matthew 7:8, ESV).

There may be reasons the door does not open at the first knock. What then? “Does the ploughman plough all day?” Then I will knock all day. I may not find at first; what then? “Does the ploughman plough all day?” Then I will seek all day. I may not receive at first; what then? “Does the ploughman plough all day?” Then I will ask all day.

Friends, if you have begun to seek the Lord, the short way is: “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved” (Acts 16:31, ESV). Do it at once. In the name of God, do it at once, and you are saved at once. May the Spirit of God bring you to faith in Jesus, and you enter the kingdom of Christ immediately. But if, in seeking the Lord, you are unsure of this or do not see your way, never give up seeking. Go to the foot of the cross, hold on to it and cry, “If I perish, I perish here.

Lord, I come to You in Jesus Christ for mercy; and if You are not pleased to look on me immediately and forgive my sins, I will cry to You until You do.”

When God’s Holy Spirit brings a person to earnest prayer that will not be denied, they are not far from peace. Careless indifference and half-hearted devotion hold people in bondage. They find peace when their hearts are roused to strong resolve; to seek until they find. I like to see people study the Scriptures until they learn the way of salvation, and hear the gospel until their souls live by it. If they are determined to drive the plough through doubts, fears and difficulties until they reach salvation, by God’s grace they will soon find it.

The same is true in seeking the salvation of others. “Does the ploughman plough all day?” Yes, when it is ploughing-time. Then I will work on and on — pray and preach, or pray and teach — however long the day God appoints me, for — “’Tis all my business here below The precious Gospel seed to sow.”

Brother worker, are you becoming a little weary? Never mind. Stir yourself and keep ploughing on for the love of Jesus and for dying people. Our workday has only its appointed hours, and while they last, let us fulfill our task. Ploughing is hard work, but there will be no harvest without it. So let us put forth all our strength and not grow tired until we have done our Lord’s will and, by His Holy Spirit, brought conviction to people’s hearts.

Some soils are very hard and cling together, making the labor discouraging. Others are like uncultivated wasteland, full of roots and tangled brambles. They need a steam plough, and we must pray that the Lord makes us equal to such work, for we cannot leave them untilled. Therefore, we must exert even greater effort so that the task may be completed.

I once heard of a minister who tried to visit a dying man but was refused entry. He returned the next morning, and another excuse prevented him from seeing the man. He came again and was still refused. He continued until he had called twenty times without success. But on the twenty-first visit, he was finally admitted, and by God’s grace, a soul was saved from death.

“Why do you tell your child something twenty times?” someone once asked a mother. “Because,” she replied, “nineteen times is not enough.” When a soul needs to be ploughed, even hundreds of furrows may not be enough. What then? Keep ploughing all day until the work is done. Whether you are ministers, missionaries, teachers, or personal soul-winners, do not grow weary.

Your work is noble, and its reward is eternal. The grace of God is seen in allowing us to engage in such holy service. It is magnified in sustaining us in it, and it will be most clearly displayed when He enables us to persevere until we can say, as Jesus did, “I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do” (John 17:4, ESV).

We value what costs us labor and service, and we will treasure even more those who are saved through our efforts. It is good for us to learn the value of our harvest by going out weeping at the time of sowing. When you think of the ploughman working all day, let it move you to steady, earnest effort in winning souls. Seek— “With cries, entreaties, tears to save And snatch them from the fiery wave.”

Does the ploughman plough all day for a little oats or barley? And will you not plough all day for souls who will live forever—either to adore the grace of God if saved, or to remain in outer darkness if not? By the reality of coming judgment and the glory yet to be revealed, strengthen yourselves and keep ploughing all day.

I urge every member of our churches to keep their hands on the gospel plough and their eyes straight ahead. Does the ploughman plough all day? Then let Christians do the same. Start close to the hedge and go all the way to the end of the field. Plough as near to the ditch as possible, leaving as little untouched ground as you can. Even if there are fallen women, thieves, and drunkards in the surrounding slums, do not neglect them. If you leave any stretch of land to weeds, they will soon spread into the wheat.

When you have gone from one end of the field to the other, what next? Turn around and go back to where you began. And after that? Go up and down again. And again. You have visited that district with tracts—do it again, fifty-two times a year. Multiply your furrows. We must learn to continue in doing good. Your eternal calling is to go on doing good forever, and it is wise to rehearse that calling now. So keep ploughing and expect results as the reward of faithful perseverance.

Ploughing is not done with sudden bursts of energy. It requires steady, consistent effort. Flash and excitement may be suitable elsewhere, but not in ploughing.

The work must be regular and persistent. Some give up quickly—it wears out their gloves, blisters their soft hands, tires their bodies, and makes them earn their bread with more sweat than they prefer. But those whom the Lord fills with His grace will continue year after year, and truly, they will receive their reward. Does the ploughman plough all day? Then let us do the same, confident that one day every hill and valley will be tilled and sown, every desert and wilderness will yield a harvest for our Lord, the angel reapers will descend, and the shouts of harvest joy will fill both earth and heaven.

But now, briefly, the question may also be answered differently: Does the ploughman plough all day in order to sow? No. He does not plough forever. After ploughing, he breaks up the clods, sows, reaps, and threshes. As the chapter shows, there are many other tasks in farming. The ploughman has more to do than plough. There is progress in his work. This teaches us that there is progress in God’s work—and there should be progress in ours.

First, consider God’s work. Does the ploughman plough all day? No. He moves on to other tasks.

It may be that the Lord has been using painful means to plough your heart. You feel the terrors of the law, the bitterness of sin, the holiness of God, the weakness of the flesh, and the shadow of coming judgment. Will this continue forever? Will it last until your spirit fails?

Listen: Does the ploughman plough all day? No. He ploughs in preparation for sowing. So the Lord deals with you. Be encouraged—there is an end to the wounding and the humbling, and better things lie ahead.

You may feel poor and needy, seeking water and finding none, your tongue parched with thirst.

Yet the Lord says, “The poor and needy seek water, and there is none, and their tongue is parched with thirst; I the LORD will answer them; I the God of Israel will not forsake them” (Isaiah 41:17, ESV). He will not contend forever, nor will He always be angry (see Psalm 103:9, ESV). He will turn again and have compassion. He will not always make furrows by rebuke. He will sow the precious seed of comfort, water it with the dew of heaven, and shine upon it with the sunlight of His grace. Then there will be growth—first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear (Mark 4:28, ESV). In due season, you will rejoice as at harvest.

You who feel deeply wounded, does God always send terror and conviction? Hear this: “If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land” (Isaiah 1:19, ESV).

And what is God’s call? “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved” (Acts 16:31, ESV).

You will be saved now. You can find peace now, if you stop relying on yourself and your own works and turn instead to the One who paid your ransom on the cross.

The Lord is gentle and compassionate. “He will not always chide, nor will he keep his anger forever” (Psalm 103:9, ESV). Many of your fears arise from unbelief, from Satan, or from your own weakness—not from God. Do not blame Him for what He has not sent. His purpose is your peace, not your distress. He says, “Comfort, comfort my people, says your God” (Isaiah 40:1, ESV). And again, “I have blotted out your transgressions like a cloud and your sins like mist; return to me, for I have redeemed you” (Isaiah 44:22, ESV).

He has struck, but He will heal. He has wounded, but He will bind up. He has brought low, but He will raise up. Therefore, turn to Him and receive comfort. The ploughman does not plough forever, or he would never reap a harvest. God is not always breaking hearts; He also comes to heal them.

There is progress in God’s work. He moves from painful preparation to fruitful growth. The furrows will not always remain visible—the corn will cover them with beauty. As a woman forgets her anguish for joy that a child is born, so you who are under conviction will forget your sorrow when grace bears fruit in your soul. You will also advance to joy. The ploughman may not own much, yet he whistles as he works because he looks forward to harvest. He ploughs in hope. And dear soul, God will rejoice over you when you believe in Jesus Christ, and you too will be filled with joy. Be encouraged—the better portion is ahead. Gospel sorrow leads to gospel hope, faith, and rejoicing, and that rejoicing has no end.

God will not discipline all day. He will lead you from strength to strength, from glory to glory, until you are made like Him. This is the progress in God’s work among people: from painful preparation, to fruitful grace, to joyful experience. But what if the ploughing never leads to sowing? What if your conscience is stirred, yet you continue resisting? Then God will move forward—but in judgment. He may set aside the plough and command the clouds to withhold their rain. The land will be left barren, and its end will be to be burned. There is nothing more terrifying than for a soul to be abandoned—to be left uncultivated by God Himself. Surely that is hell. “Let the evildoer still do evil, and the filthy still be filthy” (Revelation 22:11). Character becomes fixed forever. The merciful hand will no longer till the soil of the heart. What could be worse than that?

This progression is also a lesson for us, because we too must move forward. Does the ploughman plough all day? No. He ploughs in order to sow, and in due time he sows.
