They resolve to change, yet they delay. They are not hardened opponents of God. They appear open and eager. Rejoicing, we direct the message toward them, and it seems to penetrate. But there is hidden armor beneath the surface. No lasting wound is made. Scripture describes them this way: “And these are the ones sown on rocky ground: the ones who, when they hear the word, immediately receive it with joy. And they have no root in themselves, but endure for a while; then, when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word, immediately they fall away” (Mark 4:16–17, ESV). Have we not seen many who receive the word with joy? They have no deep conviction of sin, yet they quickly profess faith in Christ. Their belief appears genuine. The seed has sprouted. There is a green blade. We thank God, thinking a soul has been saved. But our joy is premature. The same lack of depth that made them respond quickly also causes them to wither when difficulty comes. We see this often. Someone asks to join the church and tells us how deeply a sermon moved them. They say they believed at once and have never felt such happiness. We ask about conviction of sin. They believe they were convicted. What they know for certain is that religion brings them great pleasure. We ask if they will continue, and they are confident that they will. Everything seems new. They claim to hate what they once loved. And all of this has happened suddenly, without deep plowing of the heart. It is as if a field were instantly covered with wheat by magic. Perhaps they are received into fellowship. Within weeks they are less regular. When gently corrected, they explain that opposition has made things difficult. Soon they disappear entirely. A little ridicule or inconvenience has driven them back. The minister feels like a farmer who saw his field green and flourishing, only to wake and find every shoot destroyed by frost. If it is tragic to be a wayside hearer, it is hardly better to be like the rock. This second group gives more initial hope. They gather eagerly, especially around a new minister. They seem devoted. But time tests everything. What appeared strong proves shallow. When trials come, they fade away. Some of you may belong to this group. You have felt deeply. You have resolved often. Yet years pass, and nothing changes. There is no depth, no steady work of the Spirit. Must it remain so? Shall one day your life be remembered as a plant that sprouted but never ripened? God forbid. May the Spirit work deeply and effectively in you, so that you may yet bear fruit for God and bring honor to Christ. III. I shall briefly treat of the third class, and may the Spirit of God help me to deal faithfully with you. “And some fell among thorns; and the thorns sprang up with it, and choked it.” Now, this was good soil. The first two characters were bad; the wayside was not the proper place, the rock was not a suitable situation for the growth of any plant; but this is good soil, for it grows thorns. Wherever a thistle will spring up and flourish, there wheat would flourish too. This was rich, fertile soil; it was no wonder therefore that the farmer dealt generously there, and threw handful after handful upon that corner of the field. See how happy he is when in a month or two he visits the spot. The seed has sprung up. True, there is a suspicious little plant down there of about the same size as the wheat. “Oh!” he thinks, “that is not much, the corn will outgrow that. When it is stronger it will choke these few thistles that have unfortunately mixed with it.” Ah, Mr. Farmer, you do not understand the power of evil, or you would not dream like this! He comes again, and the seed has grown, there is even corn in the ear; but the thistles, the thorns, and the briers have become intertwined with one another, and the poor wheat can hardly get a ray of sunshine. It is so choked with thorns on every side, that it looks quite yellow; the plant is starved. Still it keeps on growing, and it does seem as if it would bring forth a little fruit. Alas, it never comes to anything. With it the reaper never fills his arm. We have this class very largely among us. These hear the word and understand what they hear. They take the truth home; they think it over; they even go so far as to make a profession of religion. The wheat seems to spring up and form an ear; it will soon come to perfection. Do not be in a hurry; these men and women have a great deal to look after; they have the cares of a large business; their establishment employs so many hundreds; do not be mistaken about their godliness—they have no time for it. They will tell you that they must live; that they cannot neglect this world; that they must somehow look after the present, and as for the future, they will give it proper attention by and by. They continue to attend gospel preaching, and the poor little stunted blade of religion keeps on growing in a fashion. Meanwhile they have grown rich; they come to the place of worship in a carriage; they have all that heart can wish. Ah! now the seed will grow, will it not? No, no. They have no cares now; the shop is given up, they live in the country; they no longer have to ask, “Where shall the money come from to meet the next bill?” or “How shall we provide for an increasing family?” Now they have too much instead of too little, for they have riches, and they are too wealthy to be gracious. “But,” says one, “they might spend their riches for God.” Certainly they might, but they do not, for riches are deceitful. They have to entertain much company, and go along with the world, and so Christ and his church are left behind. Yes, but they begin to spend their riches, and they have surely overcome that difficulty, for they give generously to the cause of Christ, and they are liberal in charity; the little blade will grow, will it not? No, for now look at the thorns of pleasure. Their generosity to others involves generosity to themselves; their pleasures, amusements, and vanities choke the wheat of true religion; the good grains of gospel truth cannot grow because they must attend that musical party, that ball, and that soirée, and so they cannot think about the things of God. I know several examples of this class. I knew one, high in court circles, who confessed to me that he wished he were poor, for then he might enter the kingdom of heaven. He said to me, “Ah, sir, these politics, these politics, I wish I were rid of them, they are eating the life out of my heart. I cannot serve God as I would.” I know of another, burdened with riches, who said to me, “Ah, sir, it is an awful thing to be rich; one cannot keep close to the Saviour with all this earth around him.” Ah, my dear readers, I will not ask that God lay you on a bed of sickness, that he strip you of all your wealth, and bring you to poverty; but, oh, if he were to do it, and you were to save your souls, it would be the best bargain you could ever make. If those mighty ones who now complain that the thorns choke the seed could give up all their riches and pleasures, if those who live in luxury every day could take the place of Lazarus at the gate, it would be a happy change for them if their souls might be saved. A man may be honorable and rich, and yet go to heaven; but it will be hard work, for “It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.” God does cause some rich people to enter the kingdom of heaven, but hard is their struggle. Steady, young man, steady! Do not hurry to climb to wealth! It is a place where many heads are turned. Do not ask God to make you popular; those who have popularity are wearied by it. Cry with Agur, “Give me neither poverty nor riches.” God grant that I may walk in the golden mean, and may I always have in my heart that good seed, which shall bring forth fruit a hundredfold to his own glory. IV. I now close with the last character, namely, the good ground. Of the good soil, as you will notice, we have but one in four. Will one in four of our hearers, with a well-prepared heart, receive the Word? The ground is described as “good”; not that it was good by nature, but it had been made good by grace. God had ploughed it; he had stirred it up with the plough of conviction, and there it lay in ridge and furrow as it should lie. When the gospel was preached, the heart received it, for the man said, “That is exactly the blessing I want. Mercy is what a needy sinner requires.” So the preaching of the gospel brought comfort to this disturbed and ploughed soil. Down fell the seed to take good root. In some cases it produced fervent love, largeness of heart, and devotedness of purpose of a noble kind, like seed which produces a hundredfold. The man became a mighty servant for God; he spent himself and was spent. He took his place in the front ranks of Christ’s army, stood in the hottest part of the battle, and did deeds of courage which few could accomplish—the seed produced a hundredfold. It fell into another heart of the same kind; the man could not do the most, but still he did much. He gave himself to God, and in his business he had a word to say for his Lord; in his daily walk he quietly adorned the doctrine of God his Saviour—he brought forth sixtyfold. Then it fell on another, whose abilities and talents were small; he could not be a star, but he would be a glow-worm; he could not do as the greatest, but he was content to do something, however humble. The seed had brought forth in him tenfold, perhaps twentyfold. How many are there of this sort here? Is there one who prays within himself, “God be merciful to me, a sinner”? The seed has fallen in the right place. Soul, your prayer shall be heard. God never sets a person longing for mercy without intending to give it. Does another whisper, “Oh that I might be saved”? Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you, even you, will be saved. Have you been the chief of sinners? Trust Christ, and your great sins shall vanish as a millstone sinks beneath the flood. Is there no one here who will trust the Saviour? Can it be possible that the Spirit is entirely absent? that he is not moving in one soul? not giving life in one spirit? We will pray that he may now descend, that the word may not be in vain.

fields.title: The Principal Wheat
fields.body_html:
“The principal wheat.” Isaiah 28:25 The prophet mentions it as a matter of wisdom on the part of the farmer, that he knows what is the principal thing to cultivate, and makes it his chief care. The text, with the connection, runs thus: “Does not the farmer sow the principal wheat?” He does not go to the granary and take out wheat, and cummin, and barley, and rye, and scatter these about carelessly, but he estimates the value of each grain, and arranges them in his mind accordingly. He does not think that cummin and caraway, which he grows merely to flavor his meal, are of half such importance as his bread-corn; and, though rye and barley have their value, yet he does not consider even these equal to what he calls “the principal wheat.” He is a man of judgment; he arranges things; he places the most important crop in the front rank, and spends upon it the most care.

Here let us learn a lesson. Do keep things clear in your minds—not mixed and muddled by careless thought. Do not live a confused life, without care and discretion, running everything together; but sort things out, and divide and distinguish between the precious and the worthless. See what this is worth, and what the other is worth, and set your matters in rank and order, making some of them principal, and others of them secondary. I suggest to you young people especially that, in starting life, you say to yourselves, “What shall we live for? There is a principal thing for which we ought to live; what shall it be?” Have you really considered that question, or have you gone at it at random? What are you living for? What is your principal aim? Is it to be that of the old gentleman in Horace who said to his boy, “Get money; get it honestly, if you can; but, by all means, get money”? Will you be a money-maker? Shall money be your principal corn?

Or will you choose a life of pleasure—“a short life and a merry one,” as so many fools have said to their deep regret? Is it in dissipation that your life is to be spent? Are thistles to be your principal crop? Because there is a certain pleasure in looking at a Scotch thistle, do you intend to grow acres of pleasurable vice? And will you make your bed upon them when you come to die? Search and see what is worthy to be the principal object in life; and, when you have found it, then ask the Holy Spirit to help you to choose that one thing, and to give all your powers and faculties to cultivating it. The farmer, who finds that wheat ought to be his principal crop, makes it so, and directs his efforts with that end in view; learn from this to have a main object, and to give your whole mind to it.

This farmer was wise, because he counted that to be principal which was most necessary. His family could do without cummin, which was only a flavoring. Perhaps the mistress might complain, or the cook might grumble, but that did not matter so much as it would if the children cried for bread. They certainly must have wheat, for bread is the staff of life. It is bread that strengthens man’s heart, and therefore the farmer must grow wheat if he grows nothing else. What is necessary he regarded as the principal thing. Is not this simple common sense? If we were wisely to sit down and consider, should we not say, “To have my sins forgiven, to be right with God, to be holy, to be fit to live eternally in heaven, is the greatest and most necessary thing for me, and therefore I will make it the principal object of my pursuit”? A creature cannot be satisfied unless he is fulfilling the purpose for which he was created; and the purpose of every intelligent creature is first, to glorify God, and next, to enjoy God. What a joy it must be to enjoy God himself for ever and ever! Other things may be desirable, but this one thing is necessary. A sufficient income, a measure of respect among men, a degree of health—all these are the flavoring of life; but to be saved in the Lord with an everlasting salvation is life itself. Jesus Christ is the bread by which our soul’s best life is sustained. Oh, that we were all wise enough to feel that to be one with Christ is the one thing necessary; that to be at peace with God is the principal thing; that to be brought into harmony with the Most High is the true music of our being. Other herbs may take their place in proper order, but grace is the principal wheat, and we must cultivate it.

This farmer was wise, because he made that the principal thing which was most fit to be so. Of course, barley is useful as food, for nations have lived on barley bread, and lived healthily too; and rye has been the nourishment of millions; neither have they starved on oats and other grains.

Still, give me a piece of wheaten bread, for it is the best support for life’s journey. This farmer knew that wheat was the most suitable food for man, and so he did not put the inferior grain, which might serve as a substitute, into the prominent place; but he gave his wheat the preference. He did not say, “the principal barley,” or “the principal rye,” much less “the principal cummin,” or “the principal fitches,” but “the principal wheat.”

And what is there, brethren, that is so fit for the heart, the mind, the soul of man, as to know God and his Christ? Other mental foods, such as the fruits of knowledge and the delights of science, excellent though they may be, are inferior nourishment and unsuitable to build up the inner man.

In my God and my Saviour, I find my heaven and my all. My soul feeds on a crumb of truth about Jesus, and finds deep satisfaction in living upon it. The more we know God, and enjoy God, and become like God, and the more Christ is our daily bread, the more we perceive the fitness of all this for our new-born natures. O beloved, make that your principal object which is the fittest pursuit of an immortal mind.

“Religion is the chief concern Of mortals here below; May I its great importance learn, Its sovereign virtue know!” “More needful this than glittering wealth, Or aught the world bestows; Not reputation, food, or health, Can give us such repose.”

Moreover, this farmer was wise, because he made that the principal thing which was most profitable. Under certain circumstances, in our own country, wheat is not the most profitable crop a man can grow; but ordinarily, it is the best crop the earth yields, and therefore the text speaks of “the principal wheat.” Our grandfathers used to rely upon the wheat stack to pay their rent. They looked to their corn as the source of their strength; and though it may not be so now, it was so of old, and perhaps it may yet be so again.

In any case, the illustration holds true with regard to true religion. That is the most profitable thing.

I am told that rich men find it very hard to secure anything that yields five percent nowadays; but this blessed fear of the Lord is an extraordinarily profitable investment, for it does not yield a hundred percent, or a thousand percent, but a man begins with nothing and all things become his by faith.

Being freely forgiven of our sins, we are by overflowing grace greatly enriched, so that we count among our possessions heaven itself, Christ himself, God himself. All things are ours. Oh, what a blessed crop to sow! What a harvest comes from it! Godliness is profitable for the present life, and for the life to come. Godliness is a blessing to a man’s body—it keeps him from drunkenness and vice; and it is a blessing to his soul—it makes him gentle and pure. It is a blessing to him in every way. If I had to die like a dog, I would prefer to live like a Christian. If there were no hereafter, still, for comfort and joy, give me the life of one who strives to live like Christ. There is a practical everyday truth in the verse— “’It is religion that can give Sweetest pleasures while we live; ’It is religion must supply Solid comfort when we die.” Only that religion must not be of the common sort; it must have as its root a sincere faith in Jesus Christ. See to it. Our religion must be either everything or nothing, either first or nowhere. Make it “the principal wheat,” and it will richly repay you.

II. Secondly, the husbandman is a lesson to us because he gives this principal thing the principal place. I find that the Hebrew is rendered by some eminent scholars, “He puts the wheat into the principal place.” That little handful of cummin for the wife to flavor the cakes with he grows in a corner; and the various herbs he places in their proper borders. The barley he sets in its plot, and the rye in its acre; but if there is a good bit of rich soil—the best he has—he appropriates it to the principal wheat. He gives his choicest fields to that which is to be the main means of his living.

Now, here is a lesson for you and for me. Let us give to true godliness our principal powers and abilities. Let us give to the things of God our best and most intense thought.

I pray you, do not take religion at second hand from what I tell you, or from what somebody else tells you; but think it over. Read, mark, learn, and inwardly digest the word of God. The thoughtful Christian is the growing Christian. Remember, the service of God deserves our first consideration and endeavor. We are poor things at our prime, but we ought to give the Lord nothing short of our best. God would not have us serve him heedlessly, but he would have us use all the brain and intellect and mind that we have in studying and practicing his word. “Acquaint now yourself with him, and be at peace” (Job 22:21). “Meditate on these things; give yourself wholly to them” (1 Timothy 4:15). If your mind is more clear and active at one time than at another, then sow the principal wheat. If you feel more fresh and more inclined to think at one time of the day than at another, let your mind then go towards the best things.

Be sure, also, to yield to this subject your most earnest love. The best field in the little estate of manhood is not the head, but the heart; sow the principal wheat there. Oh, to have true religion in the heart; to love what we know—intensely to love it; to hold it fast as with the grip of life and death—never to let it go! The Lord says, “My son, give me your heart” (Proverbs 23:26, ESV), and he will not be contented with anything less than our heart. Oh, when your zeal is most burning, and your love is most fervent, let the warmth and the fervency all go towards the Lord your God, and to the service of him who has redeemed you with his precious blood. Let the principal wheat have the principal part of your nature. Towards God and his Christ also turn your most fervent desires. When you enlarge your desire, desire Christ; when you become ambitious let your ambition be all for God. Let your hunger and your thirst be after righteousness. Let your aspirations and your longings be all towards holiness, and the things that shall make you like to Christ. Give to this principal wheat your principal desires.

Then let the Lord have the attentive respect of your life. Let the principal wheat be sown in every action. If we are truly Christians we must be as much Christians outside the church as in it. We shall try to make our eating and our drinking, and everything we do, tend to the glory of God.

Draw no line between the secular and the religious part of your conduct, but let the secular be made religious by a devout desire to glorify God in the one as much as in the other (1 Corinthians 10:31).

Let us worship God in the commonest duties of life, even as they do who stand before his throne.

So it ought to be. Let us sow the principal wheat in all the fields of our conversation, in business, in the family, among our friends, and with our children.

May we each one feel, “For me to live is Christ. I cannot live without Christ, or for anything but Christ” (Philippians 1:21, ESV). Let your whole nature yield itself to Jesus, and to none else.

We should give to this principal wheat our most earnest labors. We should spend ourselves for the spread of the gospel. A Christian man ought to lay himself out to serve Jesus. I hate to see a professing man zealous in politics and lukewarm in devotion; all on fire at a parish vestry, and chill as winter when he comes to a prayer-meeting. Some fly like eagles when they are serving the world, but they have a broken wing in the service of God. This should not be. If anything could rouse us up, and make the lion within us roar in his strength, it should be when we confront the foes of Jesus or fight in his cause. Our Lord's service is the principal wheat; let us labor most in connection with it.

This, I think, should also take possession of us so as to lead to our greatest sacrifices. The love of Christ ought to be so strong as to swallow up self, and make sacrifice our daily joy. For Christ's name's sake we should be willing to endure poverty, reproach, slander, exile, death. Nothing should be dear to a Christian in comparison with Christ. Now, I will put it to you whether it is so or no. Is the love of Jesus the principal wheat with us? Are we giving our religion the chief place or not? I am afraid some people treat religion as certain gentlemen treat an off-hand farm; they put a bailiff into it, and only give an eye to it now and then. Their minister is the bailiff, and they expect him to see to it for them. These off-hand farms are losing concerns.

Look at these half-and-half brethren. They have religion? Certainly. But they are like the man of whom the child spoke at the Sunday-school. “Is your father a Christian?” said the teacher. “Yes,” said the child, “but he has not worked much at it lately.” I could point out several of this sort, who are sowing their wheat very sparingly, and choosing the most barren patch to sow it in. They profess to be Christians, but religion is a tenth-rate article on their farm. Some have a large acreage for the world, and a poor little plot for Christ. They are growers of worldly pleasure and self-indulgence, and they sow a little religion by the roadside for appearance’s sake. This will not do.

God will not thus be mocked (Galatians 6:7). If we despise him and his truth we shall be lightly esteemed. O come, let us give our principal time, talent, thought, effort to that which is the chief concern of immortal spirits. May we imitate the husbandman who gives the principal wheat the principal place in his farm.

III. Let us learn a third lesson. The husbandman selects the principal seed-corn when he is sowing his wheat. When a farmer is setting aside wheat for sowing, he does not choose the tail corn and the worst of his produce, but if he is a sensible man he likes to sow the best wheat in the world.

Many farmers search the country round for a good sample of wheat for sowing, for they do not expect to get a good harvest out of bad seed. The husbandman is taught of God to put into the ground “the principal wheat.” Let me learn that if I am going to sow to the Lord and be a Christian, I should sow the best kind of Christianity.

I should try to do this, first, by believing the weightiest doctrines. I would believe not this “ism,” nor that, but the unadulterated truth which Jesus taught; for a holy character will only grow by the Spirit of God out of true doctrine. Falsehood breeds sin; truth begets and fosters holiness. You and I therefore ought to select our seed carefully, and cast out all error. If we are wise we shall think most of the most important truths, for I have known people attach the greatest importance to the smallest things. They fight over the fitches, and leave the wheat to the crows. As for me, those who will may dispute over vials and trumpets; I shall mainly preach the doctrine of the precious blood and the glorious truths of substitution and atonement. These doctrines are the principal wheat, and therefore these shall have my choice.

Next to that, we ought to sow the noblest examples. Many men are dwarfed because they choose a bad model to start with. They imitate dear old Mr. So-and-so till they grow wonderfully like him with the best of him left out. A minister happens to be of a gloomy turn of mind, and he preaches the deep experience of the children of God, and in consequence a band of good people think it their duty to be melancholy. Why need they fall into a ditch because their leader has splashed himself?

We should never copy any man's infirmities. To be like Paul there is no need to have weak eyes; to be like Thomas there is no necessity to doubt. If you copy any good man, there is a point at which you ought to stop short. If I must have a human model, I would prefer one of the bravest of the saints of God; but oh how much better to follow that perfect pattern which you have in Christ Jesus!

We should sow the best wheat by seeing that we have the purest spirit. Alas! how soon do spirits become soiled by self or pride, or despondency or sloth, or some earthly taint. But what a grand thing it is to live in the spirit of Christ! May we be humble, lowly, bold, self-sacrificing, pure, chaste, and holy.

And then, there is one more mode of sowing selected seed. We should endeavor to live in the closest communion with God. A dear brother prayed just now that we might have as much grace as we were capable of receiving, and that God would bring us into such a state that we might not hinder him in anything which he willed to do by us. This is a good prayer. It should be our desire to rise to the highest form of spiritual life. If you sow this principal wheat, get the best sort of it.

There is a spirit and a spirit; and there are doctrines and doctrines; the best is the best for you. O young men, if you mean to have piety, go in for it thoroughly. Do not sneak through the world as if you were ashamed of your Lord. If you are Christ's, show your colors. Rally to his banner, gather to his trumpet call, and then stand up, stand up for Jesus. If there is any manhood in you, this great cause calls for it all; exhibit it, and may the Spirit of God help you so to do.

IV. Fourthly, the husbandman grows the principal wheat with the principal care. Some critics say that the proper translation is that the husbandman plants his wheat in rows. It is said that the large crops in Palestine in olden times were due to the fact that they planted the wheat. They set it in lines so that it was not checked or suffocated by being too thick in one place, neither was there any fear of its being too thin in another. The wheat was planted, and then streams of water were turned by the foot to each particular plant. No wonder, therefore, that the land brought forth abundantly.

This is a lesson for us. We must not give a careless, half-hearted attention to the things of God.

The principal wheat requires careful cultivation—our hearts, minds, and lives must be deliberately trained for holiness. As it is written, “And some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked it” (Matthew 13:7). Let us avoid sowing the best of our hearts in a distracted, worldly manner, or we shall find our fruitfulness choked.

Just as the husbandman waters each row, so must we nurture every part of our spiritual life. “But the seed falling on good soil refers to someone who hears the word and understands it. This is the one who produces a crop, yielding a hundred, sixty, or thirty times what was sown” (Matthew 13:23). The care we give to our principal wheat—our devotion to Christ, our love for God, our obedience—determines the abundance of the harvest. Do not neglect the principal; give your best thought, your deepest love, your strongest efforts, to the cultivation of your soul in Christ.

Let the principal wheat have the principal care in your life. Let your heart, mind, and conduct all be devoted to God. Sow diligently, water faithfully, guard carefully. Then you will see the blessing of a fruitful harvest, and your life will yield abundantly to God’s glory.

We should give our main attention to the most important thing. Our godliness should be carried out with care and thoughtfulness. Brothers, are we careful enough in our spiritual walk? Have you examined the depth of your profession? Why are you a member of a particular church? Because your mother was? That is some reason, but it is not enough to justify you before God. I urge you to honestly assess your standing. If any Christian minister is afraid to call you to this duty, I question him. I am not afraid. I ask you to examine everything I teach, for I do not want to be responsible for another man’s beliefs. Like the Bereans, check and see whether these things are true according to Scripture (Acts 17:11).

One of the greatest blessings for the church would be a spirit of inquiry that tests everything against the Word of God. If people speak contrary to Scripture, it is because there is no light in them. Serve God as carefully as an Eastern farmer planted his wheat, placing it in orderly rows with care and precision. You serve a precise God, so serve Him precisely. He is a jealous God, so be careful to avoid even the smallest error or form of self-worship (Exodus 20:5).

Also, water every part of your spiritual life as the farmer waters each plant. Pray for grace from above, so that no part of your faith, hope, or love ever dries up. Serve each part of your soul as a farmer serves his wheat. Make grace your main concern, for it deserves it.

With this I conclude: focus on this, because from it you can expect your main harvest. If religion is the most important thing, you can expect your main reward from it. The harvest will come in various ways. You will achieve the greatest success in life if you live wholly for God’s glory.

Success or failure depends largely on the focus of our efforts. It is useless for me to try to conduct a choir—I am not made for that—but I may succeed in preaching, because that is my calling.

Christian, if you live for the world, you will not prosper, for you are not made for it. Grace has made you unsuitable for sin. If you live for God with all your heart, you will succeed, because God made you for this purpose. Just as He made the fish for water and the birds for air, He made the believer for holiness and for serving Him. You will be out of your element, like a fish out of water or a bird in the stream, if you abandon God’s service. The Eastern farmer’s success depends on his wheat; yours depends on your devotion to God. Look to godliness for your joy. Is there any happiness like knowing you are in Christ and loved by the Lord? It is in your faith that you will find comfort on a sick and dying bed, and that time may come soon.

In the life to come, what a harvest will result from serving the Lord! What does the world give?

Only smoke. A man may make a million dollars and die—what has he gained? A man’s fame may spread across the earth, yet he dies—what remains? Living for the world is like children playing in the street for coins or shells. Life for God is real and lasting; everything else is waste. Let us remember this and dedicate ourselves to serving the Lord. May the Spirit help us to sow the “principal wheat” and live in joyful expectation of reaping a harvest, as promised: “Those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy” (Psalm 126:5).
fields.body_text: “The principal wheat.” Isaiah 28:25 The prophet mentions it as a matter of wisdom on the part of the farmer, that he knows what is the principal thing to cultivate, and makes it his chief care. The text, with the connection, runs thus: “Does not the farmer sow the principal wheat?” He does not go to the granary and take out wheat, and cummin, and barley, and rye, and scatter these about carelessly, but he estimates the value of each grain, and arranges them in his mind accordingly. He does not think that cummin and caraway, which he grows merely to flavor his meal, are of half such importance as his bread-corn; and, though rye and barley have their value, yet he does not consider even these equal to what he calls “the principal wheat.” He is a man of judgment; he arranges things; he places the most important crop in the front rank, and spends upon it the most care. Here let us learn a lesson. Do keep things clear in your minds—not mixed and muddled by careless thought. Do not live a confused life, without care and discretion, running everything together; but sort things out, and divide and distinguish between the precious and the worthless. See what this is worth, and what the other is worth, and set your matters in rank and order, making some of them principal, and others of them secondary. I suggest to you young people especially that, in starting life, you say to yourselves, “What shall we live for? There is a principal thing for which we ought to live; what shall it be?” Have you really considered that question, or have you gone at it at random? What are you living for? What is your principal aim? Is it to be that of the old gentleman in Horace who said to his boy, “Get money; get it honestly, if you can; but, by all means, get money”? Will you be a money-maker? Shall money be your principal corn? Or will you choose a life of pleasure—“a short life and a merry one,” as so many fools have said to their deep regret? Is it in dissipation that your life is to be spent? Are thistles to be your principal crop? Because there is a certain pleasure in looking at a Scotch thistle, do you intend to grow acres of pleasurable vice? And will you make your bed upon them when you come to die? Search and see what is worthy to be the principal object in life; and, when you have found it, then ask the Holy Spirit to help you to choose that one thing, and to give all your powers and faculties to cultivating it. The farmer, who finds that wheat ought to be his principal crop, makes it so, and directs his efforts with that end in view; learn from this to have a main object, and to give your whole mind to it. This farmer was wise, because he counted that to be principal which was most necessary. His family could do without cummin, which was only a flavoring. Perhaps the mistress might complain, or the cook might grumble, but that did not matter so much as it would if the children cried for bread. They certainly must have wheat, for bread is the staff of life. It is bread that strengthens man’s heart, and therefore the farmer must grow wheat if he grows nothing else. What is necessary he regarded as the principal thing. Is not this simple common sense? If we were wisely to sit down and consider, should we not say, “To have my sins forgiven, to be right with God, to be holy, to be fit to live eternally in heaven, is the greatest and most necessary thing for me, and therefore I will make it the principal object of my pursuit”? A creature cannot be satisfied unless he is fulfilling the purpose for which he was created; and the purpose of every intelligent creature is first, to glorify God, and next, to enjoy God. What a joy it must be to enjoy God himself for ever and ever! Other things may be desirable, but this one thing is necessary. A sufficient income, a measure of respect among men, a degree of health—all these are the flavoring of life; but to be saved in the Lord with an everlasting salvation is life itself. Jesus Christ is the bread by which our soul’s best life is sustained. Oh, that we were all wise enough to feel that to be one with Christ is the one thing necessary; that to be at peace with God is the principal thing; that to be brought into harmony with the Most High is the true music of our being. Other herbs may take their place in proper order, but grace is the principal wheat, and we must cultivate it. This farmer was wise, because he made that the principal thing which was most fit to be so. Of course, barley is useful as food, for nations have lived on barley bread, and lived healthily too; and rye has been the nourishment of millions; neither have they starved on oats and other grains. Still, give me a piece of wheaten bread, for it is the best support for life’s journey. This farmer knew that wheat was the most suitable food for man, and so he did not put the inferior grain, which might serve as a substitute, into the prominent place; but he gave his wheat the preference. He did not say, “the principal barley,” or “the principal rye,” much less “the principal cummin,” or “the principal fitches,” but “the principal wheat.” And what is there, brethren, that is so fit for the heart, the mind, the soul of man, as to know God and his Christ? Other mental foods, such as the fruits of knowledge and the delights of science, excellent though they may be, are inferior nourishment and unsuitable to build up the inner man. In my God and my Saviour, I find my heaven and my all. My soul feeds on a crumb of truth about Jesus, and finds deep satisfaction in living upon it. The more we know God, and enjoy God, and become like God, and the more Christ is our daily bread, the more we perceive the fitness of all this for our new-born natures. O beloved, make that your principal object which is the fittest pursuit of an immortal mind. “Religion is the chief concern Of mortals here below; May I its great importance learn, Its sovereign virtue know!” “More needful this than glittering wealth, Or aught the world bestows; Not reputation, food, or health, Can give us such repose.” Moreover, this farmer was wise, because he made that the principal thing which was most profitable. Under certain circumstances, in our own country, wheat is not the most profitable crop a man can grow; but ordinarily, it is the best crop the earth yields, and therefore the text speaks of “the principal wheat.” Our grandfathers used to rely upon the wheat stack to pay their rent. They looked to their corn as the source of their strength; and though it may not be so now, it was so of old, and perhaps it may yet be so again. In any case, the illustration holds true with regard to true religion. That is the most profitable thing. I am told that rich men find it very hard to secure anything that yields five percent nowadays; but this blessed fear of the Lord is an extraordinarily profitable investment, for it does not yield a hundred percent, or a thousand percent, but a man begins with nothing and all things become his by faith. Being freely forgiven of our sins, we are by overflowing grace greatly enriched, so that we count among our possessions heaven itself, Christ himself, God himself. All things are ours. Oh, what a blessed crop to sow! What a harvest comes from it! Godliness is profitable for the present life, and for the life to come. Godliness is a blessing to a man’s body—it keeps him from drunkenness and vice; and it is a blessing to his soul—it makes him gentle and pure. It is a blessing to him in every way. If I had to die like a dog, I would prefer to live like a Christian. If there were no hereafter, still, for comfort and joy, give me the life of one who strives to live like Christ. There is a practical everyday truth in the verse— “’It is religion that can give Sweetest pleasures while we live; ’It is religion must supply Solid comfort when we die.” Only that religion must not be of the common sort; it must have as its root a sincere faith in Jesus Christ. See to it. Our religion must be either everything or nothing, either first or nowhere. Make it “the principal wheat,” and it will richly repay you. II. Secondly, the husbandman is a lesson to us because he gives this principal thing the principal place. I find that the Hebrew is rendered by some eminent scholars, "He puts the wheat into the principal place." That little handful of cummin for the wife to flavor the cakes with he grows in a corner; and the various herbs he places in their proper borders. The barley he sets in its plot, and the rye in its acre; but if there is a good bit of rich soil—the best he has—he appropriates it to the principal wheat. He gives his choicest fields to that which is to be the main means of his living. Now, here is a lesson for you and for me. Let us give to true godliness our principal powers and abilities. Let us give to the things of God our best and most intense thought. I pray you, do not take religion at second hand from what I tell you, or from what somebody else tells you; but think it over. Read, mark, learn, and inwardly digest the word of God. The thoughtful Christian is the growing Christian. Remember, the service of God deserves our first consideration and endeavor. We are poor things at our prime, but we ought to give the Lord nothing short of our best. God would not have us serve him heedlessly, but he would have us use all the brain and intellect and mind that we have in studying and practicing his word. "Acquaint now yourself with him, and be at peace" (Job 22:21). "Meditate on these things; give yourself wholly to them" (1 Timothy 4:15). If your mind is more clear and active at one time than at another, then sow the principal wheat. If you feel more fresh and more inclined to think at one time of the day than at another, let your mind then go towards the best things. Be sure, also, to yield to this subject your most earnest love. The best field in the little estate of manhood is not the head, but the heart; sow the principal wheat there. Oh, to have true religion in the heart; to love what we know—intensely to love it; to hold it fast as with the grip of life and death—never to let it go! The Lord says, "My son, give me your heart" (Proverbs 23:26, ESV), and he will not be contented with anything less than our heart. Oh, when your zeal is most burning, and your love is most fervent, let the warmth and the fervency all go towards the Lord your God, and to the service of him who has redeemed you with his precious blood. Let the principal wheat have the principal part of your nature. Towards God and his Christ also turn your most fervent desires. When you enlarge your desire, desire Christ; when you become ambitious let your ambition be all for God. Let your hunger and your thirst be after righteousness. Let your aspirations and your longings be all towards holiness, and the things that shall make you like to Christ. Give to this principal wheat your principal desires. Then let the Lord have the attentive respect of your life. Let the principal wheat be sown in every action. If we are truly Christians we must be as much Christians outside the church as in it. We shall try to make our eating and our drinking, and everything we do, tend to the glory of God. Draw no line between the secular and the religious part of your conduct, but let the secular be made religious by a devout desire to glorify God in the one as much as in the other (1 Corinthians 10:31). Let us worship God in the commonest duties of life, even as they do who stand before his throne. So it ought to be. Let us sow the principal wheat in all the fields of our conversation, in business, in the family, among our friends, and with our children. May we each one feel, "For me to live is Christ. I cannot live without Christ, or for anything but Christ" (Philippians 1:21, ESV). Let your whole nature yield itself to Jesus, and to none else. We should give to this principal wheat our most earnest labors. We should spend ourselves for the spread of the gospel. A Christian man ought to lay himself out to serve Jesus. I hate to see a professing man zealous in politics and lukewarm in devotion; all on fire at a parish vestry, and chill as winter when he comes to a prayer-meeting. Some fly like eagles when they are serving the world, but they have a broken wing in the service of God. This should not be. If anything could rouse us up, and make the lion within us roar in his strength, it should be when we confront the foes of Jesus or fight in his cause. Our Lord's service is the principal wheat; let us labor most in connection with it. This, I think, should also take possession of us so as to lead to our greatest sacrifices. The love of Christ ought to be so strong as to swallow up self, and make sacrifice our daily joy. For Christ's name's sake we should be willing to endure poverty, reproach, slander, exile, death. Nothing should be dear to a Christian in comparison with Christ. Now, I will put it to you whether it is so or no. Is the love of Jesus the principal wheat with us? Are we giving our religion the chief place or not? I am afraid some people treat religion as certain gentlemen treat an off-hand farm; they put a bailiff into it, and only give an eye to it now and then. Their minister is the bailiff, and they expect him to see to it for them. These off-hand farms are losing concerns. Look at these half-and-half brethren. They have religion? Certainly. But they are like the man of whom the child spoke at the Sunday-school. "Is your father a Christian?" said the teacher. "Yes," said the child, "but he has not worked much at it lately." I could point out several of this sort, who are sowing their wheat very sparingly, and choosing the most barren patch to sow it in. They profess to be Christians, but religion is a tenth-rate article on their farm. Some have a large acreage for the world, and a poor little plot for Christ. They are growers of worldly pleasure and self-indulgence, and they sow a little religion by the roadside for appearance’s sake. This will not do. God will not thus be mocked (Galatians 6:7). If we despise him and his truth we shall be lightly esteemed. O come, let us give our principal time, talent, thought, effort to that which is the chief concern of immortal spirits. May we imitate the husbandman who gives the principal wheat the principal place in his farm. III. Let us learn a third lesson. The husbandman selects the principal seed-corn when he is sowing his wheat. When a farmer is setting aside wheat for sowing, he does not choose the tail corn and the worst of his produce, but if he is a sensible man he likes to sow the best wheat in the world. Many farmers search the country round for a good sample of wheat for sowing, for they do not expect to get a good harvest out of bad seed. The husbandman is taught of God to put into the ground "the principal wheat." Let me learn that if I am going to sow to the Lord and be a Christian, I should sow the best kind of Christianity. I should try to do this, first, by believing the weightiest doctrines. I would believe not this "ism," nor that, but the unadulterated truth which Jesus taught; for a holy character will only grow by the Spirit of God out of true doctrine. Falsehood breeds sin; truth begets and fosters holiness. You and I therefore ought to select our seed carefully, and cast out all error. If we are wise we shall think most of the most important truths, for I have known people attach the greatest importance to the smallest things. They fight over the fitches, and leave the wheat to the crows. As for me, those who will may dispute over vials and trumpets; I shall mainly preach the doctrine of the precious blood and the glorious truths of substitution and atonement. These doctrines are the principal wheat, and therefore these shall have my choice. Next to that, we ought to sow the noblest examples. Many men are dwarfed because they choose a bad model to start with. They imitate dear old Mr. So-and-so till they grow wonderfully like him with the best of him left out. A minister happens to be of a gloomy turn of mind, and he preaches the deep experience of the children of God, and in consequence a band of good people think it their duty to be melancholy. Why need they fall into a ditch because their leader has splashed himself? We should never copy any man's infirmities. To be like Paul there is no need to have weak eyes; to be like Thomas there is no necessity to doubt. If you copy any good man, there is a point at which you ought to stop short. If I must have a human model, I would prefer one of the bravest of the saints of God; but oh how much better to follow that perfect pattern which you have in Christ Jesus! We should sow the best wheat by seeing that we have the purest spirit. Alas! how soon do spirits become soiled by self or pride, or despondency or sloth, or some earthly taint. But what a grand thing it is to live in the spirit of Christ! May we be humble, lowly, bold, self-sacrificing, pure, chaste, and holy. And then, there is one more mode of sowing selected seed. We should endeavor to live in the closest communion with God. A dear brother prayed just now that we might have as much grace as we were capable of receiving, and that God would bring us into such a state that we might not hinder him in anything which he willed to do by us. This is a good prayer. It should be our desire to rise to the highest form of spiritual life. If you sow this principal wheat, get the best sort of it. There is a spirit and a spirit; and there are doctrines and doctrines; the best is the best for you. O young men, if you mean to have piety, go in for it thoroughly. Do not sneak through the world as if you were ashamed of your Lord. If you are Christ's, show your colors. Rally to his banner, gather to his trumpet call, and then stand up, stand up for Jesus. If there is any manhood in you, this great cause calls for it all; exhibit it, and may the Spirit of God help you so to do. IV. Fourthly, the husbandman grows the principal wheat with the principal care. Some critics say that the proper translation is that the husbandman plants his wheat in rows. It is said that the large crops in Palestine in olden times were due to the fact that they planted the wheat. They set it in lines so that it was not checked or suffocated by being too thick in one place, neither was there any fear of its being too thin in another. The wheat was planted, and then streams of water were turned by the foot to each particular plant. No wonder, therefore, that the land brought forth abundantly. This is a lesson for us. We must not give a careless, half-hearted attention to the things of God. The principal wheat requires careful cultivation—our hearts, minds, and lives must be deliberately trained for holiness. As it is written, “And some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked it” (Matthew 13:7). Let us avoid sowing the best of our hearts in a distracted, worldly manner, or we shall find our fruitfulness choked. Just as the husbandman waters each row, so must we nurture every part of our spiritual life. “But the seed falling on good soil refers to someone who hears the word and understands it. This is the one who produces a crop, yielding a hundred, sixty, or thirty times what was sown” (Matthew 13:23). The care we give to our principal wheat—our devotion to Christ, our love for God, our obedience—determines the abundance of the harvest. Do not neglect the principal; give your best thought, your deepest love, your strongest efforts, to the cultivation of your soul in Christ. Let the principal wheat have the principal care in your life. Let your heart, mind, and conduct all be devoted to God. Sow diligently, water faithfully, guard carefully. Then you will see the blessing of a fruitful harvest, and your life will yield abundantly to God’s glory. We should give our main attention to the most important thing. Our godliness should be carried out with care and thoughtfulness. Brothers, are we careful enough in our spiritual walk? Have you examined the depth of your profession? Why are you a member of a particular church? Because your mother was? That is some reason, but it is not enough to justify you before God. I urge you to honestly assess your standing. If any Christian minister is afraid to call you to this duty, I question him. I am not afraid. I ask you to examine everything I teach, for I do not want to be responsible for another man’s beliefs. Like the Bereans, check and see whether these things are true according to Scripture (Acts 17:11). One of the greatest blessings for the church would be a spirit of inquiry that tests everything against the Word of God. If people speak contrary to Scripture, it is because there is no light in them. Serve God as carefully as an Eastern farmer planted his wheat, placing it in orderly rows with care and precision. You serve a precise God, so serve Him precisely. He is a jealous God, so be careful to avoid even the smallest error or form of self-worship (Exodus 20:5). Also, water every part of your spiritual life as the farmer waters each plant. Pray for grace from above, so that no part of your faith, hope, or love ever dries up. Serve each part of your soul as a farmer serves his wheat. Make grace your main concern, for it deserves it. With this I conclude: focus on this, because from it you can expect your main harvest. If religion is the most important thing, you can expect your main reward from it. The harvest will come in various ways. You will achieve the greatest success in life if you live wholly for God’s glory. Success or failure depends largely on the focus of our efforts. It is useless for me to try to conduct a choir—I am not made for that—but I may succeed in preaching, because that is my calling. Christian, if you live for the world, you will not prosper, for you are not made for it. Grace has made you unsuitable for sin. If you live for God with all your heart, you will succeed, because God made you for this purpose. Just as He made the fish for water and the birds for air, He made the believer for holiness and for serving Him. You will be out of your element, like a fish out of water or a bird in the stream, if you abandon God’s service. The Eastern farmer’s success depends on his wheat; yours depends on your devotion to God. Look to godliness for your joy. Is there any happiness like knowing you are in Christ and loved by the Lord? It is in your faith that you will find comfort on a sick and dying bed, and that time may come soon. In the life to come, what a harvest will result from serving the Lord! What does the world give? Only smoke. A man may make a million dollars and die—what has he gained? A man’s fame may spread across the earth, yet he dies—what remains? Living for the world is like children playing in the street for coins or shells. Life for God is real and lasting; everything else is waste. Let us remember this and dedicate ourselves to serving the Lord. May the Spirit help us to sow the “principal wheat” and live in joyful expectation of reaping a harvest, as promised: “Those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy” (Psalm 126:5).

fields.title: Spring In The Heart
fields.body_html:
“You visit the earth and water it; you greatly enrich it; the river of God is full of water; you provide their grain, for so you prepare the land.” Psalm 65:9-10 Though other seasons may excel in fullness, spring stands out for freshness and beauty. We thank God when harvest time comes and golden grain is ready, but we should also thank Him for spring, which prepares the harvest. April showers bring May flowers, and winter’s cold and wet bring the beauty of summer. God blesses the spring, just as He provides for summer; therefore, we should praise Him all year.

Spiritual spring is a blessed time in a church. Young faith is developing, and we hear joyfully, “We have found the Lord.” Our children spring up like grass and willows by the water. We marvel and ask, “Who are these that come like clouds, like doves to their windows?” During revival, when God brings many to Himself, the church rejoices and can say, “You bless the springing of it” (Psalm 65:9-10, ESV).

I will focus on individual cases. There is a time when grace begins to spring, just as a bud breaks through the cold, hard earth. I want to speak about the blessing given to the green blade of new godliness, to those beginning to hope in the Lord.

1. Work Before the Spring The text shows that God alone must do some work before springing comes, and He works through us too. There is work for us. Before new life appears in a soul, there must be plowing, harrowing, and sowing. The ground must be prepared, but we do not expect to reap immediately.

Blessed be God, sometimes the reaper overtakes the plowman, but not always. In some hearts, God convicts long and deeply; the law digs deeply until every part of the soul is plowed. Conviction reaches the core of the spirit, wounding it. When God works, the soil of the heart is broken by His presence.

Then comes sowing. For springing to occur, something must be sown. After the preacher uses the plow of the law, he applies for the gospel’s seed. Promises of the gospel, doctrines, and clear teaching on free grace and the atonement are scattered like handfuls of seed. Some fall on the path and are lost, but others fall on prepared soil and remain.

Next is the harrowing. We cannot leave the seed after sowing; it must be prayed over. The prayers of the preacher and the church cover the seed, hiding it in the heart of the listener.

I emphasise this to encourage those who have not seen immediate results—not to give up—but also as a warning against expecting a harvest without preparation. Sudden revivals without prayerful labor rarely last. A lasting revival grows from much effort, longing, pleading, and watching. The servant of God preaches whether the people are ready or not, but for great success, hearts must be prepared.

2. Work Beyond Our Power After plowing, sowing, and harrowing, there must come the rain from heaven. “You visit the earth and water it” (Psalm 65:9). Our efforts are in vain without God’s blessing through the Spirit. O Holy Spirit, only You work wonders in the human heart, coming from the Father and Son to fulfill God’s purposes.

Three effects are described: Watering the ridges: Just as rain saturates the ridges, the Spirit moves and influences every part of the heart. Understanding is enlightened, conscience quickened, will controlled, and affections inflamed. We present gospel truth, but only God’s Spirit can truly affect the heart.

Settling the furrows: Heavy rain compacts the soil. Similarly, the Spirit humbles and steadies the soul. A proud, unsettled heart becomes solid and serious. Lofty thoughts and carnal pride are leveled. Genuine humility is a gracious fruit of the Spirit. “A broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise” (Psalm 51:17).

Softening with showers: Man’s heart is naturally hard, like dry soil. The Spirit softens it completely. The once-hard heart feels and responds; tears flow, tenderness grows.

All this is God’s work. God works through us, but He alone sends the rain of grace. Perhaps He is at work in some of you now, though spiritual life has not yet appeared. Your condition may seem sad, but we hope that soon the seed of grace will sprout, and may the Lord bless the springing thereof.

II. In the second place, let us give a brief description of the springing thereof. After the work of the Holy Spirit has been quietly going on for a certain time, as pleases the great Master and Farmer, there begin to appear signs of grace. Remember the apostle’s words: “First the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear” (Mark 4:28). Some are greatly disturbed because they do not see the full grain in the ear in themselves. They suppose that if they were the subjects of divine work, they would be just like certain mature Christians with whom they commune, or about whom they may have read in biographies. Beloved, this is a great mistake. When grace first enters the heart, it is not like a great tree covering acres with its shadow, but like the smallest of seeds, like a mustard seed. When it first rises in the soul, it is not the sun shining at high noon, but the first faint ray of dawn. Are you so simple as to expect the harvest before you have passed through the springing-time? I hope that by describing the earliest stage of Christian experience, you may be able to say, “I have gone as far as that,” and then take comfort from the text: “You bless the springing thereof” (Psalm 65:9-10).

What then is the springing up of piety in the heart? We think it first appears in sincere, earnest desires after salvation. The person is not yet saved in their own view, but longs to be. What was once indifferent is now a matter of intense concern. Once they despised Christians and thought them needlessly earnest, thought religion trivial, and regarded the things of this world as the only substantial matters; but now they are changed. They envy the humblest Christian, and would gladly exchange places with even the poorest believer if they could be assured of a home in heaven.

Worldly things have lost dominion, and spiritual things are uppermost. Once, like many, they cried, “Who will show us any good?” but now they cry, “Lift up the light of your face upon me, O Lord” (Psalm 4:6). Once it was grain and wine that brought comfort, but now it is God alone. Their rock of refuge must be God, for they find no comfort elsewhere. Their holy desires, once fleeting like smoke from a chimney, are now enduring, though not always equally strong.

At times, these desires become a hungering and thirsting after righteousness, yet they are not satisfied and long for a still deeper yearning after heavenly things. These desires are among the first springings of divine life in the soul.

“The springing thereof” next shows itself in prayer. It is now true prayer. Once, the words were a mockery of God, sounds without the heart; but now, though the prayer is such that no human ear might hear it, God approves it, for it is the communication of a spirit to God, not the muttering of lips to an unknown God. The prayers may be short: “Oh!” “Ah!” “Would to God!” “Lord, have mercy on me, a sinner!” and similar brief cries; yet they are prayers. “Behold, he prays” does not refer to length, but even a sigh or tear proves spiritual life. These “groanings that cannot be uttered” are part of “the springing thereof” (Romans 8:26).

There will also appear a love for the means of grace and for God’s house. The Bible, long unread and considered of little more value than an old almanac, is now treated with respect. Even if it brings little immediate comfort and much alarm, it is still the book for the soul, and the reader turns to its pages with hope. In attending God’s house, the believer listens eagerly, hoping for a message from the Lord. Previously, worship was attended as a social duty; now it is for the purpose of finding the Savior. Once there was no more religion in the soul than in a door swinging on its hinges; now the heart enters the house praying, “Lord, meet with my soul,” and if no blessing comes, it leaves sighing, “O that I knew where I might find Him, that I might come even to His seat.” This is one of the blessed signs of “the springing thereof.”

Yet another sign is that the soul begins to have faith in Jesus Christ, at least to some degree. It may not yet bring great joy or peace, but it keeps the heart from despair and prevents it from sinking under the weight of sin. I have known times when no one could perceive faith in me, and I could scarcely perceive it in myself, yet I was bold to say with Peter, “Lord, you know all things; you know that I love you” (John 21:17). What man cannot see, Christ sees. Many are so focused on their small faith that they fail to recognize it; but if they look to Christ and not to their faith, they will see both Christ and their own faith. They may compare themselves to mature believers and feel their faith is too small, but even the tiniest faith to receive Christ is enough. Remember: “To all who received him, he gave the right to become children of God” (John 1:12). Weak faith is still faith, and God blesses “the springing thereof.”

The difficulty often comes from misunderstanding or lack of trust in God. Misunderstanding is like seeing green wheat for the first time and thinking it is just grass. Yet as one becomes familiar with it, it is not strange to see wheat go through stages: first the blade, then the ear, and finally the full grain in the ear. Many newly converted believers feel they are nothing like mature Christians, but they are simply at an earlier stage. One must go through the blade stage before the ear stage, and in the ear stage, there may be doubts about ever reaching the full grain; but in due time, maturity will come. Thank God that you are in Christ at all. Whether faith is large or small, whether you can do much or little for Christ, salvation depends not on what you are but on what Jesus Christ is. Trusting in Him, however small your faith, keeps you as safe as the strongest of the saints.

Yet alongside misunderstanding, there is often unbelief. Not all is excusable ignorance; there is sinful unbelief as well. O sinner, why do you not trust Christ? God gives you His word that those who trust Him are not condemned, yet you may fear that you are. This doubts God’s truth. Be ashamed that you have doubted His promise. All other sins grieve Christ less than the sin of suspecting that He will not forgive, or that He will cast away one who trusts Him. Do not slander His gracious character. “Whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37, ESV). Come in faith, and He will receive you immediately.

I have thus described “the springing thereof.” III. Thirdly, according to the text, there is one who sees this springing: Thou, Lord—“You bless the springing thereof” (Psalm 65:9).

I wish we had keener eyes to see the beginnings of grace in others; through our lack of attentiveness, we let slip many opportunities to help the weak. If a mother tends her own children, she notices the first signs of illness immediately; how much more should we watch tenderly over precious souls. Many young believers may endure weeks or months of unnecessary distress if we who know the Lord are not attentive. Shepherds stay up all night at lambing time to catch and nurse newborn lambs; we, as shepherds for God, should watch over all the newborn in His fold, especially when many are coming to Him, for tender care is needed in the first stages of new life.

Even when we miss it, God sees “the springing thereof.”

Silent, withdrawn souls who dare not speak to anyone, take comfort: God sees your new life. Even if you only think, “I will arise and go to my Father,” He hears you. Even if it is only a desire, He registers it. “You have collected my tears in your bottle; are they not in your book?” (Psalm 56:8).

He watches your return, embraces you, and welcomes you with tender love. Be encouraged that wherever you are—in your room or in secret—God is there. “You God see me” (Genesis 16:13).

“The Lord takes pleasure in those who fear him, in those who hope in his steadfast love” (Psalm 147:11).

Even a small beginning of fear or hope delights Him. “You will perfect the thing that concerns me” (Psalm 138:8). If your soul is concerned about reconciliation with God and having an interest in Christ’s blood, it is only “the springing thereof,” yet He blesses it. “A bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not quench, until he brings justice to victory” (Matthew 12:20). On the other hand, if you have experienced few or no comforts, if the means of grace have brought little consolation, consider that a blessing. Perhaps a bit of self-righteousness remains in you, and until it is gone, you cannot find true joy and peace in Christ.

April showers bring May flowers, and winter’s cold and wet bring the beauty of summer. God blesses the spring, just as He provides for summer; therefore, we should praise Him all year. Spiritual spring is a blessed time in a church. Young faith is developing, and we hear joyfully, “We have found the Lord.” Our children spring up like grass and willows by the water. We marvel and ask, “Who are these that come like clouds, like doves to their windows?” During revival, when God brings many to Himself, the church rejoices and can say, “You bless the springing of it” (Psalm 65:9-10, ESV). I will focus on individual cases. There is a time when grace begins to spring, just as a bud breaks through the cold, hard earth. Work Before the Spring The text shows that God alone must do some work before springing comes, and He works through us too. There is work for us. Before new life appears in a soul, there must be plowing, harrowing, and sowing. The ground must be prepared, but we do not expect to reap immediately. Blessed be God, sometimes the reaper overtakes the plowman, but not always. In some hearts, God convicts long and deeply; the law digs deeply until every part of the soul is plowed. Promises of the gospel, doctrines, and clear teaching on free grace and the atonement are scattered like handfuls of seed.
