fields.title: Farm Laborers
fields.body_html:
“I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth. He who plants and he who waters are one, and each will receive his wages according to his labor. For we are God’s fellow workers. You are God’s field.” 1 Corinthians 3:6–9 I will begin at the end of my text, because I find it to be the easiest way of mapping out what I want to say. We shall first notice that the church is God’s farm: “You are God’s field.” In the margin of the Revised Version we read, “You are God’s tilled ground,” and that is the expression I want to use. “You are God’s tilled ground,” or farm. After speaking about the farm, we will then say a little about the fact that the Lord employs laborers on His estate. And when we have looked at the laborers—poor fellows as they are—we will remember that God Himself is the great worker: “We are God’s fellow workers.”

I. We begin by considering that the church is God’s farm. The Lord has made the church His own by His sovereign choice. He has also secured it for Himself by purchase, having paid an immense price for it. “But the Lord’s portion is his people, Jacob his allotted heritage.” Every acre of God’s farm cost the Savior a bloody sweat—yes, the blood of His own heart. He loved us and gave Himself for us; that is the price He paid. From now on, the church is God’s rightful possession, and He holds the title to it. It is our joy to know that we are not our own; we were bought with a price. The church is God’s farm by choice and by purchase.

And now He has made it His by enclosure. It once lay open like common land, bare and barren, covered with thorns and thistles, and the home of every wild beast; for we were “by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind.” Divine foreknowledge looked over the wasteland, and electing love marked out its portion with a full measure of grace, setting us apart to be the Lord’s own estate forever. In due time, effectual grace came with power and separated us from the rest of mankind, just as fields are hedged and ditched to separate them from open land. Has not the Lord declared that He has chosen His vineyard and fenced it?

“We are a garden walled around, Chosen and made peculiar ground; A little spot, enclosed by grace Out of the world’s wide wilderness.” The Lord has also made this farm clearly His own by cultivating it. What more could He have done for His farm? He has completely changed the nature of the soil. From being barren, He has made it fruitful. He has plowed it, dug it, enriched it, watered it, and planted it with all kinds of flowers and fruits. It has already brought forth many pleasant clusters for Him, and brighter times are coming, when angels will shout at the harvest, and Christ “shall see the fruit of the travail of his soul and be satisfied.”

This farm is preserved by the Lord’s continual protection. Not only did He enclose it and cultivate it by His miraculous power to make it His own farm, but He continually keeps it in His possession.

“I, the Lord, am its keeper; every moment I water it. Lest anyone punish it, I keep it night and day.” If it were not for God’s constant power, its hedges would soon be broken down and wild beasts would devour its fields. Wicked hands are always trying to tear down its walls and lay it waste again so that there would be no true church in the world. But the Lord is jealous for His land and will not allow it to be destroyed. A church would not remain a church for long if God did not preserve it for Himself.

What if God were to say, “And now I will tell you what I will do to my vineyard. I will remove its hedge, and it shall be devoured; I will break down its wall, and it shall be trampled down”? What a wilderness it would become. What does He say?

“Go now to my place that was in Shiloh, where I made my name dwell at first, and see what I did to it because of the evil of my people Israel.” Go to Jerusalem, where once stood the city of His glory and the place of His dwelling—what is left there today? Go to Rome, where Paul once preached the gospel with power—what is it now but the center of idolatry? The Lord can remove the lampstand and leave a place that was bright as day to become dark as night. So God’s farm remains a farm because He is always present in it, preventing it from returning to its former wild state. Almighty power is just as necessary to keep the church under cultivation as it was to reclaim it in the beginning.

Since the church is God’s own farm, He expects to receive a harvest from it. The world is wasteland, and He looks for nothing from it; but we are tilled land, and therefore a harvest is expected from us. Barrenness may suit open moorland, but on a farm it would be a disgrace. Love looks for a return of love; grace given calls for gracious fruit. Watered with the drops of the Savior’s bloody sweat, shall we not bring forth a hundredfold for His praise? Kept by the eternal Spirit of God, shall there not be fruit produced in us for His glory? The Lord’s care for us has involved great cost, labor, and thought. Should there not be a matching return? Should not the Lord have a harvest of obedience, a harvest of holiness, a harvest of usefulness, a harvest of praise?

Should it not be so?

I think some churches forget that increase is expected from every field of the Lord’s farm, because they never have a harvest or even look for one. Farmers do not plow their land or sow their fields for amusement; they mean business. They plow and sow because they want a harvest. If this truth could enter the minds of some believers, surely they would see things differently. But lately it seems as if we think God’s church is not expected to produce anything and exists only for its own comfort and personal benefit. Brothers and sisters, it must not be so. The great Farmer must have some reward for His work. Every field must yield its increase, and the whole estate must bring forth praise to Him.

We join with the bride in the Song in saying, “My vineyard, my very own, is before me; you, O Solomon, may have the thousand, and the keepers of the fruit two hundred.”

But I return to where I started. This farm is, by choice, by purchase, by enclosure, by cultivation, and by preservation, completely the Lord’s. See then how wrong it would be for any of the laborers to call even part of the estate their own.

If a wealthy man owns a large farm, what would he think if the plowman said, “I plow this farm, so it is mine. I will call this field my own”? Or if another said, “I harvested that land last year, so it belongs to me”? What if all the other workers divided the farm among themselves and named the fields after themselves? The owner would quickly remove them all. The farm belongs to its owner, and it should be called by his name. It makes no sense to call it by the names of the workers.

Should insignificant people rob God of His glory? Remember how Paul put it: “What then is Apollos? What is Paul? Servants through whom you believed, as the Lord assigned to each.” “Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?”

The whole church belongs to the One who chose it in His sovereignty, bought it with His blood, fenced it by His grace, cultivated it by His wisdom, and preserved it by His power. There is only one church on earth, and those who love the Lord should remember this. Paul is a worker, Apollos is a worker, Cephas is a worker—but the farm is not Paul’s, not even a small portion of it. No part belongs to Apollos or Cephas, for “you are Christ’s.”

The truth is that in this case the workers belong to the field, not the field to the workers: “For all things are yours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas.” “For what we proclaim is not ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, with ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake.”

II. We now move to our second point: the great Farmer employs laborers. By human agency God ordinarily carries out His plans. He can, if He chooses, by His Holy Spirit work directly in the hearts of men, but that is His work and not ours. We are given instructions like this: “For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the folly of what we preach to save those who believe.” The Master’s command is not, “Sit still and watch the Spirit of God convert the nations,” but, “Go into all the world and proclaim the gospel to the whole creation.”

Look at God’s method in providing food for the world. In answer to the prayer, “Give us this day our daily bread,” He could command the clouds to drop manna every morning at each person’s door. But He knows it is good for us to work, so He uses the hands of the plowman and the sower to supply our needs. God could cultivate His chosen farm, the church, by miracles or by angels, but in great kindness He blesses her through her own sons and daughters. He uses us for our own good, because we who labor in His fields receive far more benefit ourselves than we give. Labor strengthens our spiritual muscles and keeps us spiritually healthy. “To me, though I am the very least of all the saints, this grace was given, to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ.”

Our great Master intends that every laborer on His farm should receive some benefit from it, for it is written, “You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain.” The laborer’s daily bread comes from the soil. Though he works not for himself but for his Master, he still receives his share of food. In the Lord’s storehouse there is seed for the sower and bread for the eater. However selflessly we may serve God in the care of His church, we ourselves share in the fruit. It is great kindness on God’s part that He uses us at all, for we are poor tools at best, and often more of a hindrance than a help.

The laborers employed by God are all engaged in necessary work. Notice: “I planted, Apollos watered.” Who beat a big drum or blew his own trumpet? No one. On God’s farm, no one is kept just for decoration. I have read sermons that seemed meant only for display, because there was not a single grain of the gospel in them. They were like plows without blades, seed drills with no wheat in them, or tools made of butter. I do not believe that God pays wages to people who only walk around His fields to show themselves off. Speakers who display their eloquence in the pulpit are more like wanderers picking up chickens than faithful laborers producing a crop for their Master.

Many church members live as if their only job on the farm were to pick blackberries or gather wildflowers. They are quick to criticize how others plow and mow, but they will not lift a hand to work themselves. Come now, my friends. Why do you stand idle all day? “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few.” Those who think themselves more refined than others, if you are truly Christians, must not walk around proudly and look down on those who are working hard. If you do, I will say that you have mistaken your master. Perhaps you think you serve someone who values appearance over results, but our great Lord is practical, and on His estate His laborers do necessary work.

When you and I preach or teach, we should ask ourselves, “What good will this do? I am about to teach a difficult subject—will it truly help anyone? I have chosen a complex theological point— will it serve a useful purpose?” A laborer may work very hard on his own idea and yet accomplish nothing useful. Some sermons only show minor differences in arguments, and what good does that do? Suppose we sow fields with sawdust or sprinkle them with perfume—what would that accomplish? Will God bless our moral essays, polished speeches, and elegant phrases? We must aim at usefulness. As workers together with God, we must focus on work that truly matters. “I planted,” says one—and that is good, for planting must be done. “I watered,” says another—and that also is good and necessary. Let each of you be able to give a solid report, but let no one be satisfied with mere performance, public speaking, or organizing entertainments.

On the Lord’s farm there is a division of labor. Even Paul did not say, “I planted and watered.”

No—Paul planted. And Apollos did not say, “I planted as well as watered.” It was enough for him to water. No one has every gift. How foolish it is when people say, “I enjoy this preacher because he builds up believers in doctrine, but when he was away I could not benefit from the other preacher because he focused on converting sinners.” Yes, he was planting. You have already been planted; you do not need to be planted again. You should be thankful that others are receiving the benefit. “For here the saying holds true, ‘One sows and another reaps.’” Instead of complaining that the plowman did not bring a sickle, you should pray that he has strength to plow deeply and break up hard hearts.

On God’s farm there is unity of purpose among the workers. “He who plants and he who waters are one.” One Master employs them. Though He sends them at different times and to different parts of the field, they are united in one purpose—to work toward one harvest.

In England we do not fully understand watering, because farmers there cannot water all their land.

But in the East, farmers water almost every part of their fields. Without irrigation there would be no crop. In places like Italy, Egypt, or Palestine, there are wells, pumps, wheels, buckets, channels, small streams, and pipes that carry water to every plant. Without this, the intense heat would dry everything up. Planting requires wisdom; watering requires just as much. To bring these two together, workers must be united in mind. It is harmful when workers are at cross purposes and work against each other. This is especially harmful in the church. How can I plant successfully if my helper will not water what I have planted? Or what good is watering if nothing has been planted? Farming fails when foolish people argue over it, because from sowing to reaping it is one continuous work. Let us work together all our days, for division leads to barrenness.

We are told in our text that all the laborers together are nothing. “So neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything.” Workers are nothing without their Master. All the laborers on a farm could not manage it without someone in charge, and all the preachers and Christian workers in the world can accomplish nothing unless God is with them.

Every laborer on God’s farm has received his abilities from God. No one knows how to plant or water souls unless the Lord teaches him daily. These holy gifts are acts of free grace. All laborers must work under God’s direction, or they work in vain. Without the Spirit’s guidance, they would not know when or how to work, and without His help they cannot even think a good thought. All workers must receive their seed from God, or they will sow weeds instead of wheat. All good seed comes from God’s storehouse. If we preach, it must be the true Word of God, or nothing lasting will result.

Even the strength to sow comes from the Master. We cannot preach unless God is with us. A sermon is empty talk unless the Holy Spirit gives it life. “The preparation of the heart belongs to man, but the answer of the tongue is from the Lord.” When the good seed is sown, the entire outcome depends on God. If He withholds dew and rain, the seed will not grow. If He does not shine upon it, the green ear will not ripen. The human heart will remain barren—even if Paul himself were preaching—unless the Holy Spirit works with him and blesses the Word. Since the growth comes from God alone, keep the workers in their proper place. Do not think too highly of us, for after we have done everything, we are unworthy servants.

Yet, though Scripture says the workers are nothing, it also says they will be rewarded. God works our good works in us and then rewards us for them. “Each will receive his wages according to his labor.” The reward is based not on success, but on effort. Many discouraged workers can find comfort in this. You are not paid by results but by faithful labor. You may have hard soil to plow or difficult ground to sow, with stones, birds, thorns, travelers, and scorching sun working against you—but you are not responsible for those things. Your reward is according to your work.

“One sows and another reaps,” but the one who reaps does not receive all the reward; the one who sowed will share in the joy. Workers may be considered nothing, but they will enter into the joy of their Lord.

Together, according to the text, the workers have been successful, and that is part of their reward.

When faithful workers labor in the right spirit, God blesses them. That blessing is a great part of the reward.

If you think it is easy to win a soul, try it. Without divine help, you might as well try to create a world. You cannot create a fly—how can you create a new heart and a right spirit? Regeneration is a great mystery beyond your power. “The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. We can declare the truth of God, but applying that truth to the heart and conscience is another matter entirely.

Experience teaches us this. It is also the Lord’s work to keep the seed alive once it grows. We think we have converts, but often we are disappointed. Anyone who leads a large church and cares deeply for souls will soon be convinced that unless God works, nothing will be accomplished—no conversion, no sanctification, no perseverance, no glory to God, no satisfaction for the suffering of the Savior—unless the Lord is with us. “Apart from me you can do nothing.”

If he does his work better than I do mine, should I be jealous?

Do you remember that on one occasion the disciples could not cast out a demon? That should have humbled them. Yet soon after, they saw someone casting out demons in Christ’s name, and they tried to stop him because he was not part of their group. They could not cast out the demon themselves, yet they tried to stop someone who could. Some groups are winning souls, but because they do not do it in our style, we disapprove. Instead of criticizing, let us encourage everyone who stands with Christ. “Yet wisdom is justified by her deeds.” Workers should be satisfied with a new plowman if their Master approves of him. Have you forgotten that you are nothing? “So neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything.” A teacher may come filled with gospel truth to comfort believers, but if he does not come in full dependence on God, he too is nothing. Power belongs to God. Man is empty and his words are wind; power and wisdom belong to God alone. If we remain humble, our Lord will use us. But if we exalt ourselves, He will leave us to our nothingness. This truth also gives dignity to everyone who works in God’s field. My heart is lifted up with joy at these words: “For we are God’s fellow workers.” We are simple workers on His farm, yet we work with Him. Does the Lord truly work with us?

We know He does by the results that follow. “My Father is working until now, and I am working.”

That is true for all God’s children. When you serve Him with all your heart, God is with you. When you speak to your class about Jesus, God speaks through you. When you stop a stranger and tell him about salvation by faith, Christ speaks through you just as He spoke to the woman at the well.

When you preach forgiveness through the atoning blood in the open air, it is the God of Peter testifying about His Son, just as He did on the day of Pentecost.

Finally, this truth should drive us to our knees. Since we are nothing without God, let us cry out to Him for help in this holy work. Let both sower and reaper pray together, or they will never rejoice together. If blessing is withheld, it is because we have not asked and expected it. Fellow workers, let us come to the throne of grace, and we shall see the reapers return with their sheaves, though they may have gone out weeping when they sowed.

To our Father, who is the Farmer, be all glory, forever and ever. Amen.

Together, according to the text, the workers have been successful, and that is part of their reward. “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.” Often in prayer we say, “A Paul may plant, an Apollos may water, but it is all in vain unless God gives the growth.” That is true. But another truth is often overlooked: when Paul plants and Apollos waters, God does give the growth. We do not labor in vain. There would be no growth without God, but we are not without God. When faithful workers labor in the right spirit, God blesses them. That blessing is a great part of the reward. III. Now we return to the main point: God Himself is the great Worker. He may use whatever laborers He chooses, but the growth comes from Him alone. You know this is true in natural farming. The most skilled farmer cannot make wheat germinate, grow, and ripen. He cannot even protect a field until harvest, because many dangers threaten it. Just when a farmer expects a harvest, blight or disease may destroy it. God must give the growth. If anyone depends on God, it is the farmer. Through him, we all depend on God year by year for our food. “Even the king himself is served by the field.” God gives the increase in the barn and the haystack, and it is even more so in the spiritual field. If you think it is easy to win a soul, try it. Without divine help, you might as well try to create a world. You cannot create a fly—how can you create a new heart and a right spirit? Regeneration is a great mystery beyond your power. “The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.” What can you or I do in this matter? It is beyond us. We can declare the truth of God, but applying that truth to the heart and conscience is another matter entirely. I have preached Jesus Christ with all my heart, yet I know I have never produced saving results in an unregenerate person unless the Spirit of God opened the heart and planted the living seed of truth within it. Experience teaches us this. It is also the Lord’s work to keep the seed alive once it grows. We think we have converts, but often we are disappointed. Many are like blossoms on apple trees—beautiful but fruitless. Others are like small apples that fall before they mature. Anyone who leads a large church and cares deeply for souls will soon be convinced that unless God works, nothing will be accomplished—no conversion, no sanctification, no perseverance, no glory to God, no satisfaction for the suffering of the Savior—unless the Lord is with us. “Apart from me you can do nothing.” From this truth, I draw several practical lessons. First, if the entire farm of the church belongs to the great Master and workers are nothing without Him, this should promote unity among all He employs. If we serve one Master, let us not quarrel. It is sad when we cannot rejoice at good being done by those from other denominations who work differently from us. If a new worker arrives and uses different tools, should I become his enemy? If he does his work better than I do mine, should I be jealous? Do you remember that on one occasion the disciples could not cast out a demon? That should have humbled them. Yet soon after, they saw someone casting out demons in Christ’s name, and they tried to stop him because he was not part of their group. They could not cast out the demon themselves, yet they tried to stop someone who could. Some groups are winning souls, but because they do not do it in our style, we disapprove. They may have unusual methods, but they truly bring souls to Christ—and that is what matters most. Instead of criticizing, let us encourage everyone who stands with Christ. “Yet wisdom is justified by her deeds.” Workers should be satisfied with a new plowman if their Master approves of him. If the great Lord has employed you, it is not my place to question His choice. Can I help you? Can I show you how to improve? Or can you help me improve? That is how workers should treat each other. This truth should also make all workers deeply dependent on God. Are you about to preach, young man? “Yes, I am going to accomplish great things.” Are you? Have you forgotten that you are nothing? “So neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything.” A teacher may come filled with gospel truth to comfort believers, but if he does not come in full dependence on God, he too is nothing. Power belongs to God. Man is empty and his words are wind; power and wisdom belong to God alone. If we remain humble, our Lord will use us. But if we exalt ourselves, He will leave us to our nothingness. This truth also gives dignity to everyone who works in God’s field. My heart is lifted up with joy at these words: “For we are God’s fellow workers.” We are simple workers on His farm, yet we work with Him. Does the Lord truly work with us? We know He does by the results that follow. “My Father is working until now, and I am working.” That is true for all God’s children. When you serve Him with all your heart, God is with you. When you speak to your class about Jesus, God speaks through you. When you stop a stranger and tell him about salvation by faith, Christ speaks through you just as He spoke to the woman at the well. When you preach forgiveness through the atoning blood in the open air, it is the God of Peter testifying about His Son, just as He did on the day of Pentecost. Finally, this truth should drive us to our knees. Since we are nothing without God, let us cry out to Him for help in this holy work. Let both sower and reaper pray together, or they will never rejoice together. If blessing is withheld, it is because we have not asked and expected it. Fellow workers, let us come to the throne of grace, and we shall see the reapers return with their sheaves, though they may have gone out weeping when they sowed. To our Father, who is the Farmer, be all glory, forever and ever. Amen.

fields.title: What The Farm Laborers Can Do And What They Cannot Do
fields.body_html:
“And he said, ‘The kingdom of God is as if a man should scatter seed on the ground. He sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how. The earth produces by itself, first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. But when the grain is ripe, at once he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come.’” Mark 4:26–29 (ESV) There is a lesson here for those who are laborers together with God. It is a parable for all who are involved in the kingdom of God. It will be of little value to those who remain in the kingdom of darkness, because they are not called to sow good seed. “But to the wicked God says: ‘What right have you to recite my statutes or take my covenant on your lips?’” But all who are commissioned to scatter seed for the Royal Farmer will be glad to understand how the harvest is being prepared for the One they serve. Listen, then, you who sow beside all waters; you who diligently seek to fill the storehouses of heaven—listen, and may the Spirit of God speak to you as much as you are able to receive it.

We shall first learn from our text what we can do and what we cannot do. “The kingdom of God is as if a man should scatter seed on the ground.” This is what the gracious worker can do. “He sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how.” This is what he cannot do. Once the seed is sown, it is beyond human control, and a person can neither make it sprout nor grow. Yet before long the worker appears again: “But when the grain is ripe, at once he puts in the sickle.” We can reap in due season, and it is both our duty and our privilege to do so. You see, then, that there is a place for the worker at the beginning; though there is no place for him in the middle process, another opportunity is given to him later when what he sowed has produced fruit.

Notice, then, that we can sow. Anyone who has received the knowledge of the grace of God in their heart can teach others. I use the word “man” to include all who know the Lord, whether male or female. We cannot all teach in the same way, for we do not all have the same gifts; to one is given one talent and to another ten. Neither do we all have the same opportunities, for one lives in obscurity and another has far-reaching influence. Yet there is not within the family of God a single small hand that cannot drop its own little seed into the ground. There is not a person among us who needs to stand idle, for work suited to their strength is waiting for them. There is not a saved woman who is left without a holy task; let her do it and receive the approving word, “She has done what she could.”

We should never complain that we cannot do everything if God allows us to do this one thing; for sowing the good seed is work that requires all our wisdom, strength, love, and care. Holy seed-sowing should be embraced as our highest calling, and it is not an unworthy pursuit for the noblest life. You will need heavenly teaching so that you may carefully choose good wheat and keep it free from the weeds of error. You will need guidance to remove from it your own thoughts and opinions, for these may not align with the mind of God. People are not saved by our words but by God’s Word. We need grace to understand the gospel correctly and to teach all of it. To different people we must wisely bring forward that part of God’s Word that best speaks to their conscience, for much may depend on a word spoken at the right time.

Having selected the seed, we will have plenty of work if we go out and sow it everywhere, for every day brings opportunity and every gathering presents an opening. “In the morning sow your seed, and at evening withhold not your hand.” “Blessed are you who sow beside all waters.” Wise sowers recognise favourable opportunities and gladly seize them. There are times when sowing would clearly be wasted because the soil is not ready. After a shower, or before one, or at whatever time the experienced farmer knows is best, that is when we must be active. While we are to serve God at all times, there are seasons when speaking would be like throwing pearls before pigs, and there are other times when silence would be a serious sin. Those who are lazy during plowing and sowing season are truly lazy, because they not only waste the day but lose the year.

If you watch for souls and make use of favorable hours and softened moments, you will not complain about a lack of opportunity. Even if you are never called to water or to reap, your role is large enough if you faithfully fulfill the work of the sower.

Though it may seem small to teach the simple truth of the gospel, it is essential. How are people to hear without someone teaching them? Servants of God, the seed of the Word is not like thistle-down carried by every wind. The wheat of the kingdom requires a human hand to sow it, and without such action it will not enter people’s hearts or bring forth fruit to the glory of God. The preaching of the gospel is necessary in every age. God grant that our country may never be deprived of it. Even if the Lord were to send a famine of bread and water, may He never send a famine of His Word. “So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ.”

Scatter the seed of the kingdom, then, for this is essential to the harvest.

This seed must be sown often, for many enemies oppose the wheat, and if you do not repeat your sowing you may never see a harvest. The seed must be sown everywhere, for there are no parts of the world you can afford to leave untouched, hoping they will produce fruit on their own. You must not leave the rich and educated thinking the gospel will surely reach them without effort, for pride often keeps them from God. You must not leave the poor and uneducated thinking they will naturally sense their need for Christ. They may sink lower and lower unless you lift them with the gospel. No group of people, no type of mind, may be neglected. Everywhere we must preach the Word, in season and out of season. I have heard that Captain Cook, the well-known explorer, carried a small packet of English seeds wherever he traveled and scattered them wherever he landed, leaving flowers and herbs from his homeland across the world. Imitate him wherever you go; sow spiritual seed in every place your foot steps.

Now let us consider what you cannot do. After the seed has left your hand, you cannot cause it to produce life. You cannot make it grow, because you do not know how it grows. The text says, “He sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how.” What is beyond our understanding is certainly beyond our power. Can you make a seed germinate? You may place it in warmth and moisture so that it swells and breaks open, but the act of germination itself is beyond you. How does it happen? We do not know. After it begins to grow, can you make it develop into leaf and stem? No. When the blade becomes the ear, can you ripen it? It will ripen, but not by your power.

You cannot participate in the inner process, though you may create favorable conditions. Life is a mystery. Growth is a mystery. Ripening is a mystery. These are sealed fountains beyond human control. This is equally true of the life of God in the heart. The Word enters the soul and takes root—we do not know how. Naturally, people resist the Word, yet it enters and transforms them so that they come to love it. Their nature is renewed so that instead of producing sin, it produces repentance, faith, and love. We do not know how. How the Spirit of God works on the human mind, how He creates a new heart and right spirit, how we are born again to a living hope—we cannot explain. The Holy Spirit enters us; we do not see Him, hear Him, or feel His touch physically, yet He accomplishes a powerful work within us that becomes evident over time. We know His work is described as a new creation, a resurrection, a making alive from the dead; but these words only cover our ignorance of the method. Since we do not understand how He works, we certainly cannot take over His work. We cannot create, we cannot give life, we cannot transform, we cannot regenerate, we cannot save.

When God has carried out this hidden work in the growth of the seed, what follows? We can reap the ripe grain. After a time, God the Holy Spirit uses His servants again. When the living seed has produced first the blade of thought, then the green ear of conviction, and finally faith—like full grain in the ear—the Christian worker returns to service, for he can reap. “But when the grain is ripe, at once he puts in the sickle.” This does not refer to the final day of judgment, which is not within the scope of this parable. It clearly refers to a human sower and reaper. The reaping Jesus speaks of here is the kind He mentioned when He said to His disciples, “Lift up your eyes, and see that the fields are white for harvest.” After sowing in the hearts of the Samaritans and seeing faith begin to appear, the Lord Jesus declared, “The fields are white for harvest.” The apostle says, “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.” Our Lord said to His disciples, “I sent you to reap that for which you did not labor.” Is there not also this promise: “And let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up”?

Christian workers begin their harvest work by watching for signs of faith in Christ. They are eager to see the first blade and glad to see the ripening ear. They may hope that people believe, but they long to be sure. When they are persuaded that faith is truly present, they begin to encourage, congratulate, and comfort. They know the new believer needs to be gathered into the barn of Christian fellowship to protect them from many dangers.

No wise farmer leaves ripe grain exposed to hail, mildew, or birds. Likewise, no true believer should remain outside the fellowship of the church. They should be welcomed into the church with the joy that accompanies bringing in sheaves. The worker watches carefully, and when the right time comes, he gathers in the converts so they may be cared for by the church, separated from the world, shielded from temptation, and kept for the Lord. He does this promptly, because the text says, “at once he puts in the sickle.” He does not delay in cold suspicion. When faith is evident, he encourages open confession and says to the new believer, “Have you confessed your faith? Is it not time to do so openly? Has not Jesus commanded the believer to be baptized? If you love Him, keep His commandments.” He does not rest until the convert is brought into fellowship with the faithful. For our work is only half complete when people are made disciples and baptized. We must then encourage, instruct, strengthen, comfort, and help them in every difficulty. What does the Savior say? “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you.”

Notice, then, the scope and limit of our work. We can bring the truth to people, but the Lord alone can bless it. The living and growing of the Word within the soul belongs to God alone. When that hidden work of growth is complete, we can gather the saved into the church. For Christ to be formed in a person—the hope of glory—is not our work; that remains God’s. But when Christ has indeed been formed in them, to recognize His image and say, “Come in, you who are blessed by my Father. Inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world,” is our duty and joy. Creating divine life belongs to God; nurturing it belongs to us. Causing hidden life to grow belongs to the Lord; recognizing its development and gathering it in belongs to the faithful, just as it is written, “But when the grain is ripe, at once he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come.”

This, then, is our first lesson: we see what we can do and what we cannot do. II. Our second heading is similar to the first and concerns what we can know and what we cannot know.

First, what we can know. We can know that when we have sown the good seed of the Word, it will grow, because God has promised it. Not every grain in every place—for some will be taken by birds, some destroyed by worms, and some scorched by the sun—but as a general rule, God’s Word will not fail. As it is written, “so shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose, and shall succeed in the thing for which I sent it.” This we can know. We can also know that once the seed takes root it will continue to grow. It is not a dream or a passing image that disappears, but a living force that moves from the blade to the ear, and under God’s blessing develops into true salvation, becoming like “the full grain in the ear.” With God’s help and blessing, our work of teaching will lead not only to thought and conviction but to conversion and eternal life.

We also know, because we are told, that the reason for this growth is chiefly that there is life in the Word itself. In the Word of God there is life, for it is written, “For the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword.” It is also called “the living and abiding word of God.” Living seeds naturally grow, and the reason the Word of God grows in people’s hearts is that it is the living Word of the living God. Where the word of a king is, there is power. We know this because Scripture teaches it. Is it not written, “Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth”?

Moreover, the earth, which in this parable represents the person, “produces by itself.” We must be careful in explaining this, for human hearts do not produce faith on their own; they are like hard rock where seed would perish. What it means is this: just as the earth, under the blessing of dew and rain and by God’s hidden working upon it, becomes ready to receive and hold the seed, so the human heart is made ready to receive and embrace the gospel of Jesus Christ. An awakened heart desires exactly what the Word of God provides. Moved by divine influence, the soul embraces the truth, and the truth embraces the soul, so that it lives within the heart and is energized there. A person’s love receives the love of God; a person’s faith, worked in them by the Spirit of God, believes the truth of God; a person’s hope, produced in them by the Holy Spirit, takes hold of the promises revealed. In this way, the heavenly seed grows in the soil of the soul. The life does not come from the one who preaches the Word; it is placed within the Word by the Holy Spirit. The life is not in your hand, but in the heart that is led by the Spirit to receive the truth. Salvation does not come from the preacher’s authority, but through the hearer’s personal conviction, personal faith, and personal love. This much we can know, and is it not enough for practical purposes?

Still, there is something we cannot know—a secret into which we cannot look. As I have said before, you cannot look inside a person and see exactly how the truth takes hold of the heart, or how the heart takes hold of the truth. Some people have examined their own feelings so closely that they have become discouraged and spiritually blind. Others have examined the feelings of young believers so strictly that they have harmed them rather than helped them. In God’s work there is more room for faith than for sight. The heavenly seed grows in secret. It must be buried out of sight, or there will be no harvest. Even if you kept the seed above ground and it sprouted, you still could not see the inner life force that moves it. “The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.” Explain the new birth? Experience it, and you will know what it is.

There are secrets into which we cannot enter, because their light is too bright for human eyes. You cannot become all-knowing, for you are a creature, not the Creator. There will always be a realm that is not only unknown but unknowable to you. Your knowledge goes so far and no further. You may thank God for this, because it leaves room for faith and gives reason for prayer. Cry out to the Great Worker to do what you cannot do, so that when you see people saved you may give the Lord all the glory.

III. Thirdly, our text tells us what we may expect if we work for God, and what we may not expect.

According to this parable, we may expect to see fruit. The farmer scatters his seed, the seed sprouts and grows, and he naturally expects a harvest. I wish I could stir up the expectations of Christian workers, for I fear many work without faith. If you planted a garden or field and sowed seed, you would be greatly surprised and grieved if nothing came up. Yet many Christians seem content to work without expecting results. This is a miserable way to work—drawing up empty buckets year after year. Surely, either I must see some result of my labor and rejoice, or, if I see none, I must be deeply grieved if I am truly serving my Master. We ought to expect results. If we expected more, we would see more. Lack of expectation has been a great cause of failure among God’s workers.

But we must not expect every seed we sow to spring up immediately. Sometimes—glory be to God—the moment the Word is spoken people are converted, and the reaper overtakes the sower.

But it is not always so. Some have labored faithfully for years and seen little visible result, yet at last the harvest has come—a harvest that would never have been gathered if they had not persevered.

I believe this world will be converted to Christ—but not today, nor tomorrow, perhaps not for many generations. The sowing of centuries is not lost; it is moving toward its great conclusion.

Mushrooms may appear quickly, but an oak forest requires generations. It is ours to sow and to hope for quick reaping, yet we must remember that “Be patient, therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord. See how the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient about it, until it receives the early and the late rains.” So we must expect results, but not lose heart if we must wait.

We should expect to see the good seed grow, but not always in our preferred way. Like children, we are often impatient. A boy plants seeds one day and digs them up the next to see if they are growing. Nothing will come of that, because he will not leave them alone long enough. So it is with impatient workers. They want immediate visible results, or they begin to distrust the Word.

Some preachers are so hurried that they allow no time for reflection, no space to count the cost, no opportunity for people to consider their ways and turn to the Lord with full commitment. Every other seed is allowed time to grow, but the seed of the Word must grow instantly before their eyes or they think nothing has happened. In their eagerness, they overheat the seed with fanaticism and destroy it. They convince people they are converted when they are not, and so prevent them from coming to a true saving knowledge of the truth. Some are kept from salvation because they are told they are already saved and are filled with pride before their hearts are truly broken. Perhaps if they had been taught to look for something deeper, they would not have been satisfied with shallow soil. Their growth appears rapid, but so is their decline. Let us confidently expect growth, but let us expect it in order: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear.

We may also expect the seed to ripen. By God’s grace our work will lead to genuine faith in those upon whom He works by His Word and Spirit. But we must not expect perfection at the beginning.

Many mistakes have been made here. A young person comes under conviction, and a well-meaning, experienced believer questions them deeply and severely. He looks for full maturity at once. He enters the field early in the season and complains that he sees no grain, only grass. Of course he sees no grain yet. He refuses to accept the blade as evidence of life and insists on full maturity immediately. If he had looked for the blade, he would have found it and been encouraged.

For my part, I am thankful to see even a faint desire, a weak longing, a sense of uneasiness about sin, or a craving for mercy. Should we not allow things to begin small?

Notice the blade of desire, then watch for more. Soon conviction and resolve will follow, and then a small faith—like a mustard seed—but certain to grow. “For who has despised the day of small things?” Do not examine a newborn believer to see if they are fully sound in doctrine according to your standards. They are far from that, and difficult questions will only trouble them. Speak to them about their sin and Christ as Savior, and in doing so you will water the growing ear until it becomes full grain. It may not look like wheat yet, but later you will say, “That is wheat indeed. I recognize it. This is a true ear of grain, and I gladly gather it among my Master’s sheaves.” If you cut down the blade, how will the ear grow? Expect grace in your converts, but do not expect glory yet.

IV. Finally, we consider what kind of sleep workers may take and what kind they may not take.

The man in the parable “sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how.” Farming is said to be a good trade because it continues while the farmer sleeps. Our work is similar. When we serve our Master by sowing good seed, it grows even while we sleep.

How may a faithful worker for Christ rightly sleep? First, he may sleep with restful confidence.

Are you afraid that Christ’s kingdom will fail? Who asked you to worry for the ark of the Lord?

Are you anxious that the Almighty’s purposes will collapse? Such anxiety dishonors God. Will omnipotence be defeated? You would do better to sleep than to interfere like Uzzah. Rest patiently.

God’s purposes will stand. His kingdom will come. His chosen people will be saved. Christ “shall see of the travail of his soul and be satisfied.” Take the sweet sleep God gives to His beloved—the sleep of full confidence—like Jesus sleeping in the stern of the boat during the storm. God’s cause has never been in danger and never will be. The seed is secured by omnipotence and will produce a harvest. “In returning and rest you shall be saved; in quietness and in trust shall be your strength.”

Wait for the harvest, for the pleasure of the Lord shall prosper in the hand of Jesus.

Take also the sleep of joyful expectation that leads to a hopeful waking. Rise each morning believing that the Lord rules over all things for His purposes and for the good of those who trust Him. Expect blessing during the day, and go to bed calmly trusting Him for tomorrow. If you never rest, you will not rise refreshed and ready to work. If you spent all night anxiously worrying, you would be unfit for service in the morning. So rest and be at peace, and work steadily and calmly, because the matter is safe in the Lord’s hands. “It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep.”

Rest also because you have consciously committed your work into God’s hands. After speaking the Word, go to God in prayer, entrust the matter to Him, and do not fret. It cannot be in better hands. Leave it with Him who “works all things according to the counsel of his will.”

But do not sleep in carelessness. The farmer sows seed, but he does not forget it. He repairs fences, drives away birds, removes weeds, and guards against flooding. He does not watch the seed grow, but he has plenty else to do. He sleeps in proper measure and season, not like a lazy person. He never sleeps in indifference or inactivity, for every season demands work. One field is sown, but another waits. One crop is reaped, but another must be threshed and winnowed. A farmer’s work is never finished. His sleep is only a pause to give strength for continued labor. The parable teaches us to do all that lies within our responsibility, but not to intrude into God’s work. In teaching, we must labor diligently; but regarding the secret working of truth in the human heart, we must pray and rest, looking to the Lord for inward power.
