We need grace to understand the gospel correctly and to teach all of it. To different people we must wisely bring forward that part of God’s Word that best speaks to their conscience, for much may depend on a word spoken at the right time. Having selected the seed, we will have plenty of work if we go out and sow it everywhere, for every day brings opportunity and every gathering presents an opening. “In the morning sow your seed, and at evening withhold not your hand.” “Blessed are you who sow beside all waters.” Wise sowers recognise favourable opportunities and gladly seize them. There are times when sowing would clearly be wasted because the soil is not ready. After a shower, or before one, or at whatever time the experienced farmer knows is best, that is when we must be active. While we are to serve God at all times, there are seasons when speaking would be like throwing pearls before pigs, and there are other times when silence would be a serious sin. Those who are lazy during plowing and sowing season are truly lazy, because they not only waste the day but lose the year. If you watch for souls and make use of favorable hours and softened moments, you will not complain about a lack of opportunity. Even if you are never called to water or to reap, your role is large enough if you faithfully fulfill the work of the sower. Though it may seem small to teach the simple truth of the gospel, it is essential. How are people to hear without someone teaching them? Servants of God, the seed of the Word is not like thistle-down carried by every wind. The wheat of the kingdom requires a human hand to sow it, and without such action it will not enter people’s hearts or bring forth fruit to the glory of God. The preaching of the gospel is necessary in every age. God grant that our country may never be deprived of it. Even if the Lord were to send a famine of bread and water, may He never send a famine of His Word. “So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ.” Scatter the seed of the kingdom, then, for this is essential to the harvest. This seed must be sown often, for many enemies oppose the wheat, and if you do not repeat your sowing you may never see a harvest. The seed must be sown everywhere, for there are no parts of the world you can afford to leave untouched, hoping they will produce fruit on their own. You must not leave the rich and educated thinking the gospel will surely reach them without effort, for pride often keeps them from God. You must not leave the poor and uneducated thinking they will naturally sense their need for Christ. They may sink lower and lower unless you lift them with the gospel. No group of people, no type of mind, may be neglected. Everywhere we must preach the Word, in season and out of season. I have heard that Captain Cook, the well-known explorer, carried a small packet of English seeds wherever he traveled and scattered them wherever he landed, leaving flowers and herbs from his homeland across the world. Imitate him wherever you go; sow spiritual seed in every place your foot steps. Now let us consider what you cannot do. After the seed has left your hand, you cannot cause it to produce life. You cannot make it grow, because you do not know how it grows. The text says, “He sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how.” What is beyond our understanding is certainly beyond our power. Can you make a seed germinate? You may place it in warmth and moisture so that it swells and breaks open, but the act of germination itself is beyond you. How does it happen? We do not know. After it begins to grow, can you make it develop into leaf and stem? No. When the blade becomes the ear, can you ripen it? It will ripen, but not by your power. You cannot participate in the inner process, though you may create favorable conditions. Life is a mystery. Growth is a mystery. Ripening is a mystery. These are sealed fountains beyond human control. This is equally true of the life of God in the heart. The Word enters the soul and takes root—we do not know how. Naturally, people resist the Word, yet it enters and transforms them so that they come to love it. Their nature is renewed so that instead of producing sin, it produces repentance, faith, and love. We do not know how. How the Spirit of God works on the human mind, how He creates a new heart and right spirit, how we are born again to a living hope—we cannot explain. The Holy Spirit enters us; we do not see Him, hear Him, or feel His touch physically, yet He accomplishes a powerful work within us that becomes evident over time. We know His work is described as a new creation, a resurrection, a making alive from the dead; but these words only cover our ignorance of the method. Since we do not understand how He works, we certainly cannot take over His work. We cannot create, we cannot give life, we cannot transform, we cannot regenerate, we cannot save. When God has carried out this hidden work in the growth of the seed, what follows? We can reap the ripe grain. After a time, God the Holy Spirit uses His servants again. When the living seed has produced first the blade of thought, then the green ear of conviction, and finally faith—like full grain in the ear—the Christian worker returns to service, for he can reap. “But when the grain is ripe, at once he puts in the sickle.” This does not refer to the final day of judgment, which is not within the scope of this parable. It clearly refers to a human sower and reaper. The reaping Jesus speaks of here is the kind He mentioned when He said to His disciples, “Lift up your eyes, and see that the fields are white for harvest.” After sowing in the hearts of the Samaritans and seeing faith begin to appear, the Lord Jesus declared, “The fields are white for harvest.” The apostle says, “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.” Our Lord said to His disciples, “I sent you to reap that for which you did not labor.” Is there not also this promise: “And let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up”? Christian workers begin their harvest work by watching for signs of faith in Christ. They are eager to see the first blade and glad to see the ripening ear. They may hope that people believe, but they long to be sure. When they are persuaded that faith is truly present, they begin to encourage, congratulate, and comfort. They know the new believer needs to be gathered into the barn of Christian fellowship to protect them from many dangers. No wise farmer leaves ripe grain exposed to hail, mildew, or birds. Likewise, no true believer should remain outside the fellowship of the church. They should be welcomed into the church with the joy that accompanies bringing in sheaves. The worker watches carefully, and when the right time comes, he gathers in the converts so they may be cared for by the church, separated from the world, shielded from temptation, and kept for the Lord. He does this promptly, because the text says, “at once he puts in the sickle.” He does not delay in cold suspicion. When faith is evident, he encourages open confession and says to the new believer, “Have you confessed your faith? Is it not time to do so openly? Has not Jesus commanded the believer to be baptized? If you love Him, keep His commandments.” He does not rest until the convert is brought into fellowship with the faithful. For our work is only half complete when people are made disciples and baptized. We must then encourage, instruct, strengthen, comfort, and help them in every difficulty. What does the Savior say? “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you.” Notice, then, the scope and limit of our work. We can bring the truth to people, but the Lord alone can bless it. The living and growing of the Word within the soul belongs to God alone. When that hidden work of growth is complete, we can gather the saved into the church. For Christ to be formed in a person—the hope of glory—is not our work; that remains God’s. But when Christ has indeed been formed in them, to recognize His image and say, “Come in, you who are blessed by my Father. Inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world,” is our duty and joy. Creating divine life belongs to God; nurturing it belongs to us. Causing hidden life to grow belongs to the Lord; recognizing its development and gathering it in belongs to the faithful, just as it is written, “But when the grain is ripe, at once he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come.” This, then, is our first lesson: we see what we can do and what we cannot do. II. Our second heading is similar to the first and concerns what we can know and what we cannot know. First, what we can know. We can know that when we have sown the good seed of the Word, it will grow, because God has promised it. Not every grain in every place—for some will be taken by birds, some destroyed by worms, and some scorched by the sun—but as a general rule, God’s Word will not fail. As it is written, “so shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose, and shall succeed in the thing for which I sent it.” This we can know. We can also know that once the seed takes root it will continue to grow. It is not a dream or a passing image that disappears, but a living force that moves from the blade to the ear, and under God’s blessing develops into true salvation, becoming like “the full grain in the ear.” With God’s help and blessing, our work of teaching will lead not only to thought and conviction but to conversion and eternal life. We also know, because we are told, that the reason for this growth is chiefly that there is life in the Word itself. In the Word of God there is life, for it is written, “For the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword.” It is also called “the living and abiding word of God.” Living seeds naturally grow, and the reason the Word of God grows in people’s hearts is that it is the living Word of the living God. Where the word of a king is, there is power. We know this because Scripture teaches it. Is it not written, “Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth”? Moreover, the earth, which in this parable represents the person, “produces by itself.” We must be careful in explaining this, for human hearts do not produce faith on their own; they are like hard rock where seed would perish. What it means is this: just as the earth, under the blessing of dew and rain and by God’s hidden working upon it, becomes ready to receive and hold the seed, so the human heart is made ready to receive and embrace the gospel of Jesus Christ. An awakened heart desires exactly what the Word of God provides. Moved by divine influence, the soul embraces the truth, and the truth embraces the soul, so that it lives within the heart and is energized there. A person’s love receives the love of God; a person’s faith, worked in them by the Spirit of God, believes the truth of God; a person’s hope, produced in them by the Holy Spirit, takes hold of the promises revealed. In this way, the heavenly seed grows in the soil of the soul. The life does not come from the one who preaches the Word; it is placed within the Word by the Holy Spirit. The life is not in your hand, but in the heart that is led by the Spirit to receive the truth. Salvation does not come from the preacher’s authority, but through the hearer’s personal conviction, personal faith, and personal love. This much we can know, and is it not enough for practical purposes? Still, there is something we cannot know—a secret into which we cannot look. As I have said before, you cannot look inside a person and see exactly how the truth takes hold of the heart, or how the heart takes hold of the truth. Some people have examined their own feelings so closely that they have become discouraged and spiritually blind. Others have examined the feelings of young believers so strictly that they have harmed them rather than helped them. In God’s work there is more room for faith than for sight. The heavenly seed grows in secret. It must be buried out of sight, or there will be no harvest. Even if you kept the seed above ground and it sprouted, you still could not see the inner life force that moves it. “The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.” Explain the new birth? Experience it, and you will know what it is. There are secrets into which we cannot enter, because their light is too bright for human eyes. You cannot become all-knowing, for you are a creature, not the Creator. There will always be a realm that is not only unknown but unknowable to you. Your knowledge goes so far and no further. You may thank God for this, because it leaves room for faith and gives reason for prayer. Cry out to the Great Worker to do what you cannot do, so that when you see people saved you may give the Lord all the glory. III. Thirdly, our text tells us what we may expect if we work for God, and what we may not expect. According to this parable, we may expect to see fruit. The farmer scatters his seed, the seed sprouts and grows, and he naturally expects a harvest. I wish I could stir up the expectations of Christian workers, for I fear many work without faith. If you planted a garden or field and sowed seed, you would be greatly surprised and grieved if nothing came up. Yet many Christians seem content to work without expecting results. This is a miserable way to work—drawing up empty buckets year after year. Surely, either I must see some result of my labor and rejoice, or, if I see none, I must be deeply grieved if I am truly serving my Master. We ought to expect results. If we expected more, we would see more. Lack of expectation has been a great cause of failure among God’s workers. But we must not expect every seed we sow to spring up immediately. Sometimes—glory be to God—the moment the Word is spoken people are converted, and the reaper overtakes the sower. But it is not always so. Some have labored faithfully for years and seen little visible result, yet at last the harvest has come—a harvest that would never have been gathered if they had not persevered. I believe this world will be converted to Christ—but not today, nor tomorrow, perhaps not for many generations. The sowing of centuries is not lost; it is moving toward its great conclusion. Mushrooms may appear quickly, but an oak forest requires generations. It is ours to sow and to hope for quick reaping, yet we must remember that “Be patient, therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord. See how the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient about it, until it receives the early and the late rains.” So we must expect results, but not lose heart if we must wait. We should expect to see the good seed grow, but not always in our preferred way. Like children, we are often impatient. A boy plants seeds one day and digs them up the next to see if they are growing. Nothing will come of that, because he will not leave them alone long enough. So it is with impatient workers. They want immediate visible results, or they begin to distrust the Word. Some preachers are so hurried that they allow no time for reflection, no space to count the cost, no opportunity for people to consider their ways and turn to the Lord with full commitment. Every other seed is allowed time to grow, but the seed of the Word must grow instantly before their eyes or they think nothing has happened. In their eagerness, they overheat the seed with fanaticism and destroy it. They convince people they are converted when they are not, and so prevent them from coming to a true saving knowledge of the truth. Some are kept from salvation because they are told they are already saved and are filled with pride before their hearts are truly broken. Perhaps if they had been taught to look for something deeper, they would not have been satisfied with shallow soil. Their growth appears rapid, but so is their decline. Let us confidently expect growth, but let us expect it in order: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. We may also expect the seed to ripen. By God’s grace our work will lead to genuine faith in those upon whom He works by His Word and Spirit. But we must not expect perfection at the beginning. Many mistakes have been made here. A young person comes under conviction, and a well-meaning, experienced believer questions them deeply and severely. He looks for full maturity at once. He enters the field early in the season and complains that he sees no grain, only grass. Of course he sees no grain yet. He refuses to accept the blade as evidence of life and insists on full maturity immediately. If he had looked for the blade, he would have found it and been encouraged. For my part, I am thankful to see even a faint desire, a weak longing, a sense of uneasiness about sin, or a craving for mercy. Should we not allow things to begin small? Notice the blade of desire, then watch for more. Soon conviction and resolve will follow, and then a small faith—like a mustard seed—but certain to grow. “For who has despised the day of small things?” Do not examine a newborn believer to see if they are fully sound in doctrine according to your standards. They are far from that, and difficult questions will only trouble them. Speak to them about their sin and Christ as Savior, and in doing so you will water the growing ear until it becomes full grain. It may not look like wheat yet, but later you will say, “That is wheat indeed. I recognize it. This is a true ear of grain, and I gladly gather it among my Master’s sheaves.” If you cut down the blade, how will the ear grow? Expect grace in your converts, but do not expect glory yet. IV. Finally, we consider what kind of sleep workers may take and what kind they may not take. The man in the parable “sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how.” Farming is said to be a good trade because it continues while the farmer sleeps. Our work is similar. When we serve our Master by sowing good seed, it grows even while we sleep. How may a faithful worker for Christ rightly sleep? First, he may sleep with restful confidence. Are you afraid that Christ’s kingdom will fail? Who asked you to worry for the ark of the Lord? Are you anxious that the Almighty’s purposes will collapse? Such anxiety dishonors God. Will omnipotence be defeated? You would do better to sleep than to interfere like Uzzah. Rest patiently. God’s purposes will stand. His kingdom will come. His chosen people will be saved. Christ “shall see of the travail of his soul and be satisfied.” Take the sweet sleep God gives to His beloved—the sleep of full confidence—like Jesus sleeping in the stern of the boat during the storm. God’s cause has never been in danger and never will be. The seed is secured by omnipotence and will produce a harvest. “In returning and rest you shall be saved; in quietness and in trust shall be your strength.” Wait for the harvest, for the pleasure of the Lord shall prosper in the hand of Jesus. Take also the sleep of joyful expectation that leads to a hopeful waking. Rise each morning believing that the Lord rules over all things for His purposes and for the good of those who trust Him. Expect blessing during the day, and go to bed calmly trusting Him for tomorrow. If you never rest, you will not rise refreshed and ready to work. If you spent all night anxiously worrying, you would be unfit for service in the morning. So rest and be at peace, and work steadily and calmly, because the matter is safe in the Lord’s hands. “It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep.” Rest also because you have consciously committed your work into God’s hands. After speaking the Word, go to God in prayer, entrust the matter to Him, and do not fret. It cannot be in better hands. Leave it with Him who “works all things according to the counsel of his will.” But do not sleep in carelessness. The farmer sows seed, but he does not forget it. He repairs fences, drives away birds, removes weeds, and guards against flooding. He does not watch the seed grow, but he has plenty else to do. He sleeps in proper measure and season, not like a lazy person. He never sleeps in indifference or inactivity, for every season demands work. One field is sown, but another waits. One crop is reaped, but another must be threshed and winnowed. A farmer’s work is never finished. His sleep is only a pause to give strength for continued labor. The parable teaches us to do all that lies within our responsibility, but not to intrude into God’s work. In teaching, we must labor diligently; but regarding the secret working of truth in the human heart, we must pray and rest, looking to the Lord for inward power.

fields.title: The Sheep Before The Shearers
fields.body_html:
“Like a sheep before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth.” — Isaiah 53:7 (ESV) Our Lord Jesus took our place so completely that, in this chapter, we are compared to sheep: “All we like sheep have gone astray” (Isaiah 53:6, ESV), and he also is compared to a sheep “As a sheep before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth.” It is remarkable how complete the exchange of positions was between Christ and his people. He became what they were so that they might become what he is. We can easily understand how we are the sheep and he the Shepherd; but to compare the Son of the Most High to a sheep would have been unacceptable presumption if his own Spirit had not chosen this humble picture.

Although this image is gracious, its use here is not unusual. Long before Isaiah’s day, our Lord was foreshadowed in the lamb of the Passover. Later he was proclaimed as “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29, ESV), and even in his glory he is described as the Lamb in the midst of the throne.

In unfolding this divine picture, I invite you first to consider our Saviour’s patience, shown in the image of a sheep silent before its shearers.

Our Lord was brought before the shearers to be stripped of his comfort, stripped of his honour, stripped even of his good name, and at last stripped of his very life; yet under the shearers he was silent like a sheep. Think of how patient he was before Pilate, Herod, and Caiaphas, and upon the cross. There is no record of him crying out in impatience at the pain and shame he suffered at the hands of those wicked men. Not one bitter word escaped him.

Pilate said, “Have you no answer to make? See how many charges they bring against you” (Mark 15:4, ESV). Herod was deeply disappointed because he hoped to see some miracle performed by him. The few words our Lord did speak were gentle and submissive, like the quiet sound of a sheep, yet infinitely full of meaning. He said, “For this purpose I was born and for this purpose I have come into the world—to bear witness to the truth” (John 18:37, ESV), and, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34, ESV). Apart from this, he remained patient and silent.

Notice first that our Lord was silent and did not open his mouth against his enemies. He did not accuse a single one of cruelty or injustice. They slandered him, but he did not reply. False witnesses rose up, but he did not answer them. You might think he would have spoken when they spat in his face. Could he not have said, “Friend, why are you doing this? For which of my works do you insult me?” But the time for such questions had passed. When they struck him on the face with their hands, it would not have been surprising if he had asked, “Why do you strike me?” But no— he acted as though he did not hear their insults. He brought no accusation before his Father. He needed only to lift his eyes to heaven, and legions of angels would have driven away the mocking soldiers. One flash of a seraph’s wing, and Herod would have perished; Pilate could have fallen under the judgement he deserved as an unjust judge. The hill of the cross could have become like the mouth of a volcano to swallow up the crowd that stood there mocking and jeering at him. But there was no such display of power. Rather, there was a far greater display of power over himself.

He restrained omnipotence itself with a strength beyond measure.

Again, as he spoke no word against his enemies, so he spoke no word against any of us. You remember how Zipporah said to Moses, “Surely you are a bridegroom of blood to me!” (Exodus 4:25, ESV), as she saw her child bleeding. Surely Jesus could have said to his church, “You are a costly bride to me, bringing me all this shame and bloodshed.” But “God gives generously to all without reproach” (James 1:5, ESV). He opened the very fountain of his heart and did not rebuke us. He had counted the full cost beforehand. Therefore he endured the cross, despising the shame.

“This was compassion like a God, That when the Saviour knew, The price of pardon was his blood, His pity never withdrew.” Without doubt he looked across the ages, for his eyes were not dim, even when filled with blood upon the tree. He must have foreseen your indifference and mine, our cold hearts and our unfaithfulness. He could have left behind words such as these: “I am suffering for those who are unworthy of my love. Their love will be a poor return for mine. Though I give my whole heart to them, how lukewarm their love will be towards me. I am weary of them; it grieves me to lay down my life for such a people.” But there is no trace of such a thought. No. “Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end” (John 13:1, ESV). He did not speak a single word that sounded like regret or complaint for suffering on their behalf, nor any sorrow that he had begun the work.

And as there was no word against his enemies, and no word against you or me, so there was no word against his Father, nor a syllable of complaint about the severity of the punishment laid upon him for our sake. You and I have complained under far lighter troubles, feeling that we have been treated unfairly. We have even dared to cry out to God, “My face is red with weeping, and on my eyelids is deep darkness, although there is no violence in my hands, and my prayer is pure” (Job 16:16–17, ESV). But not so the Saviour. No complaint was found in his mouth. We cannot begin to understand how deeply the Father pressed and crushed him, yet there was no rebellion. “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46, ESV) was a cry of astonished sorrow, not a complaint. It showed true humanity in weakness, but not humanity in revolt. Jeremiah wrote many laments, but Jesus spoke few. Jesus wept, and Jesus sweat great drops of blood, yet he never murmured or rebelled in his heart.

Look at your Lord and Saviour lying in quiet surrender beneath the shearers, as they take away everything dear to him, yet he does not open his mouth. Here we see his complete submission. He gave himself fully; there was no holding back. The sacrifice did not need to be tied with ropes to the horns of the altar. How different from you and me. He stood willing to suffer, to be spat upon, to be shamefully treated, and to die, for he was fully surrendered. He was entirely given to do the Father’s will and to accomplish our redemption. There was complete self-control as well. No part of him rose up to demand freedom or to escape the suffering. No part of his body, no thought of his mind, no power of his spirit resisted.

All submitted to the will of God. The whole Christ gave his whole being to God so that he might offer himself perfectly, without blemish, for our redemption. There was not only self-control, but complete focus on his mission. The sheep lying there does not think of the pastures; it yields itself to the shearer. The zeal for God’s house consumed our Lord in Pilate’s hall as much as anywhere else, for there he made the good confession. His only concern was to uphold the honour of God and to save his chosen people. Brothers and sisters, I wish we could reach this point: to surrender our whole spirit to God, to learn self-control, and to give our conquered selves entirely to him.

The calmness and submission of our Lord are illustrated even more clearly if it is true that sheep in the East are more docile than ours. Those who have seen the noise and rough handling at many of our sheep shearings may struggle to believe the testimony of the ancient writer Philo Judaeus, who said that sheep came willingly to be shorn. He wrote that wool-covered rams, heavy with thick fleeces, place themselves into the shepherd’s hands to have their wool cut, as if paying their yearly tribute to man, their natural ruler. The sheep stands in a quiet, bowed posture, unconstrained under the hand of the shearer. This may sound strange to those unfamiliar with the gentle nature of sheep, but he insists it is true. How wonderful was such submission in our Lord’s case. Let us admire it and seek to follow his example.

I have tried, however imperfectly, to describe the patience of our beloved Master. Now, secondly, let us consider our own situation under the same image used of our Lord.

Did I not say at the beginning that because we are sheep, he was willing to compare himself to a sheep? Let us look at it from another angle. Our Lord was a sheep before the shearers, and as he is, so are we in this world. Though we will never be offered like lambs in the temple as an atoning sacrifice, yet for ages the saints have been treated as a flock for slaughter. As it is written, “For your sake we are being killed all the day long; we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered” (Romans 8:36, ESV). Jesus sends us out as sheep in the midst of wolves (Matthew 10:16, ESV), and we are to see ourselves as living sacrifices, ready to be offered. But I want to focus especially on this second image: we are brought like sheep under the shearer’s hand.

Just as a sheep is taken by the shearer and its wool is cut off, so the Lord sometimes takes his people and shears them, removing their earthly comforts and leaving them stripped.

I wish that when our time comes to go through this shearing, it could be said of us as it was of our Lord, “As a sheep before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth.” I fear we speak far too much and complain endlessly, often without real cause, or for very small reasons. But now let us consider the image itself.

First, remember that a sheep repays its owner for all his care and effort by allowing itself to be shorn. As far as I know, there is nothing else a sheep can do in return. It provides food when it is killed, but while it is alive the one payment it can make to the shepherd is to give its fleece at the proper time. Some of God’s people can offer Christ the tribute of gratitude through active service, and they should do so gladly every day of their lives. But many others cannot do much in active service, and almost the only return they can give to their Lord is to surrender their fleece through suffering when he calls them to suffer, quietly yielding to be stripped of personal comfort when the time comes for patient endurance.

Here comes the shearer. He takes the sheep and begins to cut, cut, cut, cutting away the wool in great handfuls. Affliction is often the large pair of shears. A husband, or perhaps a wife, is taken away. Little children are removed. Property is cut off, and health is gone. Sometimes the shears remove a person’s good name; slander arises and comforts disappear. Well, this is your shearing time, and it may be that you cannot glorify God in any great outward way except by going through this process. If that is so, should we not, like good sheep belonging to Christ, surrender ourselves willingly, saying, “I lay myself down with this intention: that you may take from me anything and everything, and do what you will with me; for I am not my own, for I was bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20, ESV)?

Notice that the sheep itself benefits from the act of shearing. Before the sheep are shorn, the wool is long and old, and every bush and briar tears at it until the sheep looks ragged and miserable.

If the wool were left on when the heat of summer came, the sheep would hardly be able to bear it.

It would be so overloaded with fleece that it would be as uncomfortable as we are when we keep on our heavy winter clothes far too late in the season. So, brothers and sisters, when the Lord shears us, we do not enjoy the process any more than the sheep do; but first, it is for his glory, and second, it is for our good. Therefore we are bound to submit willingly. There are many things we would have liked to keep which, if we had kept them, would not have been blessings but curses.

A blessing that has gone stale becomes a curse. The manna, though it came from heaven, was good only as long as God commanded it to be kept for the proper time. When it was kept beyond that time, it “bred worms and stank” (Exodus 16:20, ESV), and then it was no blessing at all. Many people would keep their mercies until they rot, but God will not allow it. Up to a certain point, your wealth was a blessing; beyond that point it would not have been, and so the Lord took it away.

Up to that point, your child was a gift; beyond that, it would not have been so, and therefore sickness came and the child died. You may not be able to see it, but it is true: when God removes a blessing from his people, he takes it away because it would not have remained a blessing.

Before sheep are shorn, they are always washed. Have you ever seen the scene when they are driven down to the brook? Men stand in rows leading to the shepherd who waits in the water. The sheep are driven down; the men seize them, throw them into the pool, keep their heads above water, and swirl them round and round to wash the wool before cutting it off. Then you see them come out on the other side trembling, poor creatures, wondering what will happen next. I want to suggest to you, brothers and sisters, that whenever a trial threatens to come upon you, you should ask the Lord to sanctify it to you. If the good Shepherd is about to cut off your wool, ask him to wash it before he removes it. Ask to be cleansed in spirit, soul, and body. Christian people have the good habit of asking a blessing on their meals before eating bread. Is it not even more necessary to ask a blessing on our troubles before we enter them? Your dear child may be near death; will you not, dear parents, come together and ask God to bless even the death of that child, if it must happen? The harvest fails; would it not be right to say, “Lord, sanctify this poverty, this loss, this bad harvest. Make it a means of grace to us”? Why not ask a blessing on the cup of bitterness as well as on the cup of thanksgiving? Ask to be washed before you are shorn, and if the shearing must come, let it be your chief concern to offer clean wool.

After the washing, when the sheep has dried, it loses what was its comfort. It is thrown down, and the shearers begin their work. The poor creature loses its warm fleece. You too will have to part with your comforts. Remember this: the next time you receive a fresh blessing, call it a loan. Poor sheep, there is no wool on your back that will not one day be cut off. Child of God, there is no earthly comfort in your possession that will not either leave you, or you will leave it. Nothing truly belongs to us except our God. “Why,” someone says, “not our sin?” Sin was ours, but Jesus took it upon himself, and it is gone.

Nothing is truly ours but our God, for all his gifts are held on loan and can be recalled at his sovereign will. We foolishly think our mercies belong to us, and when the Lord takes them away, we begin to complain. A loan, it is said, should go home laughing, and so should we rejoice when the Lord takes back what he lent us. All our possessions are brief favours borrowed for a time. As the sheep yields its wool and loses its comfort, so must we give up all our earthly possessions. Or if they remain with us until death, we shall leave them then. We shall not carry a single one of them across the river of death.

The shearers take care not to harm the sheep. They cut as close as possible, but they do not cut the skin. If they can help it, they do not draw blood, not even the smallest amount. When a cut does happen, it is usually because the sheep does not lie still. A careful shearer keeps his shears free from blood. Of this Thomson wrote in his poem The Seasons, and the lines beautifully illustrate the whole subject: “How meek, how patient, the mild creature lies! What softness in its melancholy face, What silent, suffering innocence appears!

Fear not, you gentle flocks! It is not the knife Of dreadful slaughter raised above you; No, it is the shepherd’s careful, guided shears, Who, having borrowed your fleece As payment for his yearly care, Will send you back to the hills light and free.” It is the kicking and struggling that make the shearing difficult. If we are silent before the shearers, no harm will come. The Lord may cut very close. I have known him strip some so completely that they seemed to have nothing left, like Job when he said, “Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return” (Job 1:21, ESV). Yet they have also said with Job, “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21, ESV).

Notice that shearers always choose the right time. It would be cruel and foolish to begin shearing in winter. There is a saying about God “tempering the wind to the shorn lamb.” Whether or not that is accurate, it would indeed be cruel to shear lambs when bitter winds are blowing. Sheep are shorn in warm, pleasant weather, when they can afford to lose their fleece and are better without it. As summer approaches, shearing time comes. Have you not noticed that when the Lord afflicts us, he chooses the best possible time? He taught his disciples to pray, “Pray that your flight may not be in winter” (Matthew 24:20, ESV). The spirit of that prayer can be seen in the timing of our sorrows. He does not send our heaviest trials at our weakest moments. If your soul is already deeply depressed, the Lord does not add the heaviest burden then. He keeps such loads for times when “the joy of the Lord” is your strength. We often feel that when joy increases, a trial may be near; and when sorrow deepens, deliverance may be approaching. The Lord does not send two burdens at once, or if he does, he gives double strength. His shearing time is chosen with gentle wisdom.

There is something else to remember. As with the sheep, new wool grows. Whenever the Lord removes earthly comforts with one hand—one, two, three—he restores with the other hand six, twenty, a hundred. We cry and complain about the small loss, yet that loss is necessary so that we may receive a greater gain. Yes, it will be so. We shall have reason to rejoice, for “weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning” (Psalm 30:5, ESV). If we lose one position, another awaits us. If we are driven from one place, a better refuge is prepared. Providence opens a second door when it closes the first. If the Lord took away the manna from Israel, it was because they ate the produce of the land of Canaan. If the water from the rock did not follow them any longer, it was because they drank from the Jordan and from the streams. O sheep of the Lord’s fold, new wool is coming. Therefore do not be anxious about the shearing. I have said these things briefly so that we may come to the final point.

Let us try to follow the example of our blessed Lord when our time comes to be shorn. Let us be silent before the shearers, submissive and still, as he was.

Everything I have said gives a reason for doing so. Our shearing through affliction glorifies God, honours the Shepherd, and benefits ourselves. The Lord measures and tempers our trials and sends them at the right time. In many ways I have shown that it is wise to submit as the sheep does, and that the more completely we do so, the better.

We struggle far too much, and we often excuse ourselves for doing so. Sometimes we say, “This is too painful; I cannot be patient. I could have borne anything but this.” When a father disciplines his child, does he choose something pleasant? No. The pain is part of the discipline. In the same way, the bitterness of sorrow is part of our correction. “By the wounds a heart is healed” (see Proverbs 20:30, ESV). Do not complain because your trial feels sharp and unusual. That would be like saying, “If everything goes my way, I will submit; but if it does not, I will rebel.” That is not the spirit of a child of God.

Sometimes we complain about our weakness. “Lord, if I were stronger I would not mind this heavy loss; but I am frail, like a dry leaf blown by the storm.” But who decides what trial suits you—God or you? Since the Lord judges this trial suitable for your weakness, you can be sure it is so. Lie still. Lie still. “But my grief comes from a cruel source,” you say. “This trouble did not come directly from God. It came through my cousin or my brother, who should have treated me better.

If it had been an enemy, I could have borne it.” My brother, trial does not truly come from an enemy. God stands behind all your trouble. Look past secondary causes to the great First Cause. It is a serious mistake to focus on the human instrument that strikes us and forget the hand that holds the rod. If I strike a dog, he bites the stick. Poor creature, he knows no better. If he could think more clearly, he would either bite me or quietly accept the blow. You must not start biting the stick. It is your heavenly Father who uses it. Whether the rod is made of ebony or thorn, it is in his hand. It is best to stop trying to choose our trials and to leave everything in the hands of infinite wisdom.

The heart of my message is this: believer, yield yourself. Lie quietly in God’s hands. Do not struggle. There is no point in struggling. If the great Shearer intends to shear, he will do so. As I said before, when the sheep struggles, it may be cut by the shears. If we struggle against God, we may receive two blows instead of one. In truth, there is not half as much pain in a trial as there is in fighting against it. The Eastern farmer uses a goad to guide the ox. The gentle prod does little harm, but if the ox kicks, it drives the goad into itself and bleeds. So it is with us. It is hard “to kick against the goads” (Acts 26:14, ESV). We suffer more through rebellion than we would if we submitted to the will of God.

Have you ever earned a penny by fretting, or put bread on the table by complaining? Complaining wastes breath, and worrying wastes time. To lie quietly in God’s hand brings blessing to the soul.

Give me honour or dishonour, wealth or poverty, sickness or health, joy or sorrow, and I will gladly receive it from your hand.” A person is not far from the gates of heaven when he is fully submissive to the Lord’s will.

You who have been shorn have, I trust, received comfort through the blessed Spirit of God. May God bless you. And may the sinner also humble himself under the mighty hand of God. “Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God” (1 Peter 5:6, ESV). Submit yourselves to God (James 4:7, ESV). Let every thought be brought captive to him (2 Corinthians 10:5, ESV), and may the Lord send his blessing, for Christ’s sake. Amen.
fields.body_text: “Like a sheep before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth.” — Isaiah 53:7 (ESV) Our Lord Jesus took our place so completely that, in this chapter, we are compared to sheep: “All we like sheep have gone astray” (Isaiah 53:6, ESV), and he also is compared to a sheep “As a sheep before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth.” It is remarkable how complete the exchange of positions was between Christ and his people. He became what they were so that they might become what he is. We can easily understand how we are the sheep and he the Shepherd; but to compare the Son of the Most High to a sheep would have been unacceptable presumption if his own Spirit had not chosen this humble picture. Although this image is gracious, its use here is not unusual. Long before Isaiah’s day, our Lord was foreshadowed in the lamb of the Passover. Later he was proclaimed as “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29, ESV), and even in his glory he is described as the Lamb in the midst of the throne. In unfolding this divine picture, I invite you first to consider our Saviour’s patience, shown in the image of a sheep silent before its shearers. Our Lord was brought before the shearers to be stripped of his comfort, stripped of his honour, stripped even of his good name, and at last stripped of his very life; yet under the shearers he was silent like a sheep. Think of how patient he was before Pilate, Herod, and Caiaphas, and upon the cross. There is no record of him crying out in impatience at the pain and shame he suffered at the hands of those wicked men. Not one bitter word escaped him. Pilate said, “Have you no answer to make? See how many charges they bring against you” (Mark 15:4, ESV). Herod was deeply disappointed because he hoped to see some miracle performed by him. The few words our Lord did speak were gentle and submissive, like the quiet sound of a sheep, yet infinitely full of meaning. He said, “For this purpose I was born and for this purpose I have come into the world—to bear witness to the truth” (John 18:37, ESV), and, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34, ESV). Apart from this, he remained patient and silent. Notice first that our Lord was silent and did not open his mouth against his enemies. He did not accuse a single one of cruelty or injustice. They slandered him, but he did not reply. False witnesses rose up, but he did not answer them. You might think he would have spoken when they spat in his face. Could he not have said, “Friend, why are you doing this? For which of my works do you insult me?” But the time for such questions had passed. When they struck him on the face with their hands, it would not have been surprising if he had asked, “Why do you strike me?” But no— he acted as though he did not hear their insults. He brought no accusation before his Father. He needed only to lift his eyes to heaven, and legions of angels would have driven away the mocking soldiers. One flash of a seraph’s wing, and Herod would have perished; Pilate could have fallen under the judgement he deserved as an unjust judge. The hill of the cross could have become like the mouth of a volcano to swallow up the crowd that stood there mocking and jeering at him. But there was no such display of power. Rather, there was a far greater display of power over himself. He restrained omnipotence itself with a strength beyond measure. Again, as he spoke no word against his enemies, so he spoke no word against any of us. You remember how Zipporah said to Moses, “Surely you are a bridegroom of blood to me!” (Exodus 4:25, ESV), as she saw her child bleeding. Surely Jesus could have said to his church, “You are a costly bride to me, bringing me all this shame and bloodshed.” But “God gives generously to all without reproach” (James 1:5, ESV). He opened the very fountain of his heart and did not rebuke us. He had counted the full cost beforehand. Therefore he endured the cross, despising the shame. “This was compassion like a God, That when the Saviour knew, The price of pardon was his blood, His pity never withdrew.” Without doubt he looked across the ages, for his eyes were not dim, even when filled with blood upon the tree. He must have foreseen your indifference and mine, our cold hearts and our unfaithfulness. He could have left behind words such as these: “I am suffering for those who are unworthy of my love. Their love will be a poor return for mine. Though I give my whole heart to them, how lukewarm their love will be towards me. I am weary of them; it grieves me to lay down my life for such a people.” But there is no trace of such a thought. No. “Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end” (John 13:1, ESV). He did not speak a single word that sounded like regret or complaint for suffering on their behalf, nor any sorrow that he had begun the work. And as there was no word against his enemies, and no word against you or me, so there was no word against his Father, nor a syllable of complaint about the severity of the punishment laid upon him for our sake. You and I have complained under far lighter troubles, feeling that we have been treated unfairly. We have even dared to cry out to God, “My face is red with weeping, and on my eyelids is deep darkness, although there is no violence in my hands, and my prayer is pure” (Job 16:16–17, ESV). But not so the Saviour. No complaint was found in his mouth. We cannot begin to understand how deeply the Father pressed and crushed him, yet there was no rebellion. “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46, ESV) was a cry of astonished sorrow, not a complaint. It showed true humanity in weakness, but not humanity in revolt. Jeremiah wrote many laments, but Jesus spoke few. He gave himself fully; there was no holding back. The sacrifice did not need to be tied with ropes to the horns of the altar. How different from you and me. He stood willing to suffer, to be spat upon, to be shamefully treated, and to die, for he was fully surrendered. He was entirely given to do the Father’s will and to accomplish our redemption. There was complete self-control as well. No part of him rose up to demand freedom or to escape the suffering. No part of his body, no thought of his mind, no power of his spirit resisted. You who have been shorn have, I trust, received comfort through the blessed Spirit of God. May God bless you. And may the sinner also humble himself under the mighty hand of God. “Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God” (1 Peter 5:6, ESV). Submit yourselves to God (James 4:7, ESV). Let every thought be brought captive to him (2 Corinthians 10:5, ESV), and may the Lord send his blessing, for Christ’s sake. Amen.

fields.title: In The Hay - Field
fields.body_html:
“He causes the grass to grow for the cattle.” — Psalm 104:14 (ESV) At the appointed season all the world is busy with gathering the grass crop, and you can scarcely ride a mile in the country without breathing the delicious fragrance of the new-mown hay and hearing the mower's scythe being sharpened. There is a gospel in the hay-field, and that gospel we intend to bring out as we may be enabled by the Holy Spirit.

Our text brings us immediately to the place, and so we need no preface. “He causes the grass to grow for the cattle” — three things we shall notice: first, that grass is in itself instructive; secondly, that grass is far more so when God is seen in it; and thirdly, that by the growth of grass for the cattle, the ways of grace may be illustrated.

First, then, “He causes the grass to grow for the cattle.” Here we have something that is in itself instructive. Hardly any symbol, apart from water and light, is used more often in Scripture than the grass of the field.

In the first place, the grass may be looked at instructively as a symbol of our mortality. “All flesh is grass.” The whole history of man can be seen in a meadow. He springs up green and tender, subject to the frosts of infancy that threaten his young life; he grows, he comes to maturity, he puts on beauty just as the grass is adorned with flowers; but after a while his strength goes and his beauty becomes wrinkled, just as the grass withers and is followed by a fresh generation that withers in its turn. Like ourselves, the grass ripens only to decay. The sons of men come to maturity in due time, and then decline and wither like the green herb.

Some grass is not left to come to ripeness at all, but the mower’s scythe removes it, just as swift-footed death overtakes the careless children of Adam. “For all flesh is as grass, and all its beauty is like the flower of the field. The grass withers, the flower fades, when the breath of the LORD blows on it; surely the people are grass.” — Isaiah 40:6-7 (ESV) This is very humbling, and we often need to be reminded of it, lest we begin to dream of immortality under the stars. We should never walk on the grass without remembering that while the green sod covers our graves, it also reminds us of them, preaching with every blade a sermon about our mortality, of which the text is, “All flesh is grass, and all its beauty is like the flower of the field.”

Second, grass is often used in Scripture as a picture of the wicked. David tells us from his own experience that the righteous man is prone to grow jealous of the wicked when he sees the prosperity of the ungodly. We have seen them spread themselves out like green trees, seemingly fixed and rooted in their places; and when we have smarted under our own troubles, feeling that all day long we have been beaten and disciplined every morning, we have been inclined to ask, “How can this be consistent with the righteous government of God?” We are reminded by the Psalmist that in a short time we shall pass by the place of the wicked, and see that he is not there; we shall carefully look for his place, and see that it is no longer known; for he is soon cut down like grass, and withers like the green herb.

“But the wicked are like the tossing sea; for it cannot be quiet, and its waters toss up mire and dirt.

‘There is no peace,’ says my God, ‘for the wicked.’” — Isaiah 57:20-21 (ESV) The grass withers, the flower fades away, and in the same way the glory of those who place their confidence in temporal things and dig for comfort in the treasures of the earth will pass away forever. As the Eastern farmer gathers up the green herb and, despite its former beauty, throws it into the furnace, such shall be your lot, O boastful sinners! Thus the Judge will command his angels, “Bind them in bundles to burn.”

“So these will I destroy with the people, and they will be included in the nethermost parts of the pit, and your name will be forgotten in the grave…” — Psalm 9:17 (ESV) Where now is your merriment? Where now is your confidence? Where now is your pride and your pomp? Where now are your boastings and your loud-mouthed blasphemies?

They are silent forever; for, just as thorns crackle under a pot but are quickly consumed and leave nothing but a handful of ashes, so it will be with the wicked in this life; the fire of God’s wrath shall devour them.

It is more pleasing to remember that grass in Scripture also pictures the elect of God. The wicked are compared to dragons of the wilderness, but God’s own people shall spring up in their place, for it is written, “In the habitation of jackals, where each lay, shall be grass with reeds and rushes.”

The elect are compared to grass because of their number in the latter days and because of the rapidity of their growth. You remember the passage, “A handful of this [grain] shall become a large cluster, and the large cluster shall become a young plant in the nation.” O that the long-expected day might soon come, when God's people shall no longer be like a lone tuft of grass, but when they shall spring up among the grass, like willows by the watercourses. Grass and willows are two of the fastest growing things we know; so shall a nation be born in a day, and crowds be converted at once. When the Spirit of God is mightily at work in the church, men shall turn to Christ as doves fly to their dove-cotes, so that the astonished church shall exclaim, “Where did these come from?” O that we might live to see the age of gold, the time prophets have foretold, when the company of God’s people shall be countless as blades of grass in the meadows, and grace and truth shall flourish.

How like grass are God’s people for this reason: they are utterly dependent on the influences of heaven. Our fields become dry if spring showers and gentle dew are withheld; and what are our souls without the gracious visitations of the Spirit? Sometimes through severe trials our wounded hearts are like mown grass, and then we have the promise, “He will come down like rain upon the mown grass, like showers that water the earth.” Our sharp troubles have taken away our beauty, and then the Lord visits us and we revive again. Thank God for the old saying, which teaches a gracious truth as well as a true proverb, “Each blade of grass has its own drop of dew.” God is pleased to give his own special mercies to each one of his servants: “The blessing of the LORD makes rich, and he adds no sorrow with it.”

Once again, grass is like the food with which the Lord supplies the needs of his chosen ones. Take the twenty-third Psalm, and you have the image worked out in the sweetest form of pastoral song: “He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters.”

Just as the sheep has nourishment suited to its nature, and this nourishment is provided in abundance by its shepherd so that it not only feeds but lies down in the midst of the fodder, satisfied with plenty and perfectly at ease, so are the people of God when Jesus Christ leads them into the pastures of the covenant and reveals to them the precious truths upon which their souls are fed.

Beloved, have we not found that promise true, “On this mountain the LORD of hosts will make for all peoples a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wine, of rich food full of marrow, of aged wine well refined”? My soul has sometimes fed on Christ until I felt I could receive no more, and then I have lain down in the abundance of my God to take my rest, satisfied with his favour and full of the goodness of the Lord.

Thus you see that the grass itself is not without instruction for those who will incline their ear. In the second place, God is seen in the growing of the grass. He is seen first as a worker — “He causes the grass to grow”. He is seen secondly as a caretaker — “He causes the grass to grow for the cattle”.

First, as a worker, God can be seen in every blade of grass if we have eyes to perceive him. The world is blind when it talks about ‘natural laws’ and ‘natural causes’ and forgets that laws cannot operate by themselves, and that so-called natural causes are not causes at all unless the First Cause sets them in motion. The old Romans used to say, God thundered; God rained. We say, it thunders; it rains. What “it”? All such expressions are attempts to avoid the thought of God. We commonly say, “How wonderful are the works of nature!” But what is “nature”? I remember an unbeliever in the street, speaking about nature, being asked by a Christian whether he could define what nature was. He gave no answer. The production of grass is not the result of natural law apart from the actual work of God; mere law would be powerless unless the great Master himself sent the force through the matter that is governed by the law — much like a steam engine that supplies power to all the wheels of a cotton mill. I find rest on the grass as on a royal couch now that I know my God is there at work for his creatures.

Having asked you to see God as a worker, I want you to make use of this — therefore I urge you to see God in everyday things. He makes the grass grow — grass is common. You see it everywhere, yet God is in it. Study it, break it apart; the attributes of God are shown in every single flower of the field and in every green leaf.

In the same way, see God in your everyday experiences — in your daily troubles, your common joys, your regular mercies. Do not say, “I must see a miracle before I see God.” In truth, everything is full of wonder. See God in the bread on your table and the water in your cup. It will be the happiest way to live if in every event you can say, “My Father has done all this.” See God also in small things. The little things of life are often the greatest troubles. A man will hear that his house has burned down more quietly than he will complain when he sees an ill-cooked joint of meat on his table when he expected it to be perfect. It is the little stone in the shoe that makes the pilgrim limp. To see God in small things as well as in the great — to believe that the guidance of every drop of spray when a wave breaks on the rock is under God’s hand, as much as the movement of the mightiest planet in its orbit — all this is true wisdom.

Think also of God working among solitary things; for grass does not grow only where people tend it, but even on the side of the lonely mountain where no traveller has ever been. Where only the eye of a wild bird has seen the green grass and moss, God’s works show their beauty; for God’s works are fair even to eyes other than those of humans. And you, solitary child of God, living unseen and unknown in a remote village — you are not forgotten by the love of heaven. He makes grass grow all alone; shall he not make you flourish despite loneliness? He can develop your graces and prepare you for heaven in solitude and neglect. Grass lies beneath our feet, and nobody thinks of the fact that it is crushed by the foot, yet God makes it grow. Perhaps you are oppressed and worn down, but do not let that depress you, for God executes righteousness for all those who are oppressed: he causes the grass to grow, and he can make your heart flourish under all the pressures and afflictions of life, so that you will still be joyful and holy even if all the world tramples over you, living in the immortal life that God himself gives you, even if hell itself set its heel upon you.

Poor and needy one, unnoticed, oppressed, and trodden down, God makes the grass grow, and he will care for you.

But I said we should see in the text God also as a great caretaker. “He causes the grass to grow for the cattle.” Does God take care of oxen? Or is this only for our sake? “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain.” That shows that God cares for the beasts of the field; but it shows even more: that he wants those who work for him to be fed as they work. God cares for the cattle and makes grass grow for them. Then, my soul, though sometimes you have said with David, “I was senseless and ignorant; I was like a beast before you,” yet God cares for you.

“He gives to the beast its food, and to the young ravens when they cry.” There you have an example of God’s care for birds, and here we have his care for cattle; and though you, my listener, may see yourself as black and defiled as a raven and as far from anything spiritually good as beasts are, yet take comfort from this text: he gives grass to cattle, and he will give grace to you, though you think yourself to be like a beast before him.

Notice that he cares for these beasts who are helpless in caring for themselves. The cattle cannot plant the grass or cause it to grow. Though they can do nothing in the matter, yet he does it all for them: he causes the grass to grow. You who are as helpless as cattle to help yourselves, who can only stand and groan in misery yet do not know what to do, God can support you with his loving-kindness and favour you with his tenderness. Let the bleating of your prayers go up to heaven; let the meaning of your desires go up to him, and help will come to you though you cannot help yourselves. Beasts are dumb, speechless creatures, yet God makes the grass grow for them. Will he hear those who cannot speak and not hear those who can? Since our God gives careful attention even to the cattle in the field, he will surely have compassion on his own sons and daughters when they desire to seek his face.

There is this also to be said: God not only cares for cattle, but the food he provides for them is suitable—he causes grass to grow for the cattle, exactly the kind of food ruminants need. In the same way, the Lord God provides appropriate sustenance for his people. Depend on him by faith and wait upon him in prayer, and you will receive food suitable for you. You will find in God’s mercy exactly what your nature requires—provisions matched to your unique needs.

This “suitable” food the Lord ensures for the cattle, for no one else eats the cattle’s food. There is grass for them, and nobody else takes it; it is kept for them. In the same way, God has a special provision for his own people: “The secret of the LORD is with those who fear him, and he will show them his covenant” — Psalm 25:14 (ESV). Though the grass is technically free for anyone to eat, no creature cares for it except the cattle for which it was prepared. Similarly, though God’s grace is freely offered to all, only the elect pay attention and are prepared to receive it. There is as much reserve of the grass for the cattle as if walls enclosed it; likewise, though God’s grace is free, it is effectively reserved for those he has chosen.

God is seen in the grass as both worker and caretaker. Let us then observe his hand in providence at all times. See it not only when we enjoy abundance, but even when our supplies are scant; for grass is preparing for the cattle even in the depth of winter. And you, sons of sorrow, in your trials and troubles, are still under God’s care; he will accomplish his gracious purposes in you. Be still and witness the salvation of God. Every winter’s night connects directly to the joyous days of mowing and reaping; every season of grief is linked to future joy.

Our third point is most interesting: God’s work in providing grass for the cattle gives us illustrations of his grace.

I reflect on the text and say to myself, “He causes the grass to grow for the cattle. Here I see a full provision for that creature. I am also a creature, but nobler than cattle. Surely God will provide for me as well as for them. Yet naturally I feel uneasy: I cannot find what I want in this world. Even if I obtained all its riches, I would still feel discontented; even if I had all my heart could wish of temporal treasures, my soul would remain empty. There must be something somewhere that can satisfy me as a man with an immortal soul. God fully satisfies the ox; he must have something that will fully satisfy me if I receive it. There is the grass; the cattle eat it and then lie down content; all I have found on earth never satisfied me enough to rest fully. Therefore, there must be something that would satisfy me if I could reach it.” Is not this sound reasoning? I ask both Christians and unbelievers to follow me this far.

Let us proceed another step: the cattle not only have the grass provided, but they actually receive it. Why should I not also obtain what I want? My soul hungers and thirsts after something beyond what I can see or hear; there must be something to satisfy my soul. The cattle feed on what satisfies them; why should I not find satisfaction too? I begin to pray, “O Lord, satisfy my soul with good things, and renew my youth like the eagle’s” — Psalm 103:5 (ESV).

While I pray, I reflect: God has provided for cattle what fits their nature—they are flesh, and flesh eats grass. I too am flesh, but also spirit; to satisfy me I need spiritual nourishment. Where is it?

When I turn to God’s Word, I find, “The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever” — Isaiah 40:8 (ESV), and the words Jesus speaks are “spirit and life” — John 6:63 (ESV).

“Here is spiritual food for my soul,” I say; “I will rejoice in it.” O may God help me understand what that spiritual food is and enable me to receive it; for though God provides grass for cattle, they must eat it themselves. If they refuse, they are not nourished. I must imitate the cattle and receive what God provides for me. What is provided in Scripture? I am told that the Lord Jesus came to suffer, bleed, and die in my place, and if I trust him I shall be saved. Being saved, the thoughts of his love will give me solace and joy, strengthening me. What else have I to do but feed on these truths? The cattle bring nothing to the pasture except their hunger; they enter it and partake. Likewise, by faith I must live upon Christ. Lord, give me grace to feed on him; make me hungry and thirsty for him; give me the faith to receive him, so that I may be satisfied with favour and full of the goodness of the Lord.

Though the text seems small, it grows under meditation. Let me give further illustrations of divine grace. Preventive grace is symbolised here: grass grew before cattle were created. In Genesis we see that God provided grass before he made the cattle. What a mercy that God’s covenant provisions for his people were prepared before they were born! God gave his Son, Jesus Christ, as Saviour for his chosen before Adam fell; long before sin entered the world, God’s everlasting mercy foresaw it and provided a refuge for every elect soul. What comfort to know that before I hunger, God has prepared the manna; before I thirst, God has caused the rock in the wilderness to produce crystal streams to satisfy my soul’s thirst! See what sovereign grace can do! Before the cattle come to pasture, the grass is ready; before I experience my need for mercy, mercy is already prepared for me.

Here is an illustration of free grace: when the ox enters the field, it brings no money. Similarly, I, a poor, needy sinner, bring nothing but receive Christ without money and without cost. “The Lord makes the grass grow for the cattle, and so he provides grace for my needy soul, though I have no money, no merit, no excellence of my own.”

Why does God give grass to the cattle? Because they belong to him. Scripture affirms, “The silver is mine, and the gold is mine, declares the LORD of hosts, and the cattle on a thousand hills” — Haggai 2:8 (ESV). God provides grass for his cattle; likewise, grace is provided for God’s people.

Every herd of cattle is God’s: long before the farmer brands a bullock, God has marked it; so, long before the fall of Adam, the stamp of electing love was set on our brow: “Your eyes saw my unformed substance; in your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for me, when none of them as yet existed” — Psalm 139:16 (ESV).

God also feeds cattle because he has entered a covenant with them. “A covenant with cattle?”

someone asks. Indeed: when God spoke to Noah, after the flood, he said, “I establish my covenant with you, and with your offspring after you, and with every living creature that is with you, of the birds, of the livestock, and of every beast of the earth with you” — Genesis 9:9-10 (ESV). Thus a covenant was made with the cattle: seedtime and harvest would not fail; therefore the earth produces for them, and for them the Lord causes the grass to grow. If God keeps his covenant with cattle, will he not keep it with his beloved? Yes, his chosen are covenanted in Christ, and he provides for all their needs in time and eternity, satisfying them out of the fullness of his everlasting love.

God feeds the cattle, and then the cattle praise him. David writes, “Praise the LORD from the earth, you great sea creatures and all deeps, fire and hail, snow and frost, stormy wind fulfilling his command! Mountains and all hills, fruit trees and all cedars! Beasts and all livestock, creeping things and flying birds!” — Psalm 148:7-10 (ESV). The Lord feeds his people so that their glory may praise him, and not be silent. While other creatures give him glory, let the redeemed of the Lord especially proclaim it, those he has delivered from the hand of the enemy.

Yet even now, our text is not exhausted. Consider the grass itself: “He causes the grass to grow”.

Here is a doctrinal lesson: if grass cannot grow without God, how could grace arise in the human heart apart from divine action? Grace is a far more wonderful product of God’s wisdom than grass.

If grass cannot grow without a divine cause, any growth of grace must be traced to God, and all glory must be given to him.

Furthermore, if God deems it worthwhile to make grass and care for it, much more will he honourably cause his grace to grow in our hearts. If the great invisible Spirit, whose thoughts are high and lofty, condescends to watch over that humble growth by the hedge, surely he will oversee his own seed in us, “the incorruptible seed that lives and endures forever” — 1 Peter 1:23 (ESV).

Mungo Park, exploring the deserts of Africa, took comfort from a small piece of moss, seeing God’s wisdom and power even in that lonely patch of green.

Likewise, when you see fields ripe for mowing, your heart should leap with joy at how God has produced the grass, tending it through the winter cold and spring frost until rain and sunshine bring it to perfection. So, my soul, though you endure many frosts of sorrow and long winters of trial, the Lord will cause you to grow in grace and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever. Amen.
