To see God in small things as well as in the great — to believe that the guidance of every drop of spray when a wave breaks on the rock is under God’s hand, as much as the movement of the mightiest planet in its orbit — all this is true wisdom. Think also of God working among solitary things; for grass does not grow only where people tend it, but even on the side of the lonely mountain where no traveller has ever been. Where only the eye of a wild bird has seen the green grass and moss, God’s works show their beauty; for God’s works are fair even to eyes other than those of humans. And you, solitary child of God, living unseen and unknown in a remote village — you are not forgotten by the love of heaven. He makes grass grow all alone; shall he not make you flourish despite loneliness? He can develop your graces and prepare you for heaven in solitude and neglect. Grass lies beneath our feet, and nobody thinks of the fact that it is crushed by the foot, yet God makes it grow. Perhaps you are oppressed and worn down, but do not let that depress you, for God executes righteousness for all those who are oppressed: he causes the grass to grow, and he can make your heart flourish under all the pressures and afflictions of life, so that you will still be joyful and holy even if all the world tramples over you, living in the immortal life that God himself gives you, even if hell itself set its heel upon you. Poor and needy one, unnoticed, oppressed, and trodden down, God makes the grass grow, and he will care for you. But I said we should see in the text God also as a great caretaker. “He causes the grass to grow for the cattle.” Does God take care of oxen? Or is this only for our sake? “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain.” That shows that God cares for the beasts of the field; but it shows even more: that he wants those who work for him to be fed as they work. God cares for the cattle and makes grass grow for them. Then, my soul, though sometimes you have said with David, “I was senseless and ignorant; I was like a beast before you,” yet God cares for you. “He gives to the beast its food, and to the young ravens when they cry.” There you have an example of God’s care for birds, and here we have his care for cattle; and though you, my listener, may see yourself as black and defiled as a raven and as far from anything spiritually good as beasts are, yet take comfort from this text: he gives grass to cattle, and he will give grace to you, though you think yourself to be like a beast before him. Notice that he cares for these beasts who are helpless in caring for themselves. The cattle cannot plant the grass or cause it to grow. Though they can do nothing in the matter, yet he does it all for them: he causes the grass to grow. You who are as helpless as cattle to help yourselves, who can only stand and groan in misery yet do not know what to do, God can support you with his loving-kindness and favour you with his tenderness. Let the bleating of your prayers go up to heaven; let the meaning of your desires go up to him, and help will come to you though you cannot help yourselves. Beasts are dumb, speechless creatures, yet God makes the grass grow for them. Will he hear those who cannot speak and not hear those who can? Since our God gives careful attention even to the cattle in the field, he will surely have compassion on his own sons and daughters when they desire to seek his face. There is this also to be said: God not only cares for cattle, but the food he provides for them is suitable—he causes grass to grow for the cattle, exactly the kind of food ruminants need. In the same way, the Lord God provides appropriate sustenance for his people. Depend on him by faith and wait upon him in prayer, and you will receive food suitable for you. You will find in God’s mercy exactly what your nature requires—provisions matched to your unique needs. This “suitable” food the Lord ensures for the cattle, for no one else eats the cattle’s food. There is grass for them, and nobody else takes it; it is kept for them. In the same way, God has a special provision for his own people: “The secret of the LORD is with those who fear him, and he will show them his covenant” — Psalm 25:14 (ESV). Though the grass is technically free for anyone to eat, no creature cares for it except the cattle for which it was prepared. Similarly, though God’s grace is freely offered to all, only the elect pay attention and are prepared to receive it. There is as much reserve of the grass for the cattle as if walls enclosed it; likewise, though God’s grace is free, it is effectively reserved for those he has chosen. God is seen in the grass as both worker and caretaker. Let us then observe his hand in providence at all times. See it not only when we enjoy abundance, but even when our supplies are scant; for grass is preparing for the cattle even in the depth of winter. And you, sons of sorrow, in your trials and troubles, are still under God’s care; he will accomplish his gracious purposes in you. Be still and witness the salvation of God. Every winter’s night connects directly to the joyous days of mowing and reaping; every season of grief is linked to future joy. Our third point is most interesting: God’s work in providing grass for the cattle gives us illustrations of his grace. I reflect on the text and say to myself, “He causes the grass to grow for the cattle. Here I see a full provision for that creature. I am also a creature, but nobler than cattle. Surely God will provide for me as well as for them. Yet naturally I feel uneasy: I cannot find what I want in this world. Even if I obtained all its riches, I would still feel discontented; even if I had all my heart could wish of temporal treasures, my soul would remain empty. There must be something somewhere that can satisfy me as a man with an immortal soul. God fully satisfies the ox; he must have something that will fully satisfy me if I receive it. There is the grass; the cattle eat it and then lie down content; all I have found on earth never satisfied me enough to rest fully. Therefore, there must be something that would satisfy me if I could reach it.” Is not this sound reasoning? I ask both Christians and unbelievers to follow me this far. Let us proceed another step: the cattle not only have the grass provided, but they actually receive it. Why should I not also obtain what I want? My soul hungers and thirsts after something beyond what I can see or hear; there must be something to satisfy my soul. The cattle feed on what satisfies them; why should I not find satisfaction too? I begin to pray, “O Lord, satisfy my soul with good things, and renew my youth like the eagle’s” — Psalm 103:5 (ESV). While I pray, I reflect: God has provided for cattle what fits their nature—they are flesh, and flesh eats grass. I too am flesh, but also spirit; to satisfy me I need spiritual nourishment. Where is it? When I turn to God’s Word, I find, “The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever” — Isaiah 40:8 (ESV), and the words Jesus speaks are “spirit and life” — John 6:63 (ESV). “Here is spiritual food for my soul,” I say; “I will rejoice in it.” O may God help me understand what that spiritual food is and enable me to receive it; for though God provides grass for cattle, they must eat it themselves. If they refuse, they are not nourished. I must imitate the cattle and receive what God provides for me. What is provided in Scripture? I am told that the Lord Jesus came to suffer, bleed, and die in my place, and if I trust him I shall be saved. Being saved, the thoughts of his love will give me solace and joy, strengthening me. What else have I to do but feed on these truths? The cattle bring nothing to the pasture except their hunger; they enter it and partake. Likewise, by faith I must live upon Christ. Lord, give me grace to feed on him; make me hungry and thirsty for him; give me the faith to receive him, so that I may be satisfied with favour and full of the goodness of the Lord. Though the text seems small, it grows under meditation. Let me give further illustrations of divine grace. Preventive grace is symbolised here: grass grew before cattle were created. In Genesis we see that God provided grass before he made the cattle. What a mercy that God’s covenant provisions for his people were prepared before they were born! God gave his Son, Jesus Christ, as Saviour for his chosen before Adam fell; long before sin entered the world, God’s everlasting mercy foresaw it and provided a refuge for every elect soul. What comfort to know that before I hunger, God has prepared the manna; before I thirst, God has caused the rock in the wilderness to produce crystal streams to satisfy my soul’s thirst! See what sovereign grace can do! Before the cattle come to pasture, the grass is ready; before I experience my need for mercy, mercy is already prepared for me. Here is an illustration of free grace: when the ox enters the field, it brings no money. Similarly, I, a poor, needy sinner, bring nothing but receive Christ without money and without cost. “The Lord makes the grass grow for the cattle, and so he provides grace for my needy soul, though I have no money, no merit, no excellence of my own.” Why does God give grass to the cattle? Because they belong to him. Scripture affirms, “The silver is mine, and the gold is mine, declares the LORD of hosts, and the cattle on a thousand hills” — Haggai 2:8 (ESV). God provides grass for his cattle; likewise, grace is provided for God’s people. Every herd of cattle is God’s: long before the farmer brands a bullock, God has marked it; so, long before the fall of Adam, the stamp of electing love was set on our brow: “Your eyes saw my unformed substance; in your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for me, when none of them as yet existed” — Psalm 139:16 (ESV). God also feeds cattle because he has entered a covenant with them. “A covenant with cattle?” someone asks. Indeed: when God spoke to Noah, after the flood, he said, “I establish my covenant with you, and with your offspring after you, and with every living creature that is with you, of the birds, of the livestock, and of every beast of the earth with you” — Genesis 9:9-10 (ESV). Thus a covenant was made with the cattle: seedtime and harvest would not fail; therefore the earth produces for them, and for them the Lord causes the grass to grow. If God keeps his covenant with cattle, will he not keep it with his beloved? Yes, his chosen are covenanted in Christ, and he provides for all their needs in time and eternity, satisfying them out of the fullness of his everlasting love. God feeds the cattle, and then the cattle praise him. David writes, “Praise the LORD from the earth, you great sea creatures and all deeps, fire and hail, snow and frost, stormy wind fulfilling his command! Mountains and all hills, fruit trees and all cedars! Beasts and all livestock, creeping things and flying birds!” — Psalm 148:7-10 (ESV). The Lord feeds his people so that their glory may praise him, and not be silent. While other creatures give him glory, let the redeemed of the Lord especially proclaim it, those he has delivered from the hand of the enemy. Yet even now, our text is not exhausted. Consider the grass itself: “He causes the grass to grow”. Here is a doctrinal lesson: if grass cannot grow without God, how could grace arise in the human heart apart from divine action? Grace is a far more wonderful product of God’s wisdom than grass. If grass cannot grow without a divine cause, any growth of grace must be traced to God, and all glory must be given to him. Furthermore, if God deems it worthwhile to make grass and care for it, much more will he honourably cause his grace to grow in our hearts. If the great invisible Spirit, whose thoughts are high and lofty, condescends to watch over that humble growth by the hedge, surely he will oversee his own seed in us, “the incorruptible seed that lives and endures forever” — 1 Peter 1:23 (ESV). Mungo Park, exploring the deserts of Africa, took comfort from a small piece of moss, seeing God’s wisdom and power even in that lonely patch of green. Likewise, when you see fields ripe for mowing, your heart should leap with joy at how God has produced the grass, tending it through the winter cold and spring frost until rain and sunshine bring it to perfection. So, my soul, though you endure many frosts of sorrow and long winters of trial, the Lord will cause you to grow in grace and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever. Amen.

fields.title: The Joy Of Harvest
fields.body_html:
“They rejoice before you as with joy at the harvest” — Isaiah 9:3 (ESV) The other day I kept the feast with a company who shouted “Harvest Home.” I was glad to see the rich and poor rejoicing together; and when the cheerful meal was ended, I was glad to turn one of the tables into a pulpit, and in the large barn to preach the gospel of the ever-blessed God to an earnest audience. My heart was merry in harmony with the occasion, and I shall now keep in the same key, and talk to you a little upon the joy of harvest. Londoners forget that it is harvest time; living in this great desert of dingy bricks we hardly know what a wheat-ear is like, except as we see it dry and white in the window of a corn dealer's shop; yet let us all remember that there is such a season as harvest, when by God's goodness the fruits of the earth are gathered in.

What is the joy of harvest which is here taken as the simile of the joy of the saints before God? I am afraid that to the mere selfish order of spirits the joy of harvest is simply that of personal gratification at the increase of wealth. Sometimes the farmer only rejoices because he sees the reward of his toils, and is so much the richer man. I hope that with many there mingles the second cause of joy; namely, gratitude to God that an abundant harvest will give bread to the poor, and remove complaining from our streets. There is a lawful joy in harvest, no doubt, to the man who is enriched by it; for any man who works hard has a right to rejoice when at last he gains his desire.

It would be well if men would always recollect that their last and greatest harvest will be to them according to their labor. He who sows to his flesh will from the flesh reap corruption, but he who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life.

A young man commences life by sowing what he calls his wild oats, which he had better never have sown, for they will bring him a terrible harvest. He expects that from these wild oats he will gather a harvest of true pleasure, but it cannot be; the truest pleasures of life spring from the good seed of righteousness, and not from the hemlock of sin. As a man who sows thistles in his furrows must not expect to reap the golden wheatsheaf, so he who follows the ways of vice must not expect happiness.

On the contrary, they sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind. When a sinner feels the pangs of conscience he may well say, “This is what I sowed.” When he shall at last receive the punishment of his evil deeds he will blame no one but himself; he sowed tares and he must reap tares. On the other hand, the Christian man, though his salvation is not of works, but of grace, will have a gracious reward given to him by his Master. He who goes out weeping, bearing the seed for sowing, shall come home with shouts of joy, bringing his sheaves with him. The joy of harvest in part consists of the reward of labor; may such be our joy in serving the Lord.

The joy of harvest has another element in it, namely, that of gratitude to God for favors bestowed.

We are singularly dependent on God; far more so than most of us imagine. When the children of Israel were in the wilderness they went forth every morning and gathered the manna. Our manna does not come to us every morning, but it comes once a year. It is as much a heavenly supply as if it lay like a hoarfrost round about the camp. If we went out into the field and gathered food which dropped from the clouds we should think it a great miracle; and is it not as great a marvel that our bread should come up from the earth as that it should come down from the sky? The same God who bade the heavens drop with angels' food bids the dull earth in its due season yield corn for mankind. Therefore whenever we find that harvest comes, let us be grateful to God, and let us not suffer the season to pass over without psalms of thanksgiving. I believe I shall be correct if I say that there is never in the world, as a rule, more than sixteen months' supply of food; that is to say, when the harvest is gathered in, there may be sixteen months' supply; but at the time of harvest there is not usually enough wheat in the whole world to last the population more than four or five months; so that if the harvest did not come we should be on the verge of famine. We live still from hand to mouth. Let us pause and bless God, and let the joy of harvest be the joy of gratitude.

To the Christian it should be great joy, by means of the harvest, to receive an assurance of God's faithfulness. The Lord has promised that while the earth remains, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, shall not cease. and when you see the loaded wain carrying in the crop you may say to yourself, “God is true to his promise.

Despite the dreary winter and the damp spring, autumn has come with its golden grain.” Depend upon it, that as the Lord keeps this promise he will keep all the rest. All his promises are yea and amen in Christ Jesus; if he keeps his covenant to the earth, much more will he keep his covenant with his own people, whom he hath loved with an everlasting love. Go, Christian, to the mercy-seat with the promise on your lip and plead it. Be assured it is not a dead letter. Let not unbelief cause you to stammer when you mention the promise before the throne, but say it boldly—“Fulfil this word unto thy servant on which thou hast caused me to hope.” Shame upon us that we so little believe our God. The world is full of proofs of his goodness. Every rising sun, every falling shower, every revolving season certifies his faithfulness. Wherefore do we doubt him? If we never doubt him till we have cause for it we shall never know distrust again. Encouraged by the return of harvest, let us resolve in the strength of the Spirit of God that we will not waver, but will believe in the divine word and rejoice in it.

Once more. To the Christian, in the joy of harvest there will always be the joy of expectation. As there is a harvest to the husbandman for which he waits patiently, so there is a harvest for all faithful waiters who are looking for the coming and the appearing of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. The mature Christian, like the ripe ear of corn, hangs down his head with holy humility.

When he was but green in the things of God he stood erect and was somewhat boastful, but now that he has become full of the blessing of the Lord he is humbled thereby, and bows himself down; he is waiting for the sickle, and he dreads it not, for no common reaper shall come to gather Christ's people—he himself shall reap the harvest of the world.

The Lord leaves the destroying angel to reap the vintage and to cast it into the wine-vat to be trodden with vengeance; but as for the grain which he himself has sown, he will gather it himself with his own golden sickle. We are looking for this. We are growing among the tares, and sometimes we are half afraid lest the tares should be stronger than ourselves and choke the wheat; but we shall be separated by-and-by, and when the corn is well winnowed and stored in the garner, we shall be there. It is this expectation which even now makes our hearts throb with joy. We have gone to the grave with precious sheaves that belonged to our Master, and when we were there we thought we could almost say, “Lord, if they sleep they shall do well. Let us die with them.” Our joy of harvest is the hope of being at rest with all the saints, and forever with the Lord.

A view of these shadowy harvests upon earth should make us exceedingly glad, because they are the image and foreshadowing of the eternal harvest above.

So much about the joy of harvest; but I hasten onward. What joys are those which to the believer are as the joy of harvest? It is a common notion that Christians are an unhappy people. It is true that we are tried, but it is false that we are miserable. With all their trials, believers have such a compensation in the love of Christ that they are still a blessed generation, and it may be said of them, “Happy art thou, O Israel.”

One of the first seasons in which we knew a joy equal to the joy of harvest—a season which has continued with us ever since it commenced—was when we found the Saviour, and so obtained salvation. You recollect for yourselves, brethren and sisters, the time of the ploughing of your souls. My heart was fallow, and covered with weeds; but on a certain day the great Husbandman came and began to plough my soul. Ten black horses were his team, and it was a sharp ploughshare that he used, and the ploughers made deep furrows. The ten commandments were those black horses, and the justice of God, like a ploughshare, tore my spirit. I was condemned, undone, destroyed, lost, helpless, hopeless—I thought hell was before me. Then there came a cross ploughing, for when I went to hear the gospel it did not comfort me; it made me wish I had a part in it, but I feared that such a boon was out of the question.

The choicest promises of God frowned at me, and his threatenings thundered at me. I prayed, but found no answer of peace. It was long with me thus. After the ploughing came the sowing. God who ploughed the heart made it conscious that it needed the gospel, and the gospel seed was joyfully received. Do you recollect that auspicious day when at last you began to have some little hope? It was very little—like a green blade that peeps up from the soil; you scarce knew whether it was grass or corn, whether it was presumption or true faith. It was a little hope, but it grew very pleasantly. Alas, a frost of doubt came; snow of fear fell; cold winds of despondency blew on you, and you said, “There can be no hope for me.” But what a glorious day was that when at last the wheat which God had sown ripened, and you could say, “I have looked to him and have been lightened; I have laid my sins on Jesus, where God laid them of old, and they are taken away, and I am saved.” I remember well that day, and so no doubt do many of you. O sirs! no husbandman ever shouted for joy as our heart shouted when a precious Christ was ours, and we could grasp him with full assurance of salvation in him.

Many days have passed since then, but the joy of it is still fresh with us. And, blessed be God, it is not the joy of the first day only that we look back upon; it is the joy of every day since then, more or less; for our joy no man taketh from us; still we are walking in Christ, even as we received him.

Even now all our hope on him is stayed, all our help from him we bring; and our joy and peace continue with us because they are based upon an immovable foundation. We rejoice in the Lord, yea, and we will rejoice.

The joy of harvest generally shows itself by the farmer giving a feast to his friends and neighbors; and, usually, those who find Christ express their joy by telling their friends and their neighbors how great things the Lord hath done for them. The grace of God is communicative. A man cannot be saved, and always hold his tongue about it; as well look for dumb choirs in heaven as for a silent church on earth. If a man has been thirsty, and has come to the living stream, his first impulse will be to cry, “Ho! everyone that thirsts!” Do you feel the joy of harvest, the joy that makes you wish that others should share with you? If so, do not repress the impulse to proclaim your happiness. Speak of Christ to brothers and sisters, to friends and kinsfolk; and, if the language be stammering, the message in itself is so important that the words in which you couch it will be a secondary consideration. Tell it, tell it out far and wide—that there is a Saviour, that you have found him, and that his blood can wash away transgression. Tell it everywhere; and so the joy of harvest shall spread o'er land and sea, and God shall be glorified.

We have another joy which is like the joy of harvest. We frequently have it, too. It is the joy of answered prayer. I hope you know what it is to pray in faith. Some prayer is not worth the words used in presenting it, because there is no faith mixed with it. “With all your sacrifices you shall offer salt”, and the salt of faith is needful if we would have our sacrifices accepted. Those who are familiar with the mercy-seat know that prayer is a reality, and that the doctrine of divine answers to prayer is no fiction. Sometimes God will delay to answer for wise reasons; then his children must cry, and cry, and cry again. They are in the condition of the husbandman who must wait for the precious fruits of the earth; and when at last the answer to prayer comes, they are then in the husbandman's position when he receives the harvest. Remember Hannah's wail and Hannah's word. In the bitterness of her soul she cried to God, and when her child was given to her she called him “Samuel,” meaning, “Asked of God;” “For this child I prayed, and the LORD has granted me my petition that I made to him.” 1 Samuel 1:27.

He was a dear child to her, because he was a child of prayer. Any mercy that comes to you in answer to prayer will be your Samuel mercy, your darling mercy. You will say of it, “For this mercy I prayed,” and it will bring the joy of harvest to your spirit.

We have another joy of harvest in ourselves when we conquer a temptation. We know what it is to get under a cloud sometimes; sin within us rises with a darkening force, or an external adversity beclouds us, and we miss the plain path we were accustomed to walk in. A child of God at such times will cry mightily for help; for he is fearful of himself and fearful of his surroundings. Some of God's people have been by the week and month together exposed to the double temptation, from without and from within, and have cried to God in bitter anguish. It is a very hard struggle; the sinful action has been painted in very fascinating colors, and the siren voice of temptation has almost enchanted them. But when at last they have got through the valley of the shadow of death without having slipped with their feet; when, after all, they have not been destroyed by Apollyon, but have come forth again into the daylight, they feel a joy unspeakable, compared with which the joy of harvest is mere childish merriment. Those know deep joy who have felt bitter sorrow. As the man feels that he is the stronger for the conflict, as he feels that he has gathered experience and stronger faith from having passed through the trial, he lifts up his heart, and rejoices, not in himself, but before his God, with the joy of harvest. Brethren beloved, you know what that means.

Again, there is such a thing as the joy of harvest when we have been rendered useful. The master passion of every Christian is to be useful. There should be a burning zeal within us for the glory of God. When the man who desires to be useful has laid his plans and set about his work, he begins to look out for the results; but perhaps it will be weeks, or years, before results will come. The worker is not to be blamed that there are no fruits as yet, but he is to be blamed if he is content to be without fruits.

A preacher may preach without conversions, and who shall blame him? but if he be happy, who shall excuse him? It is ours to break our own hearts if we cannot by God's grace break other men's hearts, if others will not weep for their sins it should be our constant habit to weep for them. When the heart becomes earnest, warm, zealous, God usually gives a measure of success, some fiftyfold, some a hundredfold. When the success comes it is the joy of harvest indeed. I cannot help being egotistical enough to mention the joy I felt when first I heard that a soul had found peace through my youthful ministry.

I had been preaching in a village some few Sabbaths with an increasing congregation, but I had not heard of a conversion, and I thought, “Perhaps I am not called of God. He does not mean me to preach, for if he did he would give me spiritual children.” One Sabbath my good deacon said, “Don't be discouraged. A poor woman was savingly impressed last Sabbath.” How long do you suppose it was before I saw that woman? It was just as long as it took me to reach her cottage. I was eager to hear from her own lips whether it was a work of God's grace or not. I always looked upon her with interest, though only a poor laborer's wife, till she was taken away to heaven, after having lived a holy life.

Since then have I rejoiced over in the Lord, but that first seal to my ministry was peculiarly dear to me. It gave me a sip of the joy of harvest. If somebody had left me a fortune it would not have caused me one-hundredth part of the delight I had in discovering that a soul had been led to the Saviour. I am sure Christian people who have not this joy have missed one of the choicest delights that a believer can know this side heaven. In fact, when I see souls saved, I do not envy Gabriel his throne nor the angels their harps. It shall be our heaven to be out of heaven for a season if we can but bring others to know the Saviour and so add fresh jewels to the Redeemer's crown.

I will mention another delight which is like the joy of harvest, and that is fellowship with the Lord Jesus Christ. This is not so much something to talk about as something to experience and enjoy. If we try to describe what communion with Christ is, we fail. Solomon, the wisest of men, when inspired to write about the fellowship of the church with her Lord, had to use allegories and symbolic language, and though to a spiritual mind the Song of Solomon is always delightful, to a worldly mind it seems just like a love poem. The natural person does not accept the things of God, because they are spiritually discerned. 1 Corinthians 2:14 But oh, the happiness of knowing that Christ is yours, and of being close to him. To touch his side and put your finger in the mark of the nails; these are not everyday joys. But when such close and personal communion comes to us on our special days, it lifts our souls like the chariots of Amminadab, or, if you like, it allows us to walk over the world and all that it calls great or valuable.

Our circumstances mean nothing if Christ is with us—he is our God, our comfort, and our everything, and we rejoice before him like we rejoice at harvest.

I do not have time to go into more detail, because I want to end with one practical word. Many of us are eagerly longing for a harvest that would bring us intense joy. Lately, several people have shared with me how deeply they feel compassion for the souls of people. Others of us have felt a mysterious push to pray more than we ever have, and to care more than we ever did that Christ would save those who are perishing. We will not be satisfied until there is a thorough spiritual awakening in this land. We did not create this feeling ourselves, and we do not want to suppress it. We do not believe it can be suppressed; and others will feel the same heavenly concern, and will sigh and cry to God day and night until the blessing comes. This is the sowing, this is the ploughing, this is the harrowing—may it continue until the harvest. I long to hear my brothers and sisters everywhere saying, “We are full of anguish; we are in agony until souls are saved.” The cry of Rachel, “Give me children, or I die,” is the cry of your minister today, and the longing of thousands more. As that desire grows stronger, a revival approaches. We must have spiritual children for Christ, or our hearts will break because of our longing for their salvation. Oh, for more of these longings, yearnings, cravings, and efforts! If we pray until the harvest of revival comes, we will share in its joy.

Who will have the most joy? Those who have been most concerned about it. Those of you who do not pray in private, and who do not come to prayer meetings, will not have joy when the blessing comes and the church grows. You had no part in the sowing, so you will have little part in the harvest. Those who never speak to others about their souls, who do not participate in Sunday school or mission work, but just enjoy the blessings—they will have none of the joy of harvest, because they do not work for the Lord. And who would want lazy people to be happy? Instead, in our zeal and care, we feel like saying, “Curse Meroz; curse its inhabitants bitterly, because they did not come to help the LORD, to help the LORD against the mighty.” — Judges 5:23 (ESV) If you come to help the Lord by his Spirit, you will share the joy of harvest. Perhaps no one will have more joy than those who see their loved ones brought to God. Some of you have children who are a trial to you whenever you think of them; let them be a trial that drives you to constant prayer for them, and if the blessing comes, why should it not come to them? If a revival happens, why should your daughter not be converted, why should your wild son not be saved, or even your grey-headed father, who has been sceptical and unbelieving—why should God’s grace not reach him? And oh, what joy you will have then!

What happiness will fill your spirit when you see those related to you united with Christ your Lord!

Pray earnestly for them, and you will yet experience the joy of harvest in your own home, a shout of harvest home in your own family.

Perhaps, my listener, you have little to do with this joy because you are unsaved. Yet it is a wonderful thing for an unconverted person to be under a ministry blessed by God, and among people who pray for conversions. It is a blessing for you, young man, to have a Christian mother.

It is a great blessing for you, O unconverted woman, to have a godly sister. These give us hope for you. While your relatives are praying, we are hopeful for you. May the Lord Jesus be yours yet.

But, oh, if you remain unbelieving, however rich a blessing comes to others, it will not benefit you. “If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land.” — Isaiah 1:19 (ESV) But some may cry in sorrow, “The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved.” — Jeremiah 8:20 (ESV) It has been observed that those who pass through a revival and remain unconverted often become more hardened than before. I believe it, and I therefore pray that the Spirit of God comes with such power that none escape his influence.

May you pray: “Pass me not, O mighty Spirit!

You can make the blind to see; Witness of Jesus’ merit, Speak the word of power to me, Even me.”

“Have I long been sleeping in sin, Long been ignoring and grieving you?

Has the world kept my heart?

Oh forgive and rescue me, Even me.”

Oh, for earnest, persistent prayer from all believers around the world! If our churches were stirred to continuous, intense prayer, giving God no rest until he makes Zion a praise on earth, we might see God’s kingdom come and the power of Satan broken.

As many of you love Christ, I urge you by his name to pray earnestly; as many of you love the Church and desire her growth, I beg you not to hold back in this time of prayer. May the Lord lead you to pray until the joy of harvest is granted. Do you remember me saying one Sabbath, “The Lord will treat you as you treat his work during this next month”? I feel it will be true for many— that the Lord will treat you as you treat his Church. If you sow little, you will reap little; if you pray little, you will receive little favour. But if you act with zeal and faith, and pray and work much for the Lord, good measure, pressed down and overflowing, will be returned to you. If you water others with drops, you will receive drops; but if the Spirit helps you to pour rivers of living water from your soul, floods of heavenly grace will flow into your spirit. May God bring in the unconverted, and lead them to simple trust in Jesus; then they too will know the joy of harvest. We ask it in his name. Amen.
fields.body_text: "They rejoice before you as with joy at the harvest" — Isaiah 9:3 (ESV) The other day I kept the feast with a company who shouted "Harvest Home." I was glad to see the rich and poor rejoicing together; and when the cheerful meal was ended, I was glad to turn one of the tables into a pulpit, and in the large barn to preach the gospel of the ever-blessed God to an earnest audience. My heart was merry in harmony with the occasion, and I shall now keep in the same key, and talk to you a little upon the joy of harvest. Londoners forget that it is harvest time; living in this great desert of dingy bricks we hardly know what a wheat-ear is like, except as we see it dry and white in the window of a corn dealer's shop; yet let us all remember that there is such a season as harvest, when by God's goodness the fruits of the earth are gathered in. What is the joy of harvest which is here taken as the simile of the joy of the saints before God? I am afraid that to the mere selfish order of spirits the joy of harvest is simply that of personal gratification at the increase of wealth. Sometimes the farmer only rejoices because he sees the reward of his toils, and is so much the richer man. I hope that with many there mingles the second cause of joy; namely, gratitude to God that an abundant harvest will give bread to the poor, and remove complaining from our streets. There is a lawful joy in harvest, no doubt, to the man who is enriched by it; for any man who works hard has a right to rejoice when at last he gains his desire. It would be well if men would always recollect that their last and greatest harvest will be to them according to their labor. He who sows to his flesh will from the flesh reap corruption, but he who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life. A young man commences life by sowing what he calls his wild oats, which he had better never have sown, for they will bring him a terrible harvest. He expects that from these wild oats he will gather a harvest of true pleasure, but it cannot be; the truest pleasures of life spring from the good seed of righteousness, and not from the hemlock of sin. As a man who sows thistles in his furrows must not expect to reap the golden wheatsheaf, so he who follows the ways of vice must not expect happiness. On the contrary, they sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind. When a sinner feels the pangs of conscience he may well say, "This is what I sowed." When he shall at last receive the punishment of his evil deeds he will blame no one but himself; he sowed tares and he must reap tares. On the other hand, the Christian man, though his salvation is not of works, but of grace, will have a gracious reward given to him by his Master. He who goes out weeping, bearing the seed for sowing, shall come home with shouts of joy, bringing his sheaves with him. The joy of harvest in part consists of the reward of labor; may such be our joy in serving the Lord. The joy of harvest has another element in it, namely, that of gratitude to God for favors bestowed. We are singularly dependent on God; far more so than most of us imagine. When the children of Israel were in the wilderness they went forth every morning and gathered the manna. Our manna does not come to us every morning, but it comes once a year. It is as much a heavenly supply as if it lay like a hoarfrost round about the camp. If we went out into the field and gathered food which dropped from the clouds we should think it a great miracle; and is it not as great a marvel that our bread should come up from the earth as that it should come down from the sky? The same God who bade the heavens drop with angels' food bids the dull earth in its due season yield corn for mankind. Therefore whenever we find that harvest comes, let us be grateful to God, and let us not suffer the season to pass over without psalms of thanksgiving. I believe I shall be correct if I say that there is never in the world, as a rule, more than sixteen months' supply of food; that is to say, when the harvest is gathered in, there may be sixteen months' supply; but at the time of harvest there is not usually enough wheat in the whole world to last the population more than four or five months; so that if the harvest did not come we should be on the verge of famine. We live still from hand to mouth. Let us pause and bless God, and let the joy of harvest be the joy of gratitude. To the Christian it should be great joy, by means of the harvest, to receive an assurance of God's faithfulness. The Lord has promised that while the earth remains, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, shall not cease. and when you see the loaded wain carrying in the crop you may say to yourself, "God is true to his promise. Despite the dreary winter and the damp spring, autumn has come with its golden grain." Depend upon it, that as the Lord keeps this promise he will keep all the rest. All his promises are yea and amen in Christ Jesus; if he keeps his covenant to the earth, much more will he keep his covenant with his own people, whom he hath loved with an everlasting love. Go, Christian, to the mercy-seat with the promise on your lip and plead it. Be assured it is not a dead letter. Let not unbelief cause you to stammer when you mention the promise before the throne, but say it boldly—"Fulfil this word unto thy servant on which thou hast caused me to hope." Shame upon us that we so little believe our God. The world is full of proofs of his goodness. Every rising sun, every falling shower, every revolving season certifies his faithfulness. Wherefore do we doubt him? If we never doubt him till we have cause for it we shall never know distrust again. Encouraged by the return of harvest, let us resolve in the strength of the Spirit of God that we will not waver, but will believe in the divine word and rejoice in it. Once more. To the Christian, in the joy of harvest there will always be the joy of expectation. As there is a harvest to the husbandman for which he waits patiently, so there is a harvest for all faithful waiters who are looking for the coming and the appearing of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. The mature Christian, like the ripe ear of corn, hangs down his head with holy humility. When he was but green in the things of God he stood erect and was somewhat boastful, but now that he has become full of the blessing of the Lord he is humbled thereby, and bows himself down; he is waiting for the sickle, and he dreads it not, for no common reaper shall come to gather Christ's people—he himself shall reap the harvest of the world. The Lord leaves the destroying angel to reap the vintage and to cast it into the wine-vat to be trodden with vengeance; but as for the grain which he himself has sown, he will gather it himself with his own golden sickle. We are looking for this. We are growing among the tares, and sometimes we are half afraid lest the tares should be stronger than ourselves and choke the wheat; but we shall be separated by-and-by, and when the corn is well winnowed and stored in the garner, we shall be there. It is this expectation which even now makes our hearts throb with joy. We have gone to the grave with precious sheaves that belonged to our Master, and when we were there we thought we could almost say, "Lord, if they sleep they shall do well. Let us die with them." Our joy of harvest is the hope of being at rest with all the saints, and forever with the Lord. A view of these shadowy harvests upon earth should make us exceedingly glad, because they are the image and foreshadowing of the eternal harvest above. So much about the joy of harvest; but I hasten onward. What joys are those which to the believer are as the joy of harvest? It is a common notion that Christians are an unhappy people. It is true that we are tried, but it is false that we are miserable. With all their trials, believers have such a compensation in the love of Christ that they are still a blessed generation, and it may be said of them, "Happy art thou, O Israel." One of the first seasons in which we knew a joy equal to the joy of harvest—a season which has continued with us ever since it commenced—was when we found the Saviour, and so obtained salvation. You recollect for yourselves, brethren and sisters, the time of the ploughing of your souls. My heart was fallow, and covered with weeds; but on a certain day the great Husbandman came and began to plough my soul. Ten black horses were his team, and it was a sharp ploughshare that he used, and the ploughers made deep furrows. The ten commandments were those black horses, and the justice of God, like a ploughshare, tore my spirit. I was condemned, undone, destroyed, lost, helpless, hopeless—I thought hell was before me. Then there came a cross ploughing, for when I went to hear the gospel it did not comfort me; it made me wish I had a part in it, but I feared that such a boon was out of the question. The choicest promises of God frowned at me, and his threatenings thundered at me. I prayed, but found no answer of peace. It was long with me thus. After the ploughing came the sowing. God who ploughed the heart made it conscious that it needed the gospel, and the gospel seed was joyfully received. Do you recollect that auspicious day when at last you began to have some little hope? It was very little—like a green blade that peeps up from the soil; you scarce knew whether it was grass or corn, whether it was presumption or true faith. It was a little hope, but it grew very pleasantly. Alas, a frost of doubt came; snow of fear fell; cold winds of despondency blew on you, and you said, "There can be no hope for me." But what a glorious day was that when at last the wheat which God had sown ripened, and you could say, "I have looked to him and have been lightened; I have laid my sins on Jesus, where God laid them of old, and they are taken away, and I am saved." I remember well that day, and so no doubt do many of you. O sirs! no husbandman ever shouted for joy as our heart shouted when a precious Christ was ours, and we could grasp him with full assurance of salvation in him. Many days have passed since then, but the joy of it is still fresh with us. And, blessed be God, it is not the joy of the first day only that we look back upon; it is the joy of every day since then, more or less; for our joy no man taketh from us; still we are walking in Christ, even as we received him. Even now all our hope on him is stayed, all our help from him we bring; and our joy and peace continue with us because they are based upon an immovable foundation. We rejoice in the Lord, yea, and we will rejoice. The joy of harvest generally shows itself by the farmer giving a feast to his friends and neighbors; and, usually, those who find Christ express their joy by telling their friends and their neighbors how great things the Lord hath done for them. The grace of God is communicative. A man cannot be saved, and always hold his tongue about it; as well look for dumb choirs in heaven as for a silent church on earth. If a man has been thirsty, and has come to the living stream, his first impulse will be to cry, "Ho! everyone that thirsts!" Do you feel the joy of harvest, the joy that makes you wish that others should share with you? If so, do not repress the impulse to proclaim your happiness. Speak of Christ to brothers and sisters, to friends and kinsfolk; and, if the language be stammering, the message in itself is so important that the words in which you couch it will be a secondary consideration. Tell it, tell it out far and wide—that there is a Saviour, that you have found him, and that his blood can wash away transgression. Tell it everywhere; and so the joy of harvest shall spread o'er land and sea, and God shall be glorified. We have another joy which is like the joy of harvest. We frequently have it, too. It is the joy of answered prayer. I hope you know what it is to pray in faith. Some prayer is not worth the words used in presenting it, because there is no faith mixed with it. “With all your sacrifices you shall offer salt”, and the salt of faith is needful if we would have our sacrifices accepted. Those who are familiar with the mercy-seat know that prayer is a reality, and that the doctrine of divine answers to prayer is no fiction. Sometimes God will delay to answer for wise reasons; then his children must cry, and cry, and cry again. They are in the condition of the husbandman who must wait for the precious fruits of the earth; and when at last the answer to prayer comes, they are then in the husbandman's position when he receives the harvest. Remember Hannah's wail and Hannah's word. In the bitterness of her soul she cried to God, and when her child was given to her she called him "Samuel," meaning, "Asked of God;" “For this child I prayed, and the LORD has granted me my petition that I made to him.” 1 Samuel 1:27. He was a dear child to her, because he was a child of prayer. Any mercy that comes to you in answer to prayer will be your Samuel mercy, your darling mercy. You will say of it, "For this mercy I prayed," and it will bring the joy of harvest to your spirit. We have another joy of harvest in ourselves when we conquer a temptation. We know what it is to get under a cloud sometimes; sin within us rises with a darkening force, or an external adversity beclouds us, and we miss the plain path we were accustomed to walk in. A child of God at such times will cry mightily for help; for he is fearful of himself and fearful of his surroundings. Some of God's people have been by the week and month together exposed to the double temptation, from without and from within, and have cried to God in bitter anguish. It is a very hard struggle; the sinful action has been painted in very fascinating colors, and the siren voice of temptation has almost enchanted them. But when at last they have got through the valley of the shadow of death without having slipped with their feet; when, after all, they have not been destroyed by Apollyon, but have come forth again into the daylight, they feel a joy unspeakable, compared with which the joy of harvest is mere childish merriment. Those know deep joy who have felt bitter sorrow. As the man feels that he is the stronger for the conflict, as he feels that he has gathered experience and stronger faith from having passed through the trial, he lifts up his heart, and rejoices, not in himself, but before his God, with the joy of harvest. Brethren beloved, you know what that means. Again, there is such a thing as the joy of harvest when we have been rendered useful. The master passion of every Christian is to be useful. There should be a burning zeal within us for the glory of God. When the man who desires to be useful has laid his plans and set about his work, he begins to look out for the results; but perhaps it will be weeks, or years, before results will come. The worker is not to be blamed that there are no fruits as yet, but he is to be blamed if he is content to be without fruits. A preacher may preach without conversions, and who shall blame him? but if he be happy, who shall excuse him? It is ours to break our own hearts if we cannot by God's grace break other men's hearts, if others will not weep for their sins it should be our constant habit to weep for them. When the heart becomes earnest, warm, zealous, God usually gives a measure of success, some fiftyfold, some a hundredfold. When the success comes it is the joy of harvest indeed. I cannot help being egotistical enough to mention the joy I felt when first I heard that a soul had found peace through my youthful ministry. I had been preaching in a village some few Sabbaths with an increasing congregation, but I had not heard of a conversion, and I thought, "Perhaps I am not called of God. He does not mean me to preach, for if he did he would give me spiritual children." One Sabbath my good deacon said, "Don't be discouraged. A poor woman was savingly impressed last Sabbath." How long do you suppose it was before I saw that woman? It was just as long as it took me to reach her cottage. I was eager to hear from her own lips whether it was a work of God's grace or not. I always looked upon her with interest, though only a poor laborer's wife, till she was taken away to heaven, after having lived a holy life. Since then have I rejoiced over in the Lord, but that first seal to my ministry was peculiarly dear to me. It gave me a sip of the joy of harvest. If somebody had left me a fortune it would not have caused me one-hundredth part of the delight I had in discovering that a soul had been led to the Saviour. I am sure Christian people who have not this joy have missed one of the choicest delights that a believer can know this side heaven. In fact, when I see souls saved, I do not envy Gabriel his throne nor the angels their harps. It shall be our heaven to be out of heaven for a season if we can but bring others to know the Saviour and so add fresh jewels to the Redeemer's crown. I will mention another delight which is like the joy of harvest, and that is fellowship with the Lord Jesus Christ. This is not so much something to talk about as something to experience and enjoy. If we try to describe what communion with Christ is, we fail. Solomon, the wisest of men, when inspired to write about the fellowship of the church with her Lord, had to use allegories and symbolic language, and though to a spiritual mind the Song of Solomon is always delightful, to a worldly mind it seems just like a love poem. The natural person does not accept the things of God, because they are spiritually discerned. 1 Corinthians 2:14 But oh, the happiness of knowing that Christ is yours, and of being close to him. To touch his side and put your finger in the mark of the nails; these are not everyday joys. But when such close and personal communion comes to us on our special days, it lifts our souls like the chariots of Amminadab, or, if you like, it allows us to walk over the world and all that it calls great or valuable. Our circumstances mean nothing if Christ is with us—he is our God, our comfort, and our everything, and we rejoice before him like we rejoice at harvest. I do not have time to go into more detail, because I want to end with one practical word. Many of us are eagerly longing for a harvest that would bring us intense joy. Lately, several people have shared with me how deeply they feel compassion for the souls of people. Others of us have felt a mysterious push to pray more than we ever have, and to care more than we ever did that Christ would save those who are perishing. We will not be satisfied until there is a thorough spiritual awakening in this land. We did not create this feeling ourselves, and we do not want to suppress it. We do not believe it can be suppressed; and others will feel the same heavenly concern, and will sigh and cry to God day and night until the blessing comes. This is the sowing, this is the ploughing, this is the harrowing—may it continue until the harvest. I long to hear my brothers and sisters everywhere saying, "We are full of anguish; we are in agony until souls are saved." The cry of Rachel, "Give me children, or I die," is the cry of your minister today, and the longing of thousands more. As that desire grows stronger, a revival approaches. We must have spiritual children for Christ, or our hearts will break because of our longing for their salvation. Oh, for more of these longings, yearnings, cravings, and efforts! If we pray until the harvest of revival comes, we will share in its joy. Who will have the most joy? Those who have been most concerned about it. Those of you who do not pray in private, and who do not come to prayer meetings, will not have joy when the blessing comes and the church grows. You had no part in the sowing, so you will have little part in the harvest. Those who never speak to others about their souls, who do not participate in Sunday school or mission work, but just enjoy the blessings—they will have none of the joy of harvest, because they do not work for the Lord. And who would want lazy people to be happy? Instead, in our zeal and care, we feel like saying, "Curse Meroz; curse its inhabitants bitterly, because they did not come to help the LORD, to help the LORD against the mighty." — Judges 5:23 (ESV) If you come to help the Lord by his Spirit, you will share the joy of harvest. Perhaps no one will have more joy than those who see their loved ones brought to God. Some of you have children who are a trial to you whenever you think of them; let them be a trial that drives you to constant prayer for them, and if the blessing comes, why should it not come to them? If a revival happens, why should your daughter not be converted, why should your wild son not be saved, or even your grey-headed father, who has been sceptical and unbelieving—why should God’s grace not reach him? And oh, what joy you will have then! What happiness will fill your spirit when you see those related to you united with Christ your Lord! Pray earnestly for them, and you will yet experience the joy of harvest in your own home, a shout of harvest home in your own family. Perhaps, my listener, you have little to do with this joy because you are unsaved. Yet it is a wonderful thing for an unconverted person to be under a ministry blessed by God, and among people who pray for conversions. It is a blessing for you, young man, to have a Christian mother. It is a great blessing for you, O unconverted woman, to have a godly sister. These give us hope for you. While your relatives are praying, we are hopeful for you. May the Lord Jesus be yours yet. But, oh, if you remain unbelieving, however rich a blessing comes to others, it will not benefit you. "If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land." — Isaiah 1:19 (ESV) But some may cry in sorrow, "The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved." — Jeremiah 8:20 (ESV) It has been observed that those who pass through a revival and remain unconverted often become more hardened than before. You can make the blind to see; Witness of Jesus’ merit, Speak the word of power to me, Even me." "Have I long been sleeping in sin, Long been ignoring and grieving you? Has the world kept my heart? Oh forgive and rescue me, Even me." Oh, for earnest, persistent prayer from all believers around the world! If our churches were stirred to continuous, intense prayer, giving God no rest until he makes Zion a praise on earth, we might see God’s kingdom come and the power of Satan broken. As many of you love Christ, I urge you by his name to pray earnestly; as many of you love the Church and desire her growth, I beg you not to hold back in this time of prayer. May the Lord lead you to pray until the joy of harvest is granted. Do you remember me saying one Sabbath, "The Lord will treat you as you treat his work during this next month"? I feel it will be true for many— that the Lord will treat you as you treat his Church. If you sow little, you will reap little; if you pray little, you will receive little favour. But if you act with zeal and faith, and pray and work much for the Lord, good measure, pressed down and overflowing, will be returned to you. fields.title: Spiritual Gleaning
fields.body_html:
“Let her glean even among the sheaves, and do not reproach her.” — Ruth 2:15 People from the country understand gleaning. I hope this custom never disappears, so the poor always get their share of the harvest. But many who see gleaning in their parish fields every year are not yet wise enough to understand the spiritual meaning of gleaning. That is the subject today, and my text comes from the story of Ruth, known to all of you. I will use it to illustrate our case in a simple but instructive way. First, there is a great Husbandman; in Ruth’s story it was Boaz, in ours it is our heavenly Father. Second, there is a humble gleaner; Ruth was the gleaner, but she represents every believer. Third, there is a gracious permission given to Ruth: “Let her glean even among the sheaves, and do not reproach her.” The same permission is given to us spiritually.

In the first place, the God of the whole earth is a great Husbandman. This is true in natural things.

All farm operations happen by his power and wisdom. Man may plough the soil and sow the seed, but as Jesus said, “My Father is the farmer.” — John 15:1 (ESV) He controls the clouds and the sunshine; he directs the winds and distributes dew and rain; he gives frost and heat; and through all these natural processes, he provides food for humans and animals. All this farming is for the benefit of others, never for himself. He has no need of our work. “The cattle on a thousand hills are mine,” — Psalm 50:10 (ESV). The purest kindness and generosity are in God’s heart. Though all things belong to God, his works in creation and providence are not for himself, but for his creatures. This encourages us to trust him.

In spiritual matters, God is also a great Husbandman, and all his work is done for his children, so they may be nourished with the finest spiritual food. Consider the wide gospel fields our heavenly Father tends for his children. These fields are very productive. “The people of Israel shall dwell in safety; Jacob shall dwell securely in a land of grain and wine; his heavens shall drop down dew.”

— Deuteronomy 33:28 (ESV) Every field God tends yields a plentiful harvest; there are no failures or famines with him.

One part of his farm is called the Doctrine field. What full sheaves of fine wheat are there! Those allowed to glean here will gather more than enough, for the land yields abundantly. Look at the sheaf of election, full of heavy, strong ears of wheat, like Pharaoh saw in his dream. There is the sheaf of perseverance, where each ear represents the promise that God will finish what he started.

If we do not have faith to partake of these, we may glean from the sheaves of redemption by the blood of Christ. Many who cannot feed on election or perseverance can feed on the atonement and rejoice in substitution. These rich sheaves, when meditated on, provide royal food for the Lord’s family.

I wonder why some of God’s stewards lock the gate of this field, as if they think it dangerous. I want my people not just to glean here, but to carry home wagon-loads, for they cannot be too well fed when truth is the food. Are my fellow workers afraid that God’s people will become arrogant if they get too much food? I fear they may starve if the bread of sound doctrine is withheld. If we love the commandments and warnings of God, we need not fear the doctrines; we should study and feed on them with joy. The doctrines of God’s distinguishing grace must be presented alongside the rest of the Word, and those pulpits that exclude these truths are incomplete. Do not keep God’s people out of this field. Open the gate and come in, all of you children of God! In my Master’s field nothing grows that will harm you. Gospel doctrine is always safe. You can feast until you are full with no harm. Fear no revealed truth. Fear ignorance, not holy knowledge. Grow in grace and in the knowledge of Jesus Christ. Everything taught in God’s Word is meant for study; neglect nothing. Visit the Doctrine field daily and glean with the utmost diligence.

2. The great Husbandman has another field called the Promise field; I need not speak much of it, for I hope you often enter it and gather from it. Let us just take an ear or two from one of the sheaves and show them to you so that you may be encouraged to stay there all day and carry home a rich harvest at night. Here is an ear: “The mountains may depart and the hills be removed, but my steadfast love shall not depart from you, and my covenant of peace shall not be removed,” (Isaiah 54:10).

Here is another: “When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and through the rivers, they shall not overwhelm you; when you walk through fire you shall not be burned, and the flame shall not consume you,” (Isaiah 43:2). Here is another; it is small in stalk but heavy with grain: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness,” (2 Corinthians 12:9).

Another is long in the stalk but very rich in corn: “Do not let your hearts be troubled. Believe in God; believe also in me. In my Father’s house are many rooms. If it were not so, would I have told you that I go to prepare a place for you? And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also,” (John 14:1–3). What a promise that is—“I will come again.” Truly, beloved, we can say of the Promise field what cannot be said of any field in all England: it is so rich that it could not be richer, and it has so many ears of grain that you could not fit another in. As the poet sings: “What more can he say, than to you he hath said,— You who unto Jesus for refuge have fled?”

Glean in that field, you poor and needy ones, and never think you are intruding. The whole field is yours; every ear is yours. You may gather from the sheaves themselves, and the more you take, the more you may.

Then there is the Ordinance field; a great deal of good wheat grows here. The field of Baptism has been especially fruitful to some of us, for it has shown us our death, burial, and resurrection in Christ, and so has encouraged and instructed us. It has been good for us to declare ourselves on the Lord’s side, and we have found that keeping our Lord’s commandments brings great reward.

But I will not delay you long in this field, for some think the soil is damp; I wish them more light and more grace. We will move on to the field of the Lord’s Supper, where the best of the Lord’s grain grows. What rich things we have tasted in this choice spot! Have we not there enjoyed the sweetest and most sustaining spiritual food? Across the whole estate no field rivals this central and crown jewel; this is the King’s Acre. Gospel gleaner, remain in this field; glean in it on the first day of each week, and expect to see your Lord there; for it is written, “And he was recognised by them in the breaking of the bread,” (Luke 24:35). The heavenly Husbandman has a field on a hill, which is equal to the best of the others, though it may not surpass them.

You cannot truly enter any of the other fields unless you pass through this one; the road to the other fields lies through this hill farm, called Fellowship and Communion with Christ. This is the field for the Lord’s choicest ones to glean in. Some of you have only passed through it quickly, not staying long enough; but those who know how to dwell here, truly to live here, will spend their hours most profitably and pleasantly.

Only as we have fellowship and communion with Christ do ordinances, doctrines, and promises profit us. All else is dry and barren unless we enjoy Christ’s love, bear his likeness, dwell continually with him, and rejoice in his love. I regret that few Christians value this field; it is enough for them to be sound in doctrine and fairly correct in practice. They care far less than they should about intimate interaction with Christ by the Holy Spirit. If we gleaned in this field, we would have far fewer tempers, far less pride, and far less sloth. This is a sheltered, protected field, and in it you will find food better than even angels eat; indeed, you will find Jesus himself as the bread from heaven. Blessed field, may we visit it every day. The Master leaves the gate wide open for all believers; let us enter and gather the golden ears until we can carry no more. Thus we have seen the great Husbandman in his fields; let us rejoice that we have such a Husbandman near and such fields to glean in.

II. And now, secondly, we have a humble gleaner. Ruth was a gleaner, and may serve as an example of what every believer should be in the fields of God.

1. The believer is a favoured gleaner, for they may take home as much as they can carry; everything is freely given by the Lord. I use the metaphor of a gleaner because few Christians go beyond it, though they are free to do so if they are able. Some may ask, why does the believer not reap the entire field? I answer, they are welcome to do so if they can; no good thing will the Lord withhold from those who walk uprightly. If your faith is like a large wagon and can carry the whole field, you have full permission to take it. Alas, our faith is small; we glean rather than reap. We are limited, not God. May you all grow beyond the metaphor and return home with your sheaves.

2. Again, a gleaner must endure toil and fatigue. She rises early and goes to a field; if it is closed, she moves to another; if that one is gone over, she hurries further still. All day she bends down, gathering ears one by one, seldom sitting to rest. She returns home at night, heavily laden if the field was good. Beloved, let us do the same in seeking spiritual food.

Let us not fear a little fatigue in the Master’s fields; if the gleaning is rich, we must not weary in gathering the precious grain, for the reward is great. I know of a friend who walks five miles every Sunday to hear the gospel, and the same distance back. Another considers ten miles a small matter; they are wise, for no effort is too great to hear the pure Word of God. A gleaner does not expect the ears to come to her; she knows gleaning is hard work.

We may not always find the best field nearby; we may need to journey to the far end of the parish. But gleaners must not be choosy; wherever the Lord sends the gospel, there we must go.

3. Every ear the gleaner gathers requires stooping. Proud people rarely profit from the Word because they expect the corn to be lifted for them. They admire the preacher who holds truth high, out of reach, but this is no great feat. A preacher’s job is to place truth within reach of all, children and adults. Handfuls may be deliberately given to poor gleaners, and they do not mind stooping to gather them. If we only preach to the educated, the wise understand, but the illiterate do not. Preach simply to the poor, and others can understand if they choose. Those who will not stoop for plain truth should give up gleaning. I would learn from a child if it helped me understand the gospel. The gleaning in the Lord’s field is rich enough to make hard labour worthwhile. Hungry souls know this; they must not be hindered. We stoop through prayer, humility, and confession, and gather daily bread for our souls.

4. The gleaner gathers ear by ear; occasionally handfuls fall, but usually it is straw by straw.

Ruth was favoured with handfuls, but normally one stoops, gathers, and stoops again.

Where abundance is found, go there; if not, rejoice in gathering one ear at a time. Some only attend their favourite minister and refuse to hear others; remember, “not forsaking the assembling of yourselves together,” (Hebrews 10:25). Do not deprive your soul of food. If you cannot gather much at once, gather little by little. Be content to learn here a little and there a little; otherwise, you will be half-starved and then return to the despised minister to pick up what his field yields.

5. The gleaner keeps what she gathers in her hand; she does not drop it. Some hear a good thought but rush for the next, losing all before. At the end, a handful falls, and they forget all prior. A sermon is like a field; gather, tie up, and carry home, but do not lose it to idle talk. I knew a man who rushed home after a sermon, but deacons discussing it destroyed all he remembered. Avoid such losses; walk home quietly and keep your gleanings. Be like a miser who keeps all he gathers; do not lose your eternal riches through frivolous conversation.

6. Then the gleaner threshes the wheat. Threshing a sermon is wise, whoever preached it, for there is always some straw. Many “thresh” by criticising the preacher, but better is to separate truth from straw through meditation and prayer. Lay the sermon on the floor of reflection, beat it with prayer, and the wheat is yours. Do not neglect this; if a gleaner stores corn without threshing, mice will consume it. Satan, sin, and the world may waste an unprocessed sermon. He who threshes carefully and separates truth from straw becomes a wise hearer, feeding on what he hears.

7. Finally, the gleaner winnows the corn. Ruth did this in the field; we may need to do it at home. She left the chaff behind; we should separate precious from worthless, leaving the chaff. Do not take home trivialities or odd remarks from ministers. Ask, “What did the preacher say that was truly worth hearing?” Often the answer is, “I do not recall.” They have sifted the wheat and brought home chaff. Follow the opposite rule: drop the straw, retain the good grain. Judge carefully, reject false teaching, and keep true doctrine. This is the art of heavenly gleaning. May the Lord grant us wisdom so we may be “rich for all the purposes of happiness,” and our mouths be satisfied with good things, our youth renewed like the eagle’s (Psalm 103:5).

III. And now, finally, here is a gracious permission given: “Let her glean among the sheaves and reproach her not” (Ruth 2:15). Ruth had no right to go among the sheaves until Boaz gave her permission by saying, “Let her do it.” Being allowed to gather in the part of the field where the wheat was freshly cut, and none yet collected, was a great favour. But Boaz also whispered that handfuls would be deliberately dropped for her—an even greater favour. Boaz had a secret affection for Ruth, and in the same way, beloved, it is because of our Lord's eternal love that he lets us enter his best fields and glean among the sheaves. His grace allows us to receive blessings of doctrine, promises, and experience. All heavenly blessings are given freely by God; we have no right to them of ourselves—our portion is from his sovereign grace.

Let us notice that, while these meal-times come without warning, there are certain seasons when we may expect them.

Eastern reapers generally sit under the shelter of a tree or a booth to take refreshment during the heat of the day. Likewise, when trouble, hardship, persecution, and loss press most heavily upon us, it is often then that the Lord gives us the sweetest comforts. We must labour until the hot sun causes sweat to fall from our faces before we can expect rest; we must bear the burden and heat of the day before we are invited to the special meals which the Lord prepares for his true workers.

When your day of trouble is hottest, then the love of Jesus will feel the sweetest.

These meal-times sometimes occur before a trial. Elijah was fed under a broom tree because he was to travel forty days and forty nights in the strength of that food. (“And as he lay and slept under a broom tree, suddenly an angel touched him and said to him, ‘Arise and eat.’ And he looked, and behold, there was at his head a cake baked on hot stones and a jar of water. And he ate and drank and lay down again. And the angel of the LORD came again a second time and touched him and said, ‘Arise and eat, for the journey is too great for you.’ And he arose and ate and drank, and went in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights to Horeb the mount of God.” — 1 Kings 19:5–8 ESV) If you receive extraordinary seasons of communion with Jesus, be ready: you may be entering a long trial ahead. Just as a ship taking on abundant provisions is preparing for a distant journey, so these rich spiritual seasons prepare you for more difficult times. Sweet nourishment readies the soul for stern conflict.

Times of refreshing can also come after service or hardship. Christ was tempted by the devil, and afterward angels came and ministered to him. (“Then the devil left him, and behold, angels came and ministered to him.” — Matthew 4:11 ESV) Jacob wrestled with God, and afterward hosts of angels met him. (“So Jacob called the name of the place Peniel, saying, ‘For I have seen God face to face, and yet my life has been delivered.’ … And Jacob called the name of the place Mahanaim.”

— Genesis 32:30–31 ESV) Abraham defeated the kings and returned from battle, and then Melchizedek met him with bread and wine. (“And Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine. (He was priest of God Most High.) And he blessed him and said, ‘Blessed be Abram by God Most High, Possessor of heaven and earth; and blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand!’ And Abram gave him a tenth of everything.” — Genesis 14:18–20 ESV) After conflict there is contentment, after battle there is a banquet. When you have served your Lord faithfully, you may sit down, and your Master will attend you.

Let worldly people say what they will about religion being hard, we do not find it so. Reaping for Christ has its difficulties, but the bread we eat is heavenly sweet, and the wine we drink comes from the choicest vineyards.

“I would not change my bless’d estate For all the world calls good or great; And while my faith can keep her hold, I envy not the sinner’s gold.”

Now we turn to another point: the gleaner is affectionately invited to these meals. That is, the poor, trembling stranger who is too weak to reap, who has no right in the field except by mercy — the poor sinner aware of their faults, with little hope and little joy — is invited to the feast of love.

In our text the gleaner is invited to come: “At meal-time come thou hither.” (Ruth 2:14 ESV) Do not let shame about your clothes, character, poverty, or physical weakness keep you from the place of sacred feasting. “At meal-time come thou hither.” I knew a deaf woman who could never hear a sound, yet she was always in God’s house. When asked why, she said that a friend had given her the text, and God gave her many sweet thoughts of it as she sat with his people. She felt that, as a believer, she should honour God by being present with his people. She enjoyed the best company — the presence of God, holy angels, and the saints. If she found pleasure in coming, then those who can hear should never stay away. Although we feel our unworthiness, we should desire to be in God’s house, like the sick waiting at the pool of Bethesda, hoping to be healed. (“Now there is in Jerusalem by the Sheep Gate a pool, in Aramaic called Bethesda, which has five roofed colonnades… a multitude of invalids… waiting for the water to be stirred.” — John 5:2-3 ESV) Trembling soul, never let the devil’s temptations keep you from the assembly of worshippers: “At meal-time come thou hither.”

Moreover, she was invited not only to come but to eat. Whatever is sweet and comforting in the Word of God, those who are broken in spirit are invited to share it. “For Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners…” (“…Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost.” — 1 Timothy 1:15) …and “…Christ died for the ungodly.” (“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8) You may be saying in your heart, “O that I could eat the children’s bread!” — and you may. You have no right except the Lord’s invitation.
