He reminds the people how he brought them out of Egypt, defeated the Amorites, raised up prophets and Nazarites—yet they still rebelled. This struck me deeply when I first came to God as a guilty sinner—not only the visible wickedness of my life, but the particular mercies I had enjoyed. How generous God has been to some of us who never lacked anything! He never let us fall into poverty, nor leave us to infamy, nor abandon us to evil example. He preserved our morality, encouraged love for his house even when we did not love him, year after year. And how poor have been our returns! What joy, deliverance, love, and comfort we have received—and yet we have sinned openly! Well may he be like a cart pressed under a heavy load of sheaves. Notice also that the Lord’s burden is so great that he even cries out. Just as a heavily loaded cart groans under its weight, so the Lord cries under the weight of sin. Have you heard these words? "Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth: for the Lord has spoken: I have nourished and brought up children, and they have rebelled against me!" (Isaiah 1:2). Hear again: "Return, O faithless people; I will heal your faithlessness" (Jeremiah 3:22). Better still, hear the lament from Jesus, gentle as dew: "O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you, how often would I have gathered your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not!" (Matthew 23:37). Sinner, God is grieved by your sin; your Creator suffers over what you mock; your Saviour cries in his spirit over what you deem trivial. "O do not this abominable thing which I hate!" For God’s sake, do it not. Cease your evil ways; why will you die, O house of Israel? While sin is grievous to the Lord, his mercy is magnified when we see that he bears the load. As the cart does not break but is pressed, so he is pressed, yet he bears. If you and I were in God’s place, would we have borne it? Within a week we would have destroyed the world. If the law of heaven punished as swiftly as human law, where would we be? God could easily avenge his honour; countless servants stand ready to do his bidding. A mere stone, a breath of wind, a grain of dust, and all is over. Yet God restrains the servants of his anger. The heavens and the earth would gladly punish, yet God restrains. The angels are astonished at his patience. Have you seen a patient man insulted and bear it? So God bears with sinners, pressed under the weight of their guilt yet unbroken. This brings us to a profound point: some of you have never seen sin as grievous to God. Others know how bitter evil is and wish to escape it. Not only does God bear with sin, but in the person of his Son, he bore and removed it. These words gain deeper meaning in the lips of Jesus: "I am pressed under you, as a cart is pressed that is full of sheaves." God must punish sin yet desires mercy. Jesus comes as a substitute for all who trust him. The burden of human guilt is laid upon his shoulders, sheaf after sheaf. "The Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all" (Isaiah 53:6). He is despised and rejected, a man of sorrows acquainted with grief (Isaiah 53:3). He sweats great drops of blood (Luke 22:44). Herod mocks him; Pilate jeers; they strike him. "I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I did not hide my face from insult and spitting" (Isaiah 50:6). They scourge him; "the chastisement for our peace was upon him, and by his stripes we are healed" (Isaiah 53:5). Like a cart pressed under sheaves, he moves through the streets of Jerusalem. Daughters of Jerusalem, weep, though he bids you dry your tears! Abjects insult him as he bears the cross, the emblem of our sin. He is brought to Golgotha, laid upon the ground, his hands and feet nailed, the iron piercing the tender parts of his body. The cross is raised. God forsakes him; his enemies mock. The sun refuses to shine; tenfold darkness covers his soul. "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Matthew 27:46). Never was sorrow like his. Shall we treat sin lightly? Shall we toy with what made our Saviour groan? Sinner, will you give up your sins for him who suffered for them? "Yes," you say, "if I could believe he suffered for me." Trust your soul to him, and he died for you, taking your guilt and sorrows; you may go free. Christ was burdened that you might be lightened; pressed that you might be free. Believe in him. Finally, God will bear the load of our sins only a little while. If you are not in Christ at the end, that same load will crush you forever. Some translate the text differently: "I will press you as a cart full of sheaves presses the way beneath it." Just as a heavily loaded cart presses the soft roads, so will God crush you beneath your sin if you are out of Christ. You must apply this personally. Do you believe in the Lord Jesus Christ? If yes, the threat is not yours. If no, listen carefully: a Christless soul will soon be lost; they are already condemned by unbelief. How will you escape if you neglect this great salvation? "Consider your ways" (Haggai 1:5). By time, eternity, life, death, heaven, hell, I urge you to believe in Christ, who can save completely those who come to him. If you do not believe, you will die in your sins. After death comes judgment! The trumpet sounds, the multitudes, the books, the great white throne, "Come, you blessed," and "Depart, you cursed" (Matthew 25:34, 41). After judgment, hell awaits the Christless. Who among us shall endure the devouring flame? Who shall dwell with everlasting burnings? None of us can, except we flee to Christ. Fly to Jesus! I may never see your face again. My tears entreat you; let God’s long-suffering lead you to repentance. He does not wish anyone to die but to turn to him and live. This turning comes through trusting Jesus with your soul. Will you trust him? The Spirit may compel you; if not, it will not be for lack of pleading. Come now, while mercy calls. Jesus with pierced hands invites you, though you have rejected him long. His love defies your sin. Whosoever will, let them come and take of the water of life freely (Revelation 22:17). May God help you come, for the Redeemer’s glory. Amen.

fields.title: Threshing
fields.body_html:
“For the fitches are not threshed with a threshing instrument, neither is a cart wheel turned about upon the cu mmin; but the fitches are beaten out with a staff, and the cummin with a rod. Bread corn is bruised; because he will not ever be threshing it, nor break it with the wheel of his cart, nor bruise it with his horsemen” (Isaiah 28:27–28).

The art of husbandry was taught to man by God. Without this instruction, he would have starved while discovering it. Therefore, when the Lord sent him out of the Garden of Eden, he gave him a measure of elementary instruction in agriculture. As the prophet says, “His God instructs him to discretion, and teaches him” (Isaiah 28:26). God has taught man to plough, to break the clods, to sow different kinds of grain, and to thresh the various sorts of seeds.

The Eastern husbandman could not thresh with machinery as we do today, but he was ingenious and careful in his methods. Sometimes a heavy instrument was dragged over the corn to separate the grain. This is what is intended in the first clause by the “threshing instrument,” as also in the passage, “I have made you a sharp threshing instrument with teeth” (Isaiah 41:15). When the corn-drag was not used, they often turned the heavy solid wheel of a country cart over the straw.

This is alluded to in the next sentence: “Neither is a cart wheel turned about upon the cummin.”

They also had flails not unlike our own, and for still smaller seeds, such as dill and cummin, they used a simple staff or a slender rod: “The fitches are beaten out with a staff, and the cummin with a rod.”

This is not the time or place for a full dissertation on threshing. Proper books provide all the information needed on the subject. The meaning of the illustration, however, is this: just as God has taught husbandmen to distinguish between different kinds of grain in threshing, so does he, in his infinite wisdom, deal discreetly with different kinds of people. He does not test us all in the same way, as we are differently constituted. He does not put all through the same agony of conviction; we are not all threshed with terrors to the same degree. He does not give all the same family or bodily affliction; one may escape with only being beaten with a rod, while another experiences, as it were, the feet of horses in severe tribulations.

Our subject is this: threshing—first, all kinds of seeds need it; second, it is done with discretion; third, it will not last forever, for as the text says, “Bread corn is bruised; because he will not ever be threshing it, nor break it with the wheel of his cart, nor bruise it with his horsemen” (Isaiah 28:28).

I. First, all of us need threshing. Some have the foolish conceit that they have no sin, but they deceive themselves, and the truth is not in them. Even the best of men are only men at the best. Being men, they are not perfect, but remain surrounded by infirmity. What is the purpose of threshing the grain? Is it not to separate it from straw and chaff?

Even the best of men still have a measure of chaff. Not all is grain on the threshing-floor. Not all is grain even in those golden sheaves joyfully brought into the garner. Even wheat is joined to straw, which was once necessary to it. Around the kernel, the husk still clings even on the threshing-floor. Even the holiest of men have something superfluous, something which must be removed. We sin either by omission or commission—whether in spirit, motive, zeal, or discretion.

If we escape one error, we often fall into the opposite. If our actions are right before doing them, we may err in the doing, or become proud afterwards. If sin is shut out at the front door, it tries the back gate, climbs in the window, or comes down the chimney. Those who cannot perceive it in themselves are frequently blinded by its smoke. They are so immersed in sin that they do not know it is raining. In my observation, I have yet to find a person the old divines would call perfectly perfect. The fully all-round man is a being I expect to see in heaven, not in this fallen world. We all need the cleansing and purging the threshing-floor is designed to accomplish.

Threshing also loosens the connection between the good grain and the husk. Of course, if the grain slipped easily from the husk, it would only need shaking. There would be no need for a staff, a rod, much less the feet of horses or the wheel of a cart. But here is the difficulty: our souls do not merely lie in the dust—they cleave to it. There is a fearful intimacy between fallen human nature and the evil in the world, and this compact is not easily broken. In our hearts, we hate every false way, yet sorrowfully confess, “For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing” (Romans 7:19). Sometimes our spirit cries ardently after God, a holy will is present, yet we find not how to do the good. Flesh and blood have tendencies and weaknesses which, though not sinful themselves, incline toward sin. Appetites need but slight excitement to grow into lusts. It is not easy to forget our own kindred or our father’s house, even when the king desires our beauty. Our alien nature remembers Egypt and the flesh-pots while manna is still in our mouths. We were all born in a house of evil; some nursed on the lap of iniquity, our first companions among heirs of wrath. What is bred in the bone is hard to remove from the flesh.

Threshing is used to loosen our hold on earthly things and to break us away from evil. This requires a divine hand, and nothing but God’s grace can make threshing effective. Something is achieved when the soul ceases to cling to sin, when sin no longer brings pleasure or satisfaction. Yet, as threshing is never complete until the grain is entirely separated from the husk, so chastening and discipline are never complete until God’s people abandon every form of evil and abhor all iniquity.

When we are fully separated from the straw and chaff, the flail rests. It has required much threshing to bring some of us near that mark, and many more heavy blows will likely fall before total separation is reached. Some sins are easily removed by God’s grace early in our spiritual life, but once gone, another layer of evil appears, and the process repeats. Complete removal of our attachment to sin demands the divine skill and power of the Holy Spirit alone.

Threshing is necessary for usefulness: the wheat must be freed from the husk to serve. We can honour God and bless others only by being holy, harmless, undefiled, and separate from sinners.

O corn of the Lord’s threshing-floor, you must be beaten and bruised or perish as worthless!

Eminent usefulness usually comes with eminent affliction. Without such separation from sin, we cannot be gathered into the garner. God’s pure wheat must not be defiled by chaff.

Nothing that defiles can enter heaven; therefore, every imperfection must be removed for eternal blessedness and perfection. Even now, we cannot have true fellowship with the Father unless we are delivered daily from sin.

Some of us may lie on the threshing-floor today, suffering chastisement. What then? Rejoice, for this shows our value to God. If the wheat cried, “The great drag has gone over me, therefore the husbandman cares not for me,” we would reply: the farmer only drags over the precious wheat, not the weeds. Because he esteems the wheat, he deals sternly with it and spares it not. Do not judge that God hates you because of affliction; see instead that he honours you through every stroke. As the Lord says, “You only have I known of all the nations of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities” (Amos 3:2). Because Christ made full atonement for his people, God does not punish us as a judge; but because we are his children, he corrects us as a father. In love, he refines his children to perfect them in his image and make them partakers of his holiness.

“I will bring them under the rod of the covenant” (Ezekiel 20:37). “I have refined you, but not with silver; I have chosen you in the furnace of affliction” (Isaiah 48:10).

Do not judge by what you see or feel, but by faith. Just as threshing shows the value of wheat, so affliction shows God’s delight in his people. As threshing reveals impurity, so affliction indicates the Christian’s current imperfection. If we were free from evil, correction would not be needed.

The sound of the flail is never heard in heaven, for there is no threshing there—only the garner of the fully sanctified. The threshing instrument is a humbling sign, and so long as we feel it, we should humble ourselves under God’s hand, recognising that we are not yet free from the straw and chaff of fallen nature.

On the other hand, the instrument is a prophecy of our future perfection. We are undergoing a discipline from the hand of God which will not fail: by his prudence and wisdom, we shall be completely delivered from the husk of sin. We feel the blows of the staff, yet we are being effectively separated from the evil that has so long surrounded us, and we shall one day be pure and perfect. Every tendency to sin shall be removed. “Foolishness is bound in the heart of a child, but the rod of discipline drives it far from him” (Proverbs 22:15). If, while we are imperfect, we succeed with our children through our poor and limited correction, how much more shall the Father of spirits bring us to live unto himself through his holy discipline? If the corn understood the necessary use of the flail, it would welcome the thresher’s work.

Since we know to what tribulation tends, let us rejoice in it and yield ourselves cheerfully to its processes. We need threshing; it proves our value in God’s sight, and while it marks our imperfection, it secures our ultimate cleansing.

II. Secondly, God’s threshing is done with great discretion: “For the fitches are not threshed with a threshing instrument.” The poor little fitches, a small seed used to flavour cakes, are not crushed with a heavy drag, for such rough treatment would destroy them. “Neither is a cart wheel turned about upon the cummin”; this little seed, perhaps caraway, would be crushed by such weight. The fitches are removed from the stalks by being “beaten out with a staff,” and the cummin requires only a touch of a rod. For tender seeds, the farmer uses gentle means; for the hardier grains, he reserves the sterner processes. Consider the spiritual lesson here.

Reflect, my brother, that your threshing and mine are in God’s hands. Our chastening is not left to servants, nor to enemies: “We are disciplined by the Lord!” (Hebrews 12:6). The Great Husbandman himself directs the labourers, for they know neither the time nor the manner except as wisdom dictates. They would turn the wheel upon the cummin or attempt to thresh wheat with a staff. I have seen God’s servants try both these follies: crushing the weak and tender, and dealing softly with those who needed stern rebuke. Some ministers, elders, and godly men and women are rough with timid souls; yet we need not fear they will destroy the true-hearted, for the Lord preserves his chosen from such mistaken severity. How comforting is this! Many today would grind the tender to powder if they could.

As the Lord has not left us to man, neither has he left us to the devil. Satan may sift us as wheat, but he cannot thresh us as fitches. He may blow away chaff with his foul breath, but he does not manage the Lord’s corn: “The Lord preserves the righteous” (Psalm 37:17). Not a providential stroke is left to chance. The Lord ordains the timing, the measure, and the place. The divine decree leaves nothing uncertain; supreme love governs even the smallest events. Whether we endure the teeth of the corn-drag, the trampling of horses, or gentler touches, all is appointed by infallible wisdom. Let this comfort the afflicted.

Notice also that the instruments used for our threshing are chosen by the Great Husbandman. As the Eastern farmer has several instruments, so has our God. No form of threshing is pleasant; each seems objectionable to the one enduring it. We say, “I could bear anything but this trouble,” or “If it were the enemy, I could endure it.” Perhaps the cummin foolishly thinks horse-hooves would be gentler than the rod, or the fitches might prefer the wheel to the staff. Thankfully, the choice is left to One who judges perfectly. What can we know? “Ah!” cries a mother, “I could bear poverty, but to lose my child is too much!” Another laments, “I could lose all wealth, but to be slandered cuts me to the heart.” We cannot please ourselves in chastisement. When I was at school under my uncle, I had to find a cane for him; I never once chose a stick that pleased the one to be struck.

Either it was too thin or too thick, and I was threatened with punishment if I failed next time. I learned never to expect God’s children to like the rod that corrects them. You may smile at my simile, yet you may find yourself crying, “Any trial but this, Lord.” Trials are seldom pleasant; indeed, almost every useful medicine is unpleasant, almost every effective surgery painful. No trial is joyous in the present, yet it is right, and right despite its bitterness.

Notice also that God selects the place. Eastern farmers have large threshing-floors for corn or barley, but near the house, I have seen smaller circles of hardened clay or cement where garden seeds are carefully beaten. Some saints are not afflicted in common life but bear sorrow in the innermost spirit; they are threshed on a smaller, private floor, yet the effect is no less real. How foolish to rebel against the Lord’s appointment, as if we could choose our own afflictions! “Should it be according to thy mind?” Should the grain appoint its thresher? Should a child choose the rod?

Leave these matters to higher wisdom. Some complain of timing: to be crippled in youth, poor in age, or widowed with young children. Yet there is wisdom. Just as a physician arranges doses for effectiveness, so the Lord knows when we should drink the cup he prepares. A dear saint endures a trial in old age; though I would shield him, our heavenly Father knows best. The instrument, the place, the measure, the time, and the purpose are appointed by infallible love.

The text also shows the limit of threshing. The farmer beats to separate the seed, but not to destroy it. The wheel does not grind; the horse’s feet do not smash. He removes the cummin from its husk without crushing it. Likewise, the Lord measures all chastening. Courage, tried friend: you shall be afflicted as you need, but not as you deserve. Tribulation comes as you can bear it. The wheat may feel the wheel, but the fitches bear nothing heavier than a staff. No saint is tempted beyond measure; every stroke is bounded by tender wisdom.

It is easy to say this in calm reflection, harder under the flail. Yet I have experienced it in pain and mental distress. I thank God for my afflictions; I never doubted his wisdom. The Great Husbandman knows how to separate us from the husk, and his method deserves eternal praise.

It is comforting that God’s limit is absolute: “If trials six be fixed for men, They shall not suffer seven.

If God appoint afflictions ten, They shall not be eleven.”

The law allowed forty stripes save one; in all our scourging, the “save one” appears. When God multiplies sorrows, it is because previous measures failed; no power can give us one blow above the set number. The Lord never plays with his saints’ feelings. “He does not afflict willingly” (Lam. 3:33). No unnecessary blow is given.

The wisdom of the farmer in limiting threshing is far exceeded by God’s wisdom in setting a limit to grief. Some endure little, perhaps due to frailty. Delicate seeds must not be beaten; saints with weak bodies shall not be roughly handled. Perhaps their minds are fragile, and what others bear lightly would be fatal to them; they are kept as the apple of God’s eye.

If you are free from tribulation, do not ask for it. A brother recently worried because he had no trouble; I said, “Rejoice while you may.” Only a foolish child would beg for flogging. Some gentle, shining saints are spared harsh treatment; they neither need it nor could bear it. Why wish for it?

Others endure heavy pressure. Yet if they are superior grain, intended for greater use, let them not regret it. The bread corn must go under horse’s feet and the cart wheel; the most useful must undergo the sternest processes. None among us would say, “I wish I were Martin Luther or as noble as him?” Yet besides outward perils, his inward trials were such none would wish to bear.

He faced Satanic temptations and despair, riding storms of conflict, then lay broken and trembling.

We only see public heroes, not their private suffering; the bread corn is bruised, and those comforting others often suffer most. Envy no one; you do not know how they were threshed to make them right.

God uses discretion in chastening; let us do likewise with others. Be gentle with children; rebuke brothers tenderly. Do not drive horses over tender seed. Remember: cummin is beaten with a staff, not crushed with a wheel. Perhaps leave the rod to wiser hands; sow and let elders thresh.

Let us trust in God’s discretion. Do not seek escape from affliction. When praying, say, “Nevertheless, not my will.” Part freely with your chaff. To escape the flail, separate from the husk quickly: “Come out from among them” (2 Cor. 6:17). Separate from sin and sinners; the process completes sooner. God make us wise!

III. Thirdly, the threshing will not last forever. It will not occupy all our days: “Bread corn is bruised, but he will not always thresh it” (Isaiah 28:28). “For a little while I have forsaken you, but with great mercies I will gather you” (Isaiah 54:7). “He will not always rebuke, nor will he keep his anger forever” (Psalm 103:9). “Weeping may stay for the night, but joy comes in the morning” (Psalm 30:5). Rejoice, daughters of sorrow; be comforted, sons of grief; hope in God, for you shall yet praise him. The rain does not always fall, clouds do not always return; sorrow and sighing shall flee. Threshing is not needed year-round; mostly the flail rests. Bless the Lord, O my soul! He will yet bring home the banished.

Above all, tribulation will not last forever. We shall soon be taken to a better world, where there are no threshing-floors or corn-drags. I sometimes hear the herald’s call: “Up and away! Boot and saddle! Leave the camp and the battle, and return in triumph!” The night is far spent, but morning comes. The day breaks over the hills. The eternal day comes. Come, eat your bread with joy, and march with a merry heart; the land flowing with milk and honey is near. Until the day breaks, abide the Great Husbandman’s will, and may the Lord glorify himself in you. Amen.

Because he esteems the wheat, he deals sternly with it and spares it not. Do not judge that God hates you because of affliction; see instead that he honours you through every stroke. As the Lord says, “You only have I known of all the nations of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities” (Amos 3:2). Because Christ made full atonement for his people, God does not punish us as a judge; but because we are his children, he corrects us as a father. In love, he refines his children to perfect them in his image and make them partakers of his holiness. “I will bring them under the rod of the covenant” (Ezekiel 20:37). “I have refined you, but not with silver; I have chosen you in the furnace of affliction” (Isaiah 48:10). Do not judge by what you see or feel, but by faith. Just as threshing shows the value of wheat, so affliction shows God’s delight in his people. As threshing reveals impurity, so affliction indicates the Christian’s current imperfection. If we were free from evil, correction would not be needed. The sound of the flail is never heard in heaven, for there is no threshing there—only the garner of the fully sanctified. The threshing instrument is a humbling sign, and so long as we feel it, we should humble ourselves under God’s hand, recognising that we are not yet free from the straw and chaff of fallen nature. On the other hand, the instrument is a prophecy of our future perfection. We are undergoing a discipline from the hand of God which will not fail: by his prudence and wisdom, we shall be completely delivered from the husk of sin. We feel the blows of the staff, yet we are being effectively separated from the evil that has so long surrounded us, and we shall one day be pure and perfect. Every tendency to sin shall be removed. “Foolishness is bound in the heart of a child, but the rod of discipline drives it far from him” (Proverbs 22:15). If, while we are imperfect, we succeed with our children through our poor and limited correction, how much more shall the Father of spirits bring us to live unto himself through his holy discipline? If the corn understood the necessary use of the flail, it would welcome the thresher’s work. Since we know to what tribulation tends, let us rejoice in it and yield ourselves cheerfully to its processes. We need threshing; it proves our value in God’s sight, and while it marks our imperfection, it secures our ultimate cleansing. II. Secondly, God’s threshing is done with great discretion: “For the fitches are not threshed with a threshing instrument.” The poor little fitches, a small seed used to flavour cakes, are not crushed with a heavy drag, for such rough treatment would destroy them. “Neither is a cart wheel turned about upon the cummin”; this little seed, perhaps caraway, would be crushed by such weight. The fitches are removed from the stalks by being “beaten out with a staff,” and the cummin requires only a touch of a rod. For tender seeds, the farmer uses gentle means; for the hardier grains, he reserves the sterner processes. Consider the spiritual lesson here. Reflect, my brother, that your threshing and mine are in God’s hands. Our chastening is not left to servants, nor to enemies: “We are disciplined by the Lord!” (Hebrews 12:6). The Great Husbandman himself directs the labourers, for they know neither the time nor the manner except as wisdom dictates. They would turn the wheel upon the cummin or attempt to thresh wheat with a staff. I have seen God’s servants try both these follies: crushing the weak and tender, and dealing softly with those who needed stern rebuke. Some ministers, elders, and godly men and women are rough with timid souls; yet we need not fear they will destroy the true-hearted, for the Lord preserves his chosen from such mistaken severity. How comforting is this! Many today would grind the tender to powder if they could. As the Lord has not left us to man, neither has he left us to the devil. Satan may sift us as wheat, but he cannot thresh us as fitches. He may blow away chaff with his foul breath, but he does not manage the Lord’s corn: “The Lord preserves the righteous” (Psalm 37:17). Not a providential stroke is left to chance. The Lord ordains the timing, the measure, and the place. The divine decree leaves nothing uncertain; supreme love governs even the smallest events. Whether we endure the teeth of the corn-drag, the trampling of horses, or gentler touches, all is appointed by infallible wisdom. Let this comfort the afflicted. Notice also that the instruments used for our threshing are chosen by the Great Husbandman. As the Eastern farmer has several instruments, so has our God. No form of threshing is pleasant; each seems objectionable to the one enduring it. We say, “I could bear anything but this trouble,” or “If it were the enemy, I could endure it.” Perhaps the cummin foolishly thinks horse-hooves would be gentler than the rod, or the fitches might prefer the wheel to the staff. Thankfully, the choice is left to One who judges perfectly. What can we know? “Ah!” cries a mother, “I could bear poverty, but to lose my child is too much!” Another laments, “I could lose all wealth, but to be slandered cuts me to the heart.” We cannot please ourselves in chastisement. When I was at school under my uncle, I had to find a cane for him; I never once chose a stick that pleased the one to be struck. Either it was too thin or too thick, and I was threatened with punishment if I failed next time. I learned never to expect God’s children to like the rod that corrects them. You may smile at my simile, yet you may find yourself crying, “Any trial but this, Lord.” Trials are seldom pleasant; indeed, almost every useful medicine is unpleasant, almost every effective surgery painful. No trial is joyous in the present, yet it is right, and right despite its bitterness. Notice also that God selects the place. Eastern farmers have large threshing-floors for corn or barley, but near the house, I have seen smaller circles of hardened clay or cement where garden seeds are carefully beaten. Some saints are not afflicted in common life but bear sorrow in the innermost spirit; they are threshed on a smaller, private floor, yet the effect is no less real. How foolish to rebel against the Lord’s appointment, as if we could choose our own afflictions! “Should it be according to thy mind?” Should the grain appoint its thresher? Should a child choose the rod? Leave these matters to higher wisdom. Some complain of timing: to be crippled in youth, poor in age, or widowed with young children. Yet there is wisdom. Just as a physician arranges doses for effectiveness, so the Lord knows when we should drink the cup he prepares. A dear saint endures a trial in old age; though I would shield him, our heavenly Father knows best. The instrument, the place, the measure, the time, and the purpose are appointed by infallible love. The text also shows the limit of threshing. The farmer beats to separate the seed, but not to destroy it. The wheel does not grind; the horse’s feet do not smash. He removes the cummin from its husk without crushing it. Likewise, the Lord measures all chastening. Courage, tried friend: you shall be afflicted as you need, but not as you deserve. Tribulation comes as you can bear it. The wheat may feel the wheel, but the fitches bear nothing heavier than a staff. No saint is tempted beyond measure; every stroke is bounded by tender wisdom. It is easy to say this in calm reflection, harder under the flail. Yet I have experienced it in pain and mental distress. I thank God for my afflictions; I never doubted his wisdom. The Great Husbandman knows how to separate us from the husk, and his method deserves eternal praise. It is comforting that God’s limit is absolute: “If trials six be fixed for men, They shall not suffer seven. If God appoint afflictions ten, They shall not be eleven.” The law allowed forty stripes save one; in all our scourging, the “save one” appears. When God multiplies sorrows, it is because previous measures failed; no power can give us one blow above the set number. The Lord never plays with his saints’ feelings. “He does not afflict willingly” (Lam. 3:33). No unnecessary blow is given. The wisdom of the farmer in limiting threshing is far exceeded by God’s wisdom in setting a limit to grief. Some endure little, perhaps due to frailty. Delicate seeds must not be beaten; saints with weak bodies shall not be roughly handled. Perhaps their minds are fragile, and what others bear lightly would be fatal to them; they are kept as the apple of God’s eye. If you are free from tribulation, do not ask for it. A brother recently worried because he had no trouble; I said, “Rejoice while you may.” Only a foolish child would beg for flogging. Some gentle, shining saints are spared harsh treatment; they neither need it nor could bear it. Why wish for it? Others endure heavy pressure. Yet if they are superior grain, intended for greater use, let them not regret it. The bread corn must go under horse’s feet and the cart wheel; the most useful must undergo the sternest processes. None among us would say, “I wish I were Martin Luther or as noble as him?” Yet besides outward perils, his inward trials were such none would wish to bear. He faced Satanic temptations and despair, riding storms of conflict, then lay broken and trembling. We only see public heroes, not their private suffering; the bread corn is bruised, and those comforting others often suffer most. Envy no one; you do not know how they were threshed to make them right. God uses discretion in chastening; let us do likewise with others. Be gentle with children; rebuke brothers tenderly. Do not drive horses over tender seed. Remember: cummin is beaten with a staff, not crushed with a wheel. Perhaps leave the rod to wiser hands; sow and let elders thresh. Let us trust in God’s discretion. Do not seek escape from affliction. When praying, say, “Nevertheless, not my will.” Part freely with your chaff. To escape the flail, separate from the husk quickly: “Come out from among them” (2 Cor. 6:17). Separate from sin and sinners; the process completes sooner. God make us wise! III. Thirdly, the threshing will not last forever. It will not occupy all our days: “Bread corn is bruised, but he will not always thresh it” (Isaiah 28:28). “For a little while I have forsaken you, but with great mercies I will gather you” (Isaiah 54:7). “He will not always rebuke, nor will he keep his anger forever” (Psalm 103:9). “Weeping may stay for the night, but joy comes in the morning” (Psalm 30:5). Rejoice, daughters of sorrow; be comforted, sons of grief; hope in God, for you shall yet praise him. The rain does not always fall, clouds do not always return; sorrow and sighing shall flee. Threshing is not needed year-round; mostly the flail rests. Bless the Lord, O my soul! He will yet bring home the banished. Above all, tribulation will not last forever. We shall soon be taken to a better world, where there are no threshing-floors or corn-drags. I sometimes hear the herald’s call: “Up and away! Boot and saddle! Leave the camp and the battle, and return in triumph!” The night is far spent, but morning comes. The day breaks over the hills. The eternal day comes. Come, eat your bread with joy, and march with a merry heart; the land flowing with milk and honey is near. Until the day breaks, abide the Great Husbandman’s will, and may the Lord glorify himself in you. Amen.

fields.title: Wheat In The Barn
fields.body_html:
“Gather the wheat into my barn.”—Matthew 13:30 “Gather the wheat into my barn.” Then the purpose of the Son of Man will be accomplished. He sowed good seed, and he shall have his barn filled with it in the end. Do not be discouraged— Christ will not be disappointed. “He shall see the fruit of his suffering and be satisfied.” He went forth weeping, carrying precious seed, but he will return rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him.

“Gather the wheat into my barn;” then Satan's plan will fail. The enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat, hoping that the false wheat would destroy or seriously harm the true; but he failed in the end, for the wheat matured and was ready to be harvested. Christ's storehouse will be full; the weeds will not choke the wheat. The evil one will be humiliated.

In gathering the wheat, good angels will be used: “the angels are the reapers.” This highlights the defeat of the great evil angel. He sows the weeds, trying to ruin the harvest; and so the good angels are sent to celebrate his failure and to rejoice with their Lord in the success of God's work. Satan will gain very little from his interference; he will be thwarted in all his efforts, and so the threat will be fulfilled: “You will crawl on your belly and eat dust.”

By giving the angels work to do, all intelligent creatures, of whom we know, are drawn into the work of grace; whether out of malice or awe, redemption excites them all. To everyone, God's wonderful works are made visible; for these things are not done in secret.

We often forget the angels. Let us not overlook their tender concern for us; they watch the Lord rejoicing over our repentance, and they rejoice with him.

They are our guardians and the Lord's messengers of mercy; they hold us so that we do not stumble, and when we die, they carry us into the presence of our Lord. One of our joys is that we belong to a countless company of angels; let us think of them with affection.

I will now stick closely to my text, preaching almost word by word. It begins with “but,” and that is a word of separation.

Note that the weeds and the wheat will grow together until the time of harvest comes. It is a great sorrow to some of the wheat to grow side by side with weeds. The ungodly are like thorns and briers to those who fear the Lord. How often does the godly heart sigh: “Woe is me that I sojourn in Mesech, that I dwell among the tents of Kedar!” A man's enemies are often found within his own household; those who should help him most may hinder him the most; their conversation troubles and torments him. It is often futile to try to escape them, for the weeds are permitted in God's providence to grow with the wheat, and they will do so until the end.

Godly people have emigrated to distant lands to build communities of saints, and yet sinners have appeared even among them. Attempts to weed out ungodly and heretical members have led to persecution and other troubles, and the plan has largely failed. Others have secluded themselves in hermitages to avoid worldly temptations, hoping to achieve victory by fleeing; this is not the way of wisdom. The word for now is, “Let both grow together,” but a time will come when a final separation will occur. Then, dear Christian woman, your husband will no longer persecute you.

Godly sister, your brother will cease mocking you. Pious worker, the ungodly will no longer taunt you. That “but” will be an iron gate between the god-fearing and the godless; then the weeds will be cast into the fire, but the Lord of the harvest will say, “Gather the wheat into my barn.”

This separation must occur; for the wheat and the weeds growing together on earth cause much pain and harm, and this will not continue in a better world. Godly men and women might wish their unconverted children to be with them in heaven; but this cannot happen, for God will not allow his purified to be defiled, nor his glorified to be tried by the presence of the unbelieving. The weeds must be removed for the perfectness and usefulness of the wheat. Would you have weeds and wheat heaped together in the barn? That would be terrible husbandry. They cannot be put to proper use until thoroughly separated.

Likewise, the saved and unsaved may live together here, but not in the next world. The command is clear: “Gather the weeds and bind them in bundles to burn them, but gather the wheat into my barn.”

Sinner, can you hope to enter heaven? You have never loved your mother's God, and will he allow you in his heavenly courts? You have never trusted your father's Saviour, and yet you hope to see his glory forever? Will you swagger through heaven, letting fall an oath, or singing loose songs?

You grow weary of worship on the Lord's Day; do you think the Lord will tolerate unwilling worshippers in his temple above? You find the Sabbath tiresome; how can you hope to enter God's eternal rest? You have no taste for heavenly pursuits, and they would be profaned if you were allowed to partake; therefore, that “but” must come, and you must part from the Lord's people forever. Can you bear to be separated from godly friends for eternity?

That separation involves a terrible difference of destiny: “Gather the weeds in bundles to burn them.” I cannot draw the full picture; but once the bundle is bound, its only place is the fire. May you escape from all that anguish. It is no trivial matter that the Lord of love compares to being consumed by fire. No words can fully convey its terror. We often speak of the wrath to come; yet we surely understate it. What did the tender, loving, gracious Jesus mean by “Gather the weeds and bind them in bundles to burn them”? Consider the vast distinction between the fate of the Lord's people and Satan's followers. Burn the wheat? No—“Gather the wheat into my barn.” There they are safely and happily housed forever. Oh, the infinite gulf between heaven and hell—the harps and angels, the wailing and gnashing of teeth! Who can measure the distance between the glorified saint, white-robed and crowned with immortality, and the soul driven forever from God and his glory? That “but” is dreadful. Remember, it divides brother from brother, mother from child, husband from wife. “One will be taken and the other left.” And once that sword descends, there is no reunion. The separation is eternal.

But one might ask, “Why such a difference?” Because there has always been a difference. The wheat was sown by the Son of Man; the false wheat by the enemy. There has always been a difference in character—the wheat good, the weeds evil. At first this difference may not be visible, but it becomes apparent as the wheat and the weeds mature. They are entirely different plants; so too a regenerated and an unregenerated person are entirely different beings. I have heard an unregenerate man claim he is as good as a godly man; in doing so, he reveals his pride.

Surely, in God's eyes, the difference between believer and unbeliever is as great as between light and darkness, or life and death. One has life, the other does not; the difference is vital and radical.

Oh, may you never trifle with this matter, but truly be the Lord's wheat! It is not enough to bear the name of wheat—we must have its nature. God cannot be mocked; he is not pleased by those who call themselves Christians while they are not. Do not be satisfied with church membership; seek membership with Christ. Do not speak of faith; exercise it. Do not boast of experience; possess it. Be the wheat, not an imitation. The terrible “but” will roll like a sea of fire between the true and false. Oh Holy Spirit, let each of us be transformed by your power.

The second word of our text is “gather”—a word of congregation. What a blessing this gathering is! It is a pleasure to bring multitudes to hear the gospel; is it not a joy to see a house full of people, on weekdays and Sabbaths, willing to travel to hear the gospel? That is great; but the gathering of the wheat into the barn is far more wonderful. Gathering is inherently better than scattering, and I pray that the Lord Jesus may always draw people here; for he is no Divider, but “to him shall all the gathering of the people come.” Has he not said, “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself”?

Observe that the congregation in our text is chosen and assembled by skilled gatherers: “The angels are the reapers.” Ministers could not do this alone, for they do not know all the Lord's wheat and are prone to mistakes—some being too lenient, others too severe. Human judgment occasionally excludes saints and admits sinners. Angels know their Master's property. They know each saint, for they were present at their birth. Angels know when sinners repent and never forget the penitent.

They have witnessed the lives of believers and helped them in spiritual battles. Yes, angels, by a holy instinct, discern the Father's children and are not deceived. They will gather all the wheat and leave out every weed.

But they are gathered under very strict rules. According to the parable, the weeds—the false wheat—are first removed, and then the angelic reapers gather only the wheat. The seed of the serpent, fathered by Satan, is separated from the seed of the kingdom, belonging to Jesus, the promised Deliverer. This is the one distinction; no other is considered. Even the most amiable unconverted person, standing among the saints, would not be carried to heaven by the angels, for the command is, “Gather the wheat.” Even if the most honest man stood in the centre of the church, surrounded by members and ministers pleading for his mercy, if he were not a believer he could not enter the divine storehouse. There is no exception. The angels have no choice; the peremptory command is, “Gather the wheat,” and they must gather no one else.

The gathering will come from vast distances. Some wheat ripens in the South Sea Islands, in China, and in Japan. Some flourishes in France, and broad fields grow in the United States. There is hardly a land without some of God's good grain. Where all of God’s wheat grows, I cannot say. There is a remnant, according to the election of grace, among every nation and people; but the angels will gather all the good grain into one storehouse.

“Gather the wheat.” The saints will be found in every rank of society. The angels will bring a few ears from palaces, and great armfuls from cottages. Many will be collected from the humble homes of our villages and hamlets, and others will be raised from the back streets of our great cities to the metropolis of God. From the darkest corners, angels will bring those children of sweetness and light who rarely saw the sun, yet were pure in heart and knew their God. The hidden and obscure will be brought into the light, for the Lord knows those who belong to him, and his harvesters will not miss them.

It is a wonderful thought that they will come from all ages. Let us hope that our first father, Adam, will be there, and mother Eve, following in the footsteps of their dear son Abel, trusting in the same sacrifice. We shall meet Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, David, Daniel, and all the saints made perfect. What a joy to see the apostles, martyrs, and reformers! I long to see Luther, Calvin, Bunyan, and Whitefield. I love the rhyme of good old father Ryland: “They all shall be there, the great and the small, Poor I shall shake hands with the blessed St. Paul.”

I do not know exactly how it will be, but I am confident we will have fellowship with all the saints of every age in the general assembly and church of the firstborn, whose names are written in heaven.

No matter when or where the wheat grew, it shall be gathered into the one barn—never to be scattered again. They grew in different fields. Some flourished on hillsides where Episcopalians prosper, and others in lower soil where Baptists multiply and Methodists thrive. But once the wheat is in the barn, no one can tell which field the ears came from.

Then, indeed, shall the Master’s prayer have a glorious answer: “That they may all be one.” All errors removed, all mistakes corrected and forgiven, the one Lord, the one faith, and the one baptism will be fully known, and there will be no more vexing or envy. What a blessed gathering!

What a meeting! The elect of God, the finest of all centuries, of whom the world was not worthy.

I would not want to be absent. Even if there were no hell, it would be hell to miss such heavenly company. Even without wailing and gnashing of teeth, it would be dreadful to miss the presence of the Lord, the joy of praising him forever, and the bliss of meeting the noblest beings who ever lived. Amid the controversies of the age, I, who have seemed a man of strife, long for the blessed rest where all spiritual minds shall blend in eternal accord before the throne of God and of the Lamb. Oh, that we were all right, that we might all be united in one spirit!

In the text, the next word is one of designation. I have already touched on that. “Gather the wheat.”

Nothing but “the wheat” may enter the Lord’s homestead. Lend me your hearts while I urge you to a searching examination for a few minutes. The wheat was sown by the Lord. Are you sown by the Lord? Friend, if you have any religion, how did you receive it? Was it self-sown? If so, it is of no use. The true wheat was sown by the Son of Man. Are you sown by the Lord? Did the Spirit of God plant eternal life in your heart? Did it come from that hand nailed to the cross? Is Jesus your life? Does your life begin and end with him? If so, it is well.

The wheat sown by the Lord is also the object of his care. Wheat requires much attention. The farmer gains nothing if he does not watch it carefully. Are you under the Lord’s care? Does he preserve you? Is it true to your soul: “I, the Lord, keep it; I water it every moment: lest any harm it, I guard it day and night”? Do you experience such keeping? Answer honestly, for the sake of your soul.

Next, wheat is useful, a gift from God for the benefit of humanity. The false wheat was good for nothing; it could only feed swine, making them stagger as if drunk. Are you one who is wholesome in society—like bread to the world, so that if men receive your example, teaching, and life, they are blessed? Judge whether you are good or harmful in life and influence.

“Gather the wheat.” God must put the goodness, grace, strength, and usefulness into you, or you will never be wheat fit for angelic gathering. Wheat is the most dependent of all plants. I have never heard of a field of wheat that grew and ripened without a husbandman’s care.

Some ears may appear after harvest, but I have never heard of plains covered with unsown wheat.

There is no wheat without a man, and there is no grace without Christ. We owe our existence to the Father, the husbandman. Yet, dependent as it is, wheat holds honour and esteem; likewise, godly people are esteemed by those of understanding. We are nothing without Christ, but with him we are full of honour. Oh, to be among those through whom the world is preserved, the excellent of the earth, in whom the saints delight. God forbid we should be among base and worthless weeds!

Finally, a word of destination: “Gather the wheat into my barn.” The process of gathering will be completed at the day of judgment, but it is ongoing every day. Saints are gathered continually, moving heavenward even now. I rejoice to hear that departed members of my own church find joy in being harvested. Glory to God, our people die well. Living well is best, but dying well often testifies most powerfully to vital godliness. The world senses the power of a triumphant death.

Every hour, the saints are gathered into the barn. That is where they wish to be. We feel no sorrow at this ingathering, for we desire to be safely stored by our Lord. If the wheat in the field could speak, each ear would say: “The goal for which we live and grow is the barn, the granary.” For this purpose the frost and sun, the dew and rain, all labour. Every process of the wheat moves toward the granary. Likewise, everything in us works toward heaven—the gathering place, the congregation of the righteous, the vision of our Redeemer's face. Our death causes no discord; it completes our life’s symphony. For the wheat, the barn is a place of security. There is no mildew, frost, heat, drought, or wet once inside. All perils are past. It has reached perfection, rewarded the husbandman’s labour, and is safely housed. Oh, long-awaited day, begin! Oh, brethren, what a blessing when we reach maturity, and Christ sees in us the fruit of his soul’s travail.

I delight to think of heaven as his barn—what a thought! Language is poor that we must call the home of our Father, the dwelling of Jesus, a barn. Heaven is the King’s palace, yet to us a barn, a place of security, rest, and safety. It is Christ’s homestead, and we are ripening for it. Think of it with ecstatic joy; for gathering into the barn is a harvest home. Men do not weep at earthly harvests, nor follow the sheaves with tears. They clap, dance, and shout for joy. Let us do similarly for those already housed. With grave and sweet melodies, let us sing around their tombs.

The bitterness of death is past. Remember their glory, and rejoice like a woman whose child is born, “who remembers no more the anguish, for joy that a man is born into the world.” Another soul begins singing in heaven—why do you weep, heirs of immortality? Is eternal happiness the birth that follows death-pangs? Then blessed are those who die. Is glory the outcome of what fills our homes with mourning? Thank God for bereavements, for sad separations. He has promoted our dear ones to the skies! He has blessed them beyond all we could ask or imagine, taking them from this weary world to lie in his bosom forever. Blessed be his name, if for nothing else but this.

Would you keep your old father here, full of pain and weakness? Your dear wife, enduring suffering? Your husband from the immortal crown? Your child to return to earth from bliss? No.

We long to go home ourselves, but concerning the departed, we rejoice before the Lord as at harvest. “Therefore comfort one another with these words.”

THE END

That "but" will be an iron gate between the god-fearing and the godless; then the weeds will be cast into the fire, but the Lord of the harvest will say, "Gather the wheat into my barn." This separation must occur; for the wheat and the weeds growing together on earth cause much pain and harm, and this will not continue in a better world. Godly men and women might wish their unconverted children to be with them in heaven; but this cannot happen, for God will not allow his purified to be defiled, nor his glorified to be tried by the presence of the unbelieving. The weeds must be removed for the perfectness and usefulness of the wheat. Would you have weeds and wheat heaped together in the barn? That would be terrible husbandry. They cannot be put to proper use until thoroughly separated. Likewise, the saved and unsaved may live together here, but not in the next world. The command is clear: "Gather the weeds and bind them in bundles to burn them, but gather the wheat into my barn." Sinner, can you hope to enter heaven? You have never loved your mother's God, and will he allow you in his heavenly courts? You have never trusted your father's Saviour, and yet you hope to see his glory forever? Will you swagger through heaven, letting fall an oath, or singing loose songs? You grow weary of worship on the Lord's Day; do you think the Lord will tolerate unwilling worshippers in his temple above? You find the Sabbath tiresome; how can you hope to enter God's eternal rest? You have no taste for heavenly pursuits, and they would be profaned if you were allowed to partake; therefore, that "but" must come, and you must part from the Lord's people forever. Can you bear to be separated from godly friends for eternity? That separation involves a terrible difference of destiny: "Gather the weeds in bundles to burn them." I cannot draw the full picture; but once the bundle is bound, its only place is the fire. May you escape from all that anguish. It is no trivial matter that the Lord of love compares to being consumed by fire. No words can fully convey its terror. We often speak of the wrath to come; yet we surely understate it. What did the tender, loving, gracious Jesus mean by "Gather the weeds and bind them in bundles to burn them"? Consider the vast distinction between the fate of the Lord's people and Satan's followers. Burn the wheat? No—"Gather the wheat into my barn." There they are safely and happily housed forever. Oh, the infinite gulf between heaven and hell—the harps and angels, the wailing and gnashing of teeth! Who can measure the distance between the glorified saint, white-robed and crowned with immortality, and the soul driven forever from God and his glory? That "but" is dreadful. Remember, it divides brother from brother, mother from child, husband from wife. "One will be taken and the other left." And once that sword descends, there is no reunion. The separation is eternal. But one might ask, "Why such a difference?" Because there has always been a difference. The wheat was sown by the Son of Man; the false wheat by the enemy. There has always been a difference in character—the wheat good, the weeds evil. At first this difference may not be visible, but it becomes apparent as the wheat and the weeds mature. They are entirely different plants; so too a regenerated and an unregenerated person are entirely different beings. I have heard an unregenerate man claim he is as good as a godly man; in doing so, he reveals his pride. Surely, in God's eyes, the difference between believer and unbeliever is as great as between light and darkness, or life and death. One has life, the other does not; the difference is vital and radical. Oh, may you never trifle with this matter, but truly be the Lord's wheat! It is not enough to bear the name of wheat—we must have its nature. God cannot be mocked; he is not pleased by those who call themselves Christians while they are not. Do not be satisfied with church membership; seek membership with Christ. Do not speak of faith; exercise it. Do not boast of experience; possess it. Be the wheat, not an imitation. The terrible "but" will roll like a sea of fire between the true and false. Oh Holy Spirit, let each of us be transformed by your power. The second word of our text is "gather"—a word of congregation. What a blessing this gathering is! It is a pleasure to bring multitudes to hear the gospel; is it not a joy to see a house full of people, on weekdays and Sabbaths, willing to travel to hear the gospel? That is great; but the gathering of the wheat into the barn is far more wonderful. Gathering is inherently better than scattering, and I pray that the Lord Jesus may always draw people here; for he is no Divider, but "to him shall all the gathering of the people come." Has he not said, "And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself"? Observe that the congregation in our text is chosen and assembled by skilled gatherers: "The angels are the reapers." Ministers could not do this alone, for they do not know all the Lord's wheat and are prone to mistakes—some being too lenient, others too severe. Human judgment occasionally excludes saints and admits sinners. Angels know their Master's property. They know each saint, for they were present at their birth. Angels know when sinners repent and never forget the penitent. They have witnessed the lives of believers and helped them in spiritual battles. Yes, angels, by a holy instinct, discern the Father's children and are not deceived. They will gather all the wheat and leave out every weed. But they are gathered under very strict rules. According to the parable, the weeds—the false wheat—are first removed, and then the angelic reapers gather only the wheat. The seed of the serpent, fathered by Satan, is separated from the seed of the kingdom, belonging to Jesus, the promised Deliverer. This is the one distinction; no other is considered. Even the most amiable unconverted person, standing among the saints, would not be carried to heaven by the angels, for the command is, "Gather the wheat." Even if the most honest man stood in the centre of the church, surrounded by members and ministers pleading for his mercy, if he were not a believer he could not enter the divine storehouse. There is no exception. The angels have no choice; the peremptory command is, "Gather the wheat," and they must gather no one else. The gathering will come from vast distances. Some wheat ripens in the South Sea Islands, in China, and in Japan. Some flourishes in France, and broad fields grow in the United States. There is hardly a land without some of God's good grain. Where all of God’s wheat grows, I cannot say. There is a remnant, according to the election of grace, among every nation and people; but the angels will gather all the good grain into one storehouse. "Gather the wheat." The saints will be found in every rank of society. The angels will bring a few ears from palaces, and great armfuls from cottages. Many will be collected from the humble homes of our villages and hamlets, and others will be raised from the back streets of our great cities to the metropolis of God. From the darkest corners, angels will bring those children of sweetness and light who rarely saw the sun, yet were pure in heart and knew their God. The hidden and obscure will be brought into the light, for the Lord knows those who belong to him, and his harvesters will not miss them. It is a wonderful thought that they will come from all ages. Let us hope that our first father, Adam, will be there, and mother Eve, following in the footsteps of their dear son Abel, trusting in the same sacrifice. We shall meet Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, David, Daniel, and all the saints made perfect. What a joy to see the apostles, martyrs, and reformers! I long to see Luther, Calvin, Bunyan, and Whitefield. I love the rhyme of good old father Ryland: "They all shall be there, the great and the small, Poor I shall shake hands with the blessed St. Paul." I do not know exactly how it will be, but I am confident we will have fellowship with all the saints of every age in the general assembly and church of the firstborn, whose names are written in heaven. No matter when or where the wheat grew, it shall be gathered into the one barn—never to be scattered again. They grew in different fields. Some flourished on hillsides where Episcopalians prosper, and others in lower soil where Baptists multiply and Methodists thrive. But once the wheat is in the barn, no one can tell which field the ears came from. Then, indeed, shall the Master’s prayer have a glorious answer: "That they may all be one." All errors removed, all mistakes corrected and forgiven, the one Lord, the one faith, and the one baptism will be fully known, and there will be no more vexing or envy. What a blessed gathering! What a meeting! The elect of God, the finest of all centuries, of whom the world was not worthy. I would not want to be absent. Even if there were no hell, it would be hell to miss such heavenly company. Even without wailing and gnashing of teeth, it would be dreadful to miss the presence of the Lord, the joy of praising him forever, and the bliss of meeting the noblest beings who ever lived. Amid the controversies of the age, I, who have seemed a man of strife, long for the blessed rest where all spiritual minds shall blend in eternal accord before the throne of God and of the Lamb. Oh, that we were all right, that we might all be united in one spirit! In the text, the next word is one of designation. I have already touched on that. "Gather the wheat." Nothing but "the wheat" may enter the Lord’s homestead. Lend me your hearts while I urge you to a searching examination for a few minutes. The wheat was sown by the Lord. Are you sown by the Lord? Friend, if you have any religion, how did you receive it? Was it self-sown? If so, it is of no use. The true wheat was sown by the Son of Man. Are you sown by the Lord? Did the Spirit of God plant eternal life in your heart? Did it come from that hand nailed to the cross? Is Jesus your life? Does your life begin and end with him? If so, it is well. The wheat sown by the Lord is also the object of his care. Wheat requires much attention. The farmer gains nothing if he does not watch it carefully. Are you under the Lord’s care? Does he preserve you? Is it true to your soul: "I, the Lord, keep it; I water it every moment: lest any harm it, I guard it day and night"? Do you experience such keeping? Answer honestly, for the sake of your soul. Next, wheat is useful, a gift from God for the benefit of humanity. The false wheat was good for nothing; it could only feed swine, making them stagger as if drunk. Are you one who is wholesome in society—like bread to the world, so that if men receive your example, teaching, and life, they are blessed? Judge whether you are good or harmful in life and influence. "Gather the wheat." God must put the goodness, grace, strength, and usefulness into you, or you will never be wheat fit for angelic gathering. Wheat is the most dependent of all plants. I have never heard of a field of wheat that grew and ripened without a husbandman’s care. Some ears may appear after harvest, but I have never heard of plains covered with unsown wheat. There is no wheat without a man, and there is no grace without Christ. We owe our existence to the Father, the husbandman. Yet, dependent as it is, wheat holds honour and esteem; likewise, godly people are esteemed by those of understanding. We are nothing without Christ, but with him we are full of honour. Oh, to be among those through whom the world is preserved, the excellent of the earth, in whom the saints delight. God forbid we should be among base and worthless weeds! Finally, a word of destination: "Gather the wheat into my barn." The process of gathering will be completed at the day of judgment, but it is ongoing every day. Saints are gathered continually, moving heavenward even now. I rejoice to hear that departed members of my own church find joy in being harvested. Glory to God, our people die well. Living well is best, but dying well often testifies most powerfully to vital godliness. The world senses the power of a triumphant death. Every hour, the saints are gathered into the barn. That is where they wish to be. We feel no sorrow at this ingathering, for we desire to be safely stored by our Lord. If the wheat in the field could speak, each ear would say: "The goal for which we live and grow is the barn, the granary." For this purpose the frost and sun, the dew and rain, all labour. Every process of the wheat moves toward the granary. Likewise, everything in us works toward heaven—the gathering place, the congregation of the righteous, the vision of our Redeemer's face. Our death causes no discord; it completes our life’s symphony. For the wheat, the barn is a place of security. There is no mildew, frost, heat, drought, or wet once inside. All perils are past. It has reached perfection, rewarded the husbandman’s labour, and is safely housed. Oh, long-awaited day, begin! Oh, brethren, what a blessing when we reach maturity, and Christ sees in us the fruit of his soul’s travail. I delight to think of heaven as his barn—what a thought! Language is poor that we must call the home of our Father, the dwelling of Jesus, a barn. Heaven is the King’s palace, yet to us a barn, a place of security, rest, and safety. It is Christ’s homestead, and we are ripening for it. Think of it with ecstatic joy; for gathering into the barn is a harvest home. Men do not weep at earthly harvests, nor follow the sheaves with tears. They clap, dance, and shout for joy. Let us do similarly for those already housed. With grave and sweet melodies, let us sing around their tombs. The bitterness of death is past. Remember their glory, and rejoice like a woman whose child is born, "who remembers no more the anguish, for joy that a man is born into the world." Another soul begins singing in heaven—why do you weep, heirs of immortality? Is eternal happiness the birth that follows death-pangs? Then blessed are those who die. Is glory the outcome of what fills our homes with mourning? Thank God for bereavements, for sad separations. He has promoted our dear ones to the skies! He has blessed them beyond all we could ask or imagine, taking them from this weary world to lie in his bosom forever. Blessed be his name, if for nothing else but this. Would you keep your old father here, full of pain and weakness? Your dear wife, enduring suffering? Your husband from the immortal crown? Your child to return to earth from bliss? No. We long to go home ourselves, but concerning the departed, we rejoice before the Lord as at harvest. "Therefore comfort one another with these words." THE END
